article_title: CAPIT Reading
citation: CAPIT Reading: Evidence Rating (Moderate). (2024). https://www.capitlearning.com/
title: Assessment-based placement with self-paced, competency-based progression
description: The program places each student at an appropriate starting level via an initial assessment and then lets students advance individually. "Students begin with an assessment that places them at the appropriate level, allowing them to progress through the program at their own pace." The competency-based digital platform delivers "individualized instruction and immediate feedback" so progression depends on demonstrated competency rather than fixed pacing.
requirements: An initial placement assessment
A competency-based digital platform providing individualized instruction and immediate feedback
constraints: Evaluated in pre-kindergarten classrooms as a supplemental program
target_learners: PK-3 students across all three tiers of instruction
target_learning_goals: Early literacy skills, closing reading gaps
examples: In the Florida matched comparison study, pre-kindergarten students progressed through the program at their own pace after assessment-based placement.
key_sources: CAPIT Reading: Evidence Rating (Moderate). (2024). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/capit-reading/

article_title: The Effects of a Principal Professional Development Program Focused on Instructional Leadership (Study Highlights)
citation: Herrmann, M., Clark, M., James-Burdumy, S., Tuttle, C., Kautz, T., Knechtel, V., Dotter, D., Smither Wulsin, C., & Deke, J. (2019). The Effects of a Principal Professional Development Program Focused on Instructional Leadership (Study Highlights). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov
title: Do not assume intensive principal professional development focused on structured observation and targeted feedback will change leadership practice or raise achievement without direct evidence
description: This principle captures the study's central lesson: an intensive program "focused primarily on helping principals conduct structured observations of teachers' classroom instruction and provide targeted feedback" was implemented as planned yet produced no intended changes in principal practice and no achievement gains. Designers and funders of principal professional development should treat observation-and-feedback training as unproven at scale and plan for rigorous evaluation, since teacher-reported support even moved in the opposite direction.
requirements: Program theory should specify which principal practices are expected to change and how those changes are expected to improve instruction and student achievement.
constraints: The evidence comes from one intensive program for elementary school principals; the study reports null effects for this program and does not establish that all observation-and-feedback approaches are ineffective.
target_learners: Elementary school principals participating in professional development
target_learning_goals: Instructional leadership practices: conducting structured classroom observations and providing targeted feedback to teachers
examples: The study randomly assigned 100 elementary schools, half to receive the program, and compared student achievement and teachers' perceptions of principals' practices across groups.
key_sources: Herrmann, M., Clark, M., James-Burdumy, S., Tuttle, C., Kautz, T., Knechtel, V., Dotter, D., Smither Wulsin, C., & Deke, J. (2019). The Effects of a Principal Professional Development Program Focused on Instructional Leadership (Study Highlights). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/study-highlights-the-effects-of-a-principal-professional-development-program-focused

article_title: Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs
citation: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2011). Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 36, no. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs
title: Report CACE significance findings using correct variance formulas, but simplified formulas may suffice for similar conclusions
description: The article's comparison implies that analysts estimating CACE in clustered education RCTs should base significance findings on correct variance formulas that account for the relevant sources of error. Because the commonly used simplified formulas "lead to very similar significance findings" across the 10 RCTs examined, the practical stakes of formula choice may be limited, though correct formulas remain the benchmark.
requirements: Clustered RCT data with noncompliance, and variance formulas appropriate to the design
constraints: Similarity of findings is demonstrated for the 10 large-scale RCTs studied; the article does not claim universal equivalence
target_learning_goals: Accurate inference about intervention effects for compliers
examples: The authors compared significance findings for the CACE estimator across 10 large-scale RCTs using correct versus commonly used variance formulas.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2011). Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 36, no. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs

article_title: Causal Validity Considerations for Including High Quality Non-Experimental Evidence in Systematic Reviews
citation: John Deke. (2018). Causal Validity Considerations for Including High Quality Non-Experimental Evidence in Systematic Reviews. OPRE Report #2018-63, Office of Planning, Research, and Evaluation, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. https://www.acf.hhs.gov/opre
title: Systematic reviews should consider causal validity when deciding whether to include high quality non-experimental evidence
description: The report's title and framing advance a review-design principle: rather than excluding all non-experimental evidence, systematic reviews should assess the causal validity of high quality non-experimental studies when deciding what to include. The provided text states the motivation — reviews "seek to assist decision makers by rating the quality of and summarizing the findings from research evidence" — and notes RCTs cannot cover all programs. The report itself is the vehicle for developing these causal validity considerations.
requirements: Review processes must rate the quality of research evidence and summarize findings to assist decision makers
constraints: The provided text does not state the specific validity criteria; it only announces the report's purpose
target_learners: Policy makers and researchers who conduct or use federally funded systematic reviews of intervention evidence
target_learning_goals: Understanding when and how non-experimental evidence can be credibly incorporated into evidence reviews for policy decisions
examples: The OPRE report itself, titled Causal Validity Considerations for Including High Quality Non-Experimental Evidence in Systematic Reviews, is the artifact developing this principle
key_sources: John Deke. (2018). Causal Validity Considerations for Including High Quality Non-Experimental Evidence in Systematic Reviews. OPRE Report #2018-63, Office of Planning, Research, and Evaluation, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. https://www.acf.hhs.gov/opre

article_title: Changes in school composition during the COVID-19 pandemic: Implications for school-average interim test score use
citation: Jonathan Schweig, Megan Kuhfeld, Andrew McEachin, Melissa Diliberti, Louis Mariano. (2022). Changes in school composition during the COVID-19 pandemic: Implications for school-average interim test score use. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org
title: Exercise caution when comparing school-average interim test scores across pandemic and pre-pandemic periods because school composition may have changed
description: This principle holds that school-aggregate interim test scores used to monitor performance and inform recovery policies should not be taken at face value as indicators of school progress when school composition changes over time. The article motivates it by noting that faulty comparisons arise when "changes in school composition over time" contaminate COVID-19-era aggregate scores. It directs users of school-average scores to consider composition change before interpreting differences as meaningful differences in school performance.
requirements: Users must have access to information about school composition over time to judge whether aggregate-score comparisons are contaminated
constraints: The concern applies to COVID-19-era comparisons with historical and other proximal aggregate scores, per the article's framing
target_learners: K-12 students in schools using interim assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate monitoring of school performance and progress using school-average test scores
examples: The report examines NWEA MAP Growth assessment data used by states and districts during the 2020-2021 school year to investigate this issue
key_sources: Jonathan Schweig, Megan Kuhfeld, Andrew McEachin, Melissa Diliberti, Louis Mariano. (2022). Changes in school composition during the COVID-19 pandemic: Implications for school-average interim test score use. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/changes-in-school-composition-during-the-covid-19-pandemic-implications-for-school-average-interim-test-score-use/

article_title: Calibration of Spanish MAP Growth Math tests
citation: Wang, S., & Li, S. (2020). Calibration of Spanish MAP Growth math tests. Portland, OR: NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Calibrate transadapted assessment items in the target language using empirical student responses rather than borrowing source-language item parameters
description: The article argues, on psychometric scaling and validity grounds, that a test's scale and construct can only be made and verified from students' empirical responses, so borrowed English item RITs should be replaced with calibrated Spanish item RITs. Its major finding is that "calibrating Spanish math item parameters using students' empirical responses is a much better approach to constructing the Spanish MAP Growth Math tests according to psychometric scaling and validity theory". The report operationalizes this with fixed-person-score calibration designs and a six-point recommendation list for operational practice.
requirements: Enough student responses collected on the target-language items to calibrate item parameters empirically
constraints: The recommendation rests on the study's evidence of negligible old-new differences for these Spanish math items; the article frames the argument in terms of psychometric scaling and validity theory rather than a measured improvement in student outcomes
target_learning_goals: Accurate representation of student performance on transadapted assessments
examples: The recommendations list directs NWEA to replace all current English math item parameters in Spanish tests, stop using English parameters in the future, implement routine calibration, review status 12 and 13 items with content experts, keep status 10 items operational, and conduct an annual item parameter drift study
key_sources: Wang, S., & Li, S. (2020). Calibration of Spanish MAP Growth math tests. Portland, OR: NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/calibration-of-spanish-map-growth-math-tests/

article_title: Fall 2019 to fall 2020 MAP Growth attrition analysis
citation: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld. (2020). Fall 2019 to fall 2020 MAP Growth attrition analysis. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org
title: Interpret fall 2020 assessment results with considerable caution against prior typical years, checking demographic shifts among tested students
description: The brief recommends that when attrition is systematic, comparisons of post-disruption results to prior years are biased by composition change. It states "considerable caution is warranted when interpreting fall 2020 assessment results, especially in relationship to previous, typical academic years that may include a substantively different group of students." Educational leaders should consider demographic shifts among tested students when planning support and recovery efforts.
requirements: Analysts must compare the demographic composition of students tested in the current period against the prior period before interpreting score trends.
constraints: The recommendation arises specifically from COVID-19-era attrition in MAP Growth data; the brief does not claim it generalizes to all assessment contexts.
target_learners: K-12 students assessed with MAP Growth
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of achievement trends for instructional and recovery decisions
examples: The study compared characteristics of fall 2019 testers who retested in fall 2020 versus those who did not, using data for 5.2 million students.
key_sources: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld. (2020). Fall 2019 to fall 2020 MAP Growth attrition analysis. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/fall-2019-to-fall-2020-map-growth-attrition-analysis/

article_title: Is teacher value added a matter of scale? The practical consequences of treating an ordinal scale as interval for estimation of teacher effects
citation: Soland, J. (2017). Is teacher value added a matter of scale? The practical consequences of treating an ordinal scale as interval for estimation of teacher effects. Applied Measurement in Education, 30(1), 52–70. https://www.nwea.org
title: Treat ordinal test scales cautiously when using them for teacher value-added decisions
description: The article argues that assuming a test scale is equal-interval "can be problematic, especially when the assessment is being used to achieve a policy aim like evaluating growth over time," and that treating an ordinal scale as interval "might lead to erroneous conclusions about teacher quality." Because mild scale transformations can multiply classification odds by a factor of 5, users of value-added estimates should check scale sensitivity before acting on high/low classifications.
requirements: Users should verify how value-added classifications change under mild nonlinear transformations of the score scale before using them for personnel decisions
constraints: The concern applies when assessments serve policy aims such as evaluating growth over time or teacher quality
target_learners: K-12 students assessed on standardized achievement tests
target_learning_goals: Fair and accurate teacher evaluation and accountability decisions
examples: The article re-estimated teacher value added under transformed scales and found classification odds changed by up to a factor of 5 while rankings stayed largely stable
key_sources: Soland, J. (2017). Is teacher value added a matter of scale? The practical consequences of treating an ordinal scale as interval for estimation of teacher effects. Applied Measurement in Education, 30(1), 52–70. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/is-teacher-value-added-a-matter-of-scale-the-practical-consequences-of-treating-an-ordinal-scale-as-interval-for-estimation-of-teacher-effects/

article_title: Career Academies
citation: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2015, September). Dropout Prevention intervention report: Career Academies. Retrieved from http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: School-within-a-school career academy structure with sustained student-teacher clusters
description: This pattern organizes a small learning community inside a larger high school. "A small learning community is formed within the larger high school by clustering three to five teachers and 50–75 students per grade." Teachers are drawn from academic and career-related disciplines and remain with students from year to year, with one lead teacher administering the academy and liaising with administrators and employer partners. Students take two to four academy courses a year, with block-scheduled academy classes in the morning followed by regular classes in the afternoon.
requirements: Clustering three to five teachers and 50–75 students per grade
Teachers remaining with students from year to year
A lead teacher with responsibility for administration and employer liaison
Block-scheduled academy-oriented classes
constraints: The report describes this structure as implemented in the evaluated academies; the comparison group attended regular high school classes, and 7.2% of comparison students enrolled in an academy at some point
target_learners: High school students in grades 9–12 in urban districts
target_learning_goals: Integrated academic and career-technical learning
Personalized attention from teachers and peer collaboration
examples: Academies in the study used career themes such as health professions, business and finance, electronics, travel and tourism, and information technology, chosen based on local employment needs
key_sources: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2015, September). Dropout Prevention intervention report: Career Academies. Retrieved from https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/70

article_title: Noncognitive Outcomes of Liberal Arts Education
citation: Key Questions. (2016). Mellon Foundation. https://www.mellon.org
title: Framework of capacities needed in a time of widening inequality, instability, and environmental crisis
description: The article articulates a framework of human capacities it argues the current historical moment demands: recognizing "the partiality of their own perspectives", making "sense of complex phenomena", directing "thoughts, feelings, and behaviors to act responsibly for the greater social good", and working "effectively across social and cultural differences". It presents this as the rationale for studying liberal arts education's noncognitive returns, framing these capacities as what solving local, regional, and global problems requires of leaders, neighbors, co-workers, and citizens.
requirements: The framework is motivated by a historical moment the article characterizes as marked by widening socio-economic inequalities, geopolitical instability, and global environmental crises.
target_learners: traditional college-age young adults in the United States
target_learning_goals: perspective recognition
sense-making of complex phenomena
self-directed responsible action for the social good
working across social and cultural differences
examples: The article lists the capacities in its overview as the qualities needed to "solve pressing local, regional, and global problems."
key_sources: Key Questions. (2016). Mellon Foundation. https://www.mellon.org

article_title: Schools Can't Do It Alone: Envisioning a Statewide System of Support to Advance School-Based Behavioral Health in California
citation: Eisenberg, L., Krausen, K., & Caparas, R. (2024). Schools can't do it alone: Envisioning a statewide system of support to advance school-based behavioral health in California. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: California's Statewide System of Support (SSOS): a three-tiered structure for deploying technical assistance to local educational systems
description: The SSOS is California's unified structure, in place since 2017, for connecting school districts, county offices of education, and charter schools to TA, tools, and resources that build capacity for continuous improvement and reducing achievement gaps. It operates as a three-tiered model: "Tier 1 support (general assistance) is available for all LEAs and schools," Tier 2 (differentiated assistance) targets LEAs flagged by California School Dashboard performance, and Tier 3 (intensive intervention) serves persistent performance issues, though the SSOS has primarily focused on Tiers 1 and 2. COEs and Lead Agencies deliver support directly, while the CCEE, CDE, and SBE coordinate the system; the CCEE also hosts an online directory and a searchable Resource Hub.
requirements: Coordination among the three state agencies (CCEE, CDE, SBE) and designation of Lead Agencies, as tasked by the California Education Code
constraints: The SSOS explicitly focuses on educational systems; behavioral health is generally addressed only when LEAs identify it as a Dashboard-linked strategy, and behavioral health indicators are not currently included on the Dashboard
target_learners: Local educational agencies (school districts, county offices of education, charter schools)
target_learning_goals: Building local education leaders' capacity for continuous improvement and reducing achievement gaps
examples: Lead Agencies each offer support on a topic such as literacy, early math, special education, MTSS, or community engagement; Geographic Lead Agencies connect COEs and LEAs to state initiatives and resources.
key_sources: Eisenberg, L., Krausen, K., & Caparas, R. (2024). Schools can't do it alone: Envisioning a statewide system of support to advance school-based behavioral health in California. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655750

article_title: How School Facilities Impact Student Health and Performance: Advancing Equity with Green Infrastructure
citation: Perez, Alyssa. (2024). How school facilities impact student health and performance: advancing equity with green infrastructure. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Causal chains as a research framework linking school building features to student health and performance
description: The brief describes "causal chains" as a method environmental health researchers developed to evidence how building features affect people where direct causal proof is impractical. Rather than showing a maintenance practice directly causes fewer asthma attacks, "researchers can test and evidence that the practice inhibits the growth of mold. Mold, causal studies can show, impacts asthma rates." The brief uses this framework to connect indoor air quality, heat, and lighting to attendance and achievement. It applies the framework to argue that sustainable school design can improve learning and well-being.
requirements: Requires identifying an intermediate mechanism (such as mold growth or absenteeism) that causal studies can individually establish
constraints: Evidencing direct causal relationships between building features and impacts on people is difficult due to how intricately people interact with their environments
target_learners: PK-12 students in California public schools
target_learning_goals: Student health, attendance, and academic performance as outcomes of the built environment
examples: The brief's asthma example: improved IAQ reduces asthma attacks, reducing chronic absenteeism and its educational harms
key_sources: Perez, Alyssa. (2024). How school facilities impact student health and performance: advancing equity with green infrastructure. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655919

article_title: Stanislaus County Office of Education: "Project Cal-Well Journey"
citation: WestEd. (2024). Stanislaus County Office of Education: Project Cal-Well Journey. https://www.wested.org
title: Wellness spaces co-designed with students
description: Wellness spaces are dedicated school environments established to foster community and well-being. Project Cal-Well supported "six wellness spaces in the three participating districts," including the Bear Cave at Ross Middle School. The brief emphasizes that the spaces "were developed with direct input from students," aligning the physical environment with student preferences so the spaces act as inviting, supportive environments within the Tier 1 universal supports component.
requirements: Direct input from students to align the physical environment with their preferences
target_learners: middle and high school students in Hughson, Patterson, and Turlock districts
target_learning_goals: social-emotional well-being
positive school climate
examples: The well-received Bear Cave at Ross Middle School in Hughson Unified
key_sources: WestEd. (2024). Stanislaus County Office of Education: Project Cal-Well Journey. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655972

article_title: Stanislaus County Office of Education: "Project Cal-Well Journey"
citation: WestEd. (2024). Stanislaus County Office of Education: Project Cal-Well Journey. https://www.wested.org
title: Universal mental health screening systems in Cal-Well districts
description: A district-level universal screening system in which every Project Cal-Well district in Stanislaus County now administers a mental health screener, such as the Covitality screening tool. Despite pandemic-era implementation hurdles and screener-selection challenges, the districts sustained ongoing screening, and the brief notes these efforts "yielded valuable lessons that have been shared with other districts across the county."
requirements: Selection of an appropriate screener and district capacity to administer it
constraints: Initial implementation hurdles related to the COVID-19 pandemic and screener selection
target_learners: all students in participating Stanislaus County districts
target_learning_goals: early identification of mental health needs
examples: Adoption of the Covitality screening tool across the three participating districts
key_sources: WestEd. (2024). Stanislaus County Office of Education: Project Cal-Well Journey. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655972

article_title: Stanislaus County Office of Education: "Project Cal-Well Journey"
citation: WestEd. (2024). Stanislaus County Office of Education: Project Cal-Well Journey. https://www.wested.org
title: Mental and behavioral health referral pathways and community of practice
description: Referral pathways are site-level processes for routing students to behavioral and mental health supports. Hughson High created an online request-for-assistance form on its website usable by students, parents, and personnel, with designated reviewers at each site and referral discussion in Tier 2 team meetings. SCOE also established a referral-pathways learning community in which "Fourteen of the 26 districts participated and expressed an interest in continuing these sessions with SCOE."
requirements: Designated individuals at each site to review requests and route them for support
target_learning_goals: timely access to behavioral and mental health services
examples: Hughson High's online request for assistance form accessible through the school's website
key_sources: WestEd. (2024). Stanislaus County Office of Education: Project Cal-Well Journey. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655972

article_title: Strengthening English Learner Reclassification in California
citation: Strengthening English Learner Reclassification in California. (2024). Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd, U.S. Department of Education grant #S283B190053. https://nces.ed.gov/programs/coe/indicator/cgf
title: California's four reclassification criteria under Education Code 313.3
description: The California Education Code (EC 313.3) outlines four criteria for reclassification of English learners: a proficient score on the state's English language proficiency assessment, teacher evaluation, parental opinion and consultation, and "a comparison of the pupil's performance in basic skills against a range of English proficient pupils of the same age." ESSA requires states to set a single standardized set of rules for all districts, making these criteria the operational definition of exiting English learner services in California.
requirements: Under ESSA, all schools and districts must use the same criteria for reclassification
target_learners: English learners designated for reclassification decisions in California districts
target_learning_goals: Determining when students have met criteria to exit English learner services
examples: OPTEL standardizes criteria 2 and 3 of the four EC 313.3 criteria
key_sources: Strengthening English Learner Reclassification in California. (2024). Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd, U.S. Department of Education grant #S283B190053. https://nces.ed.gov/programs/coe/indicator/cgf

article_title: The Racial School-Climate Gap
citation: Voight, A. (2013). The Racial School-Climate Gap. A report from the Region IX Equity Assistance Center at WestEd. San Francisco: WestEd. http://cal-schls.wested.org
title: Cal-SCHLS survey system for assessing student and staff perceptions of school climate
description: The California School Climate, Health, and Learning Survey (Cal-SCHLS) System, developed by WestEd with funding from the California Department of Education, consists of three comparable surveys: the California Healthy Kids Survey (CHKS) for students, the California School Climate Survey (CSCS) for staff, and the California School Parent Survey. Survey items "gauged respondents’ perceptions of their school environment (e.g., supportiveness, safety), as well as students’ grades, truancy, and risk behaviors." During the analysis years the CHKS was administered in approximately 840 school districts to an average of 500,000 students per year in grades 7, 9, and 11.
requirements: Available nationally as the Healthy Kids School Climate Surveys for schools wanting to regularly assess and monitor climate by racial/ethnic group
constraints: During the years the analyzed data were collected, the CHKS was administered in grades 7, 9, and 11
target_learners: California public school students in grades 7, 9, and 11, school staff, and parents
target_learning_goals: Identifying climate-related needs and guiding school-climate improvement efforts to reduce inequity
examples: All six WestEd studies summarized in this brief used student and staff data from the Cal-SCHLS system collected from 2004 to 2010
key_sources: Voight, A. (2013). The Racial School-Climate Gap. A report from the Region IX Equity Assistance Center at WestEd. San Francisco: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED580366

article_title: Understanding the Experiences of LGBTQ Students in California
citation: Hanson, T., Zhang, G., Cerna, R., Stern, A., & Austin, G. (2019). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ students in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: California Healthy Kids Survey (CHKS)
description: The CHKS is "an anonymous modular assessment for students ages 10 (grade 5) and above" developed in 1998 by WestEd for the California Department of Education. Participation has been voluntary since 2010 except in districts receiving tobacco prevention grants; the CDE minimally requires administration in grades 7 and 9. This study uses pooled 2017-19 data from 2,749 secondary schools, with about 70 percent of California districts administering the survey to more than 1.2 million students in that period. The report calls aggregated CHKS data arguably the nation's largest data source on LGBTQ youth.
requirements: Districts must administer the survey in grades 7 and 9 at minimum to capture comparable statewide data.
constraints: Participation is voluntary since 2010 (except tobacco-grant districts), and students declining to respond to gender identity or sexual orientation questions were omitted from this study's analyses.
target_learners: Students in grade 5 and above; this study covers grades 7, 9, and 11
target_learning_goals: Assessment of school climate, safety, supports, mental health, engagement, and academic performance
examples: The study analyzed responses from 804,683 students on gender identity and 796,079 on sexual orientation across 2,749 secondary schools.
key_sources: Hanson, T., Zhang, G., Cerna, R., Stern, A., & Austin, G. (2019). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ students in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED601909

article_title: Understanding the Experiences of LGBTQ High School Students in California by Race/Ethnicity
citation: Cerna, R., Stern, A., Austin, G., Betz, J., Zhang, G., & Hashmi, S. (2021). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ high school students in California by race/ethnicity. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/lgbtq-students-in-california/
title: California Healthy Kids Survey (CHKS) as a disaggregatable school-climate and well-being assessment
description: The CHKS is an anonymous, modular student assessment developed by WestEd for the California Department of Education, administered voluntarily by districts, "usually at least every other year." It collects demographic items (race, Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, Asian group identity, gender identity, sexual orientation) and 14 perception measures across five domains: school supports, school safety, mental health, school engagement, and academic performance. This report pools 2017–19 responses from 559,120 students in grades 9 and 11 and disaggregates them intersectionally.
requirements: Districts elect to administer the survey; participation by students is voluntary, and students may decline to respond to demographic items
constraints: Tables omit students who declined to respond to the gender-identity or sexual-orientation items; some subgroup cells rest on samples smaller than 10 and are flagged for caution
target_learners: California high school students in grades 9 and 11
target_learning_goals: Measuring school supports, safety, mental health, engagement, and academic performance to guide school improvement
examples: The report pools two academic years of CHKS data because most districts administer it biennially at times of their own selection
key_sources: Cerna, R., Stern, A., Austin, G., Betz, J., Zhang, G., & Hashmi, S. (2021). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ high school students in California by race/ethnicity. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/lgbtq-students-in-california/

article_title: A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process
citation: Melinda Wallace and Sheila Arredondo. (2022). A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567789
title: Content Area Review Panels (CARPs)
description: CARPs are the Nevada panels that "Evaluate and rate instructional materials submitted by publishers." Per Table 1, they include subject-matter experts, content-area and special education teachers, curriculum directors, technology specialists, and English language development experts. Panelists correlate content standards to materials, participate in training and rubric calibration, conduct independent reviews, and take part in full-group deliberations to reach a unified recommendation.
requirements: Panelists must know and understand the NVACS, participate in training and rubric calibration, and submit ratings and summary reports on time to the panel facilitator
constraints: Panels are recruited at 5–7 panelists per content area, with RPDP representation secured for English language arts, mathematics, and science
target_learners: K-12 students who will use the adopted instructional materials
target_learning_goals: Reliable, calibrated evaluation of instructional materials for statewide adoption
examples: CARP findings were consolidated into a recommendation list presented to Cabinet and then the State Board of Education for adoption
key_sources: Melinda Wallace and Sheila Arredondo. (2022). A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628368

article_title: Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department
citation: Jenna Howard Terrell, Sarah Barzee. (2023). Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Invest in ongoing capacity building and professional learning, including intermediaries, for performance assessment design and scoring
description: The report's third lesson states that "States and districts need to invest in building the capacity of teachers and leaders to effectively design and implement performance-based assessments." Developing, piloting, and testing assessments and rubrics takes significant time plus initial and ongoing professional learning. Four states (Colorado, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Virginia) had established systems for ongoing professional learning, and intermediaries such as the New Hampshire Learning Initiative and MCIEA provided guidance, professional development, and resources.
requirements: Initial professional learning to transition teachers to a performance assessment mindset, plus ongoing professional learning, and time for developing, piloting, and testing assessments and rubrics.
constraints: States without intermediaries reported staffing and capacity limitations and relied on regional service districts or district-led professional learning, leaving some interviewees feeling disconnected from district needs.
target_learners: Teachers and school and district leaders designing and scoring performance assessments
target_learning_goals: High-quality design, scoring, and implementation of performance-based assessments

citation: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability

Figure 1 presents five competencies—self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making—nested within classrooms, schools, homes, and communities. article_title: Understanding California's Early Care and Education System
citation: Melnick, H., Tinubu Ali, T., Gardner, M., Maier, A., & Wechsler, M. (2017). Understanding California's early care and education system. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/ca-ece-report
title: California's ECE system as a patchwork of uncoordinated programs administered by many federal, state, and local agencies
description: The report characterizes California's ECE system as "a patchwork of programs with distinct purposes and designs", built incrementally over more than half a century and enrolling over half a million children each year. Programs span school readiness (state preschool, Head Start, transitional kindergarten), working-parent support (Alternative Payment vouchers, General Child Care and Development), home visiting, and special education. Most programs are accountable to multiple agencies at county, state, and federal levels, which "can create confusion and increase the burden of administrative and reporting requirements" for providers and families.

Professional growth, resilience, and career advancement for early-career administrators

citation: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402
title: California Community Schools Partnership Program (CCSPP): a $4.1 billion state grant and technical assistance investment
description: The CCSPP is the nation's largest state investment in community schools: "In 2021, California passed a historic $3 billion investment in the CCSPP, followed by an additional $1.1 billion investment in 2022." It provides three grant types—planning grants up to $200,000 per LEA for up to 2 years, implementation grants of $150,000–$500,000 annually per school for up to 5 years, and extension grants up to $100,000 annually for 2 years—plus approximately $140 million for a network of regional technical assistance centers with a lead center. article_title: School Funding Effectiveness: Evidence from California's Local Control Funding Formula
citation: Johnson, R. C. (2023). School funding effectiveness: Evidence from California's Local Control Funding Formula. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/529.194
title: California Local Control Funding Formula (LCFF)
description: The LCFF is California's school funding formula, enacted in 2013, which allocates state funding "by the proportion of unduplicated 'high-need' students in the district" rather than by district property wealth. It has three components: a base grant varying by grade span, a supplemental grant equal to 20% of the adjusted base grant per high-need student, and a concentration grant equal to 50% of the adjusted base grant per high-need student in districts with more than 55% high-need students. It rolled out from 2013 through 2019 with guaranteed multiyear distributions and minimal restrictions on district use of funds.
requirements: Districts must devise a Local Control Accountability Plan identifying how resources are principally directed to high-need students
constraints: Basic Aid districts with local revenue per pupil in excess of LCFF targets do not receive state funding and are not subject to LCFF requirements
Roughly 10% of state funding, including special education and transportation, is outside the LCFF
target_learners: K–12 public school students in California, particularly students from low-income families, English learners, and students in foster care
target_learning_goals: Reducing socioeconomic achievement gaps through equitable school funding
examples: In 2018–19, allocations totaled approximately $8,000 per pupil in base grants, $1,600 per high-need student in supplemental grants, and $5,300 per high-need student in concentration grants in districts with more than 55% high-need students

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance
citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: Four-stage adaptive cycle: Capture, Model, Adapt, Evolve
description: The paper's adaptive foundation organises how AI learns about students into a continuous four-stage cycle. "Capture" records learners' digital footprints, including LLM-generated conversational trace data, to gather evidence of engagement and understanding. "Model" builds a multi-dimensional learner model from cognitive, affective, and behavioural data, combining LLM interpretation with algorithms such as knowledge tracing. "Adapt" determines what, how, and when to adjust learning experiences, conceptualised through outer-loop task sequencing and inner-loop within-task support. "Evolve" evaluates the effectiveness of adaptations through design-loop adaptivity and closed-loop evaluation to drive continual improvement.
requirements: Integration of traditional learner-modelling algorithms with LLM interpretation; open learner model interfaces for transparency
constraints: Most current LLM applications remain stateless, making sustained adaptation to individual learners impossible without this foundation
target_learning_goals: personalised feedback
self-regulated learning
adaptive instruction
examples: The paper proposes Reinforcement Learning from Human Learning (RLHL) as a possible route to tutoring systems that continually learn from interactions with students

article_title: AI as a Partner in Learning about, Doing, and Engaging with Science: Vigilance as the Key to Productive Augmentation
citation: Marcus Kubsch. (2026). AI as a Partner in Learning about, Doing, and Engaging with Science: Vigilance as the Key to Productive Augmentation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16822
title: Calibrated epistemic vigilance framework for learning with AI
description: The paper specifies epistemic vigilance—the "evaluation of communicated information from a source"—for the AI case, dividing it into the automatic check, the disposition to honor its signal, and the calibration policy setting how much scrutiny the signal buys. Its mechanism: the check weighs a claim's coherence with prior knowledge and sets processing depth, so vigilance gates whether deep processing, where integrated conceptual knowledge forms, occurs. The AI case is distinctive because optimized fluent, confident surfaces read as trustworthy whether or not the content is, and the source side of evaluation is emptied, forcing evaluation onto content.
requirements: Adequate prior knowledge for the check to run on: checking requires the prior knowledge a claim must cohere with, not the knowledge it teaches.
constraints: The claim is scoped to integrated conceptual knowledge; facts and routine procedures are built by other processes and may genuinely suffice with correction and adoption.
target_learners: members of the public using AI for decisions
target_learning_goals: integrated conceptual science knowledge
epistemic vigilance as a capacity worth having
examples: The bouncing-ball example: a correct energy-dissipation answer passes the fast check, a plainly wrong one raises the flag, and a terminology-dressed wrong answer requires widening the web of beliefs to catch the contradiction.
key_sources: Marcus Kubsch. (2026). AI as a Partner in Learning about, Doing, and Engaging with Science: Vigilance as the Key to Productive Augmentation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16822

article_title: Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction
citation: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23177
title: Evaluate AI productivity in terms of both time and subjective cognitive effort, and treat calibration as an intervention point against overreliance
description: Because AI assistance reduces felt effort even when it saves no time, the article argues that "narratives and reports about AI productivity should also consider a more encompassing notion of cognitive offloading that takes into account the subjective experience". It further positions calibration as "a key intervention point to adjust behavioral outcomes such as overreliance", since miscalibration encouraging AI use can form a feedback loop with cognitive deskilling.
requirements: Users and designers need measures capturing both completion time and subjective effort (e.g., NASA-TLX) when judging AI-assisted efficiency
constraints: The feedback-loop risk is described as preliminary evidence; excessive offloading is cautioned to lead to cognitive deskilling and overreliance
target_learners: Adults deciding whether to offload cognitive tasks to LLM assistants
target_learning_goals: Well-calibrated decisions about when to offload cognition to AI, conserving the intended resource
examples: The article recommends future work examine how incentive structures interact with completion times and reported effort, and when people choose to use AI.
key_sources: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23177

article_title: The impact of AI anxiety on career decisions of college students
citation: Duan, N., Li, L., Lin, G. & Chen, H. (2026). The impact of AI anxiety on career decisions of college students. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-37648-y
title: Integrated mediating-moderating model of AI anxiety and career decisions grounded in Career Construction Theory
description: The article develops a model, grounded in Career Construction Theory, in which AI anxiety affects career decisions through two routes: a direct path and an indirect path via career adaptability, which the article calls "a core psychological resource for individuals to cope with career challenges and uncertainty". Career adaptability is hypothesised to mediate the anxiety-to-decision link via resource depletion, while self-efficacy is hypothesised to moderate only the direct path. The empirical test confirmed mediation but not moderation, which the authors read as showing the adaptability pathway is central to how AI anxiety shapes career construction.
requirements: Measurement of AI anxiety, career adaptability, self-efficacy, and career decision constructs with reliable scales in the target population
constraints: The article states results are most applicable to undergraduate populations in small and medium-sized cities in western China and should be cautiously generalised elsewhere
target_learning_goals: career decision-making
career adaptability
coping with technology-induced career uncertainty
examples: SEM test on survey data from 315 students at three universities in Baise City, China, with mediation tested by 5000-resample bootstrap
key_sources: Duan, N., Li, L., Lin, G. & Chen, H. (2026). The impact of AI anxiety on career decisions of college students. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-37648-y

article_title: The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization
citation: Seyed Parsa Neshaei, Abhinand Shibu, and Fatma Betül Güres. (2026). The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15902
title: Card-based design-time GenUI paradigm for educational content
description: The paper proposes organizing educational content as bounded, modality-agnostic semantic cards whose learning objective is encoded separately from any interface representation. At authoring time, a GenAI engine produces a defined set of representation variants (interactive, audio, simplified text, low-bandwidth), which the instructor reviews before delivery; approved variants are stored in repositories for deployment without runtime generation. The authors state this "embeds Universal Design for Learning principles into the authoring workflow, and removed per-learner inference costs." The card boundary is presented as what makes generation tractable and keeps a domain-knowledgeable human in the loop.
requirements: Educators define bounded learning units as cards with explicit learning objectives and content fields before any representation is generated
Generated representations are reviewed and approved by the instructor before learners see them
constraints: The assumption that card variants are interchangeable from a learning perspective is stated by the authors as an unvalidated empirical claim
Client may still invoke runtime AI for selected functions such as answering questions or feedback
target_learners: Diverse learners including those needing audio-first, simplified-text, interactive, or low-bandwidth representations
target_learning_goals: Preserving the intended learning objective across multiple interface representations
examples: The paper contrasts a card on the quadratic formula, which encodes objective, prerequisites, examples, misconceptions, and an assessment prompt without specifying presentation form, against a lesson authored as a slide deck that inherits visual-layout assumptions
key_sources: Seyed Parsa Neshaei, Abhinand Shibu, and Fatma Betül Güres. (2026). The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15902

article_title: The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization
citation: Seyed Parsa Neshaei, Abhinand Shibu, and Fatma Betül Güres. (2026). The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15902
title: Card as bounded semantic content unit
description: A card is defined as "thesmallestmeaningfulunitofinstructional content that can be authored, reviewed, sequenced, and delivered independently." It may introduce a concept, explain a procedure, present a worked example, or provide practice, and is characterized by semantic structure rather than visual appearance. Cards are structured objects with fields such as learning objective, concept description, examples, prerequisite knowledge, constraints, assessment item, and source material. Cards also support composition into sequences or graphs with prerequisite relationships, optional branches, remediation paths, and thematic clusters.
requirements: Cards encode what the learner is intended to understand separately from how it will be represented
Fields must bound generation to representations of a specific, instructor-authored unit
target_learners: Educators authoring educational material for diverse learner contexts
target_learning_goals: Authoring at the level of learning intent before representational commitments are made
examples: A card on the quadratic formula would include the learning objective, prerequisite concepts, key explanation, notation, examples, common misconceptions, and perhaps a short assessment prompt
key_sources: Seyed Parsa Neshaei, Abhinand Shibu, and Fatma Betül Güres. (2026). The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15902

article_title: The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization
citation: Seyed Parsa Neshaei, Abhinand Shibu, and Fatma Betül Güres. (2026). The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15902
title: Card repository of approved representation variants
description: Once cards and their representation variants are approved, they are stored in a card repository, "a reusable collection of semantically structured learning units and their approved representation variants." A repository would contain the semantic card, metadata, approved variants, version history, and deployment constraints. Different clients render the same repository differently: a web client might show the interactive version, a mobile-first client simplified text and audio, and a WhatsApp-based client the low-bandwidth representation. Repositories could support sharing, remixing, localization, and cross-platform deployment while preserving instructor control.
requirements: Instructor approval of representation variants before they enter the repository
Semantic cards must be authored independently of any particular interface representation
target_learners: Learners in varying deployment contexts including low-bandwidth and mobile-first settings
target_learning_goals: Consistent learning content delivered through context-appropriate interface representations
examples: The paper describes a WhatsApp-based client delivering the low-bandwidth representation of the same card a web client renders interactively
key_sources: Seyed Parsa Neshaei, Abhinand Shibu, and Fatma Betül Güres. (2026). The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15902

article_title: Psychological predictors of continued ChatGPT use among university students: the roles of AI literacy, trust, and academic self-efficacy
citation: Peichen Hu. (2026). Psychological predictors of continued ChatGPT use among university students: the roles of AI literacy, trust, and academic self-efficacy. Front. Psychol. 17:1900190. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1900190
title: Capability-to-cognition-to-behavior moderated serial mediation model of continued generative AI use
description: The article proposes and tests a model in which AI literacy (capability) relates to continued ChatGPT use through an ordered psychological sequence: literacy to trust in AI, trust to academic self-efficacy, self-efficacy to continued use, with AI anxiety moderating the first link. The authors label this the "capability-to-cognition-to-behavior pattern" and contrast it with parallel-predictor acceptance models (TAM/UTAUT) that enter constructs side by side. In the tested sample the model accounted for 40% of variance in trust and continued use and 38% in self-efficacy.
requirements: Requires measuring AI literacy, trust in AI, academic self-efficacy, and AI anxiety with multi-item scales among learners who already use the tool
constraints: The ordering is a modeling assumption cross-sectional data cannot confirm; the sample comprises existing users only, so the account applies to sustained engagement rather than first-time uptake
target_learners: University students who already use generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: Sustained, productive engagement with generative AI for academic work
examples: Tested with a full latent-variable SEM on survey data from 450 Chinese university students with prior ChatGPT experience, with Monte Carlo confidence intervals (20,000 draws) for indirect effects
key_sources: Peichen Hu. (2026). Psychological predictors of continued ChatGPT use among university students: the roles of AI literacy, trust, and academic self-efficacy. Front. Psychol. 17:1900190. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1900190

article_title: A meta-analysis of the effect of generative AI on productivity and learning in programming
citation: Maier, S., Gunzenhäuser, M., Schweisthal, J., Schneider, M., & Feuerriegel, S. (2026). A meta-analysis of the effect of generative AI on productivity and learning in programming. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04779
title: Integrate GenAI into computer science education carefully, emphasizing explanation, reasoning, and critical evaluation rather than code production alone.
description: The article recommends rethinking curricula and GenAI integration by moving beyond code production alone and placing greater emphasis on explanation, reasoning, and critical evaluation, so that students develop the skills required to work safely and effectively with GenAI assistance. This principle responds to the meta-analytic finding that GenAI use does not consistently translate into improved learning or skill development, and that unrestricted access may hinder genuine skill acquisition. The authors argue that banning GenAI tools is neither realistic nor desirable given their growing professional role, making deliberate pedagogical integration essential.
requirements: Curricula must place greater emphasis on explanation, reasoning, and critical evaluation alongside code production.
GenAI integration must be deliberate rather than unrestricted, as unrestricted access may hinder genuine skill acquisition.
constraints: Banning GenAI tools is neither realistic nor desirable given the growing role of GenAI in professional programming practice.
The evidence base for learning outcomes is limited (11 effect sizes from 10 studies) and heterogeneous (I² = 86%).
target_learners: Computer science students at university and pre-university levels
target_learning_goals: Programming skill acquisition
Code comprehension and reasoning
Critical evaluation of AI-generated code
examples: The article's meta-analysis found significant learning effects only when students retained access to GenAI during the assessment itself, suggesting observed gains reflect tool-augmented performance rather than durable skill acquisition.
The authors note that when students rely on GenAI to generate or repair code, they may bypass critical learning processes such as reasoning through errors and internalizing core concepts.
key_sources: Maier, S., Gunzenhäuser, M., Schweisthal, J., Schneider, M., & Feuerriegel, S. (2026). A meta-analysis of the effect of generative AI on productivity and learning in programming. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04779

article_title: Human–AI collaboration in academic writing instruction: A calibrated feedback model for EAP
citation: Reza Farzi. (2026). Human–AI Collaboration in Academic Writing Instruction: Calibrated Feedback Model for EAP. OLBI Journal. https://doi.org/10.18192/olbij.v15i1.7773
title: Calibrated hybrid feedback model for EAP writing instruction
description: The article proposes a hybrid model of feedback provision in which language instructors leverage generative AI to support formative assessment while maintaining pedagogical oversight. It works through calibrated prompts and pedagogical (re-)framing, so that GenAI supplies immediate comments on student writing and the instructor supplies depth and pedagogical value. The model is grounded in the study's finding that GenAI "can supplement human feedback effectively but will not replace it."
requirements: Calibrated prompts designed by the instructor
Instructor pedagogical oversight of the feedback process
constraints: GenAI supplements rather than replaces human feedback
Intended for academic writing instruction in EAP contexts
target_learners: first-year EAP students in higher education
target_learning_goals: academic argumentative writing
formative feedback on second language writing
examples: In the study, each student's two argumentative essays were evaluated independently by both the instructor and ChatGPT-3.5 across three calibration stages.

article_title: Are LLM-based Chatbots Good Enough to Support Computer Science Students in Multiple-Choice Exercises?
citation: Markos Stamatakis, Omkar Gavali, Joshua Berger, Christian Wartena, Anett Hoppe, and Ralph Ewerth. (2026). Are LLM-based Chatbots Good Enough to Support Computer Science Students in Multiple-Choice Exercises? https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15919
title: Integrate LLM-generated answers into assessment and study settings carefully, since their effect on performance depends on task domain and learners' prior knowledge
description: The article concludes that chatbot outputs in test settings can either support or hinder learning depending on the task and setup, calling for "careful educational integration" of such systems. It positions LLM output as possible scaffolding for lower-prior-knowledge learners while warning of cognitive offloading for higher-prior-knowledge learners, and recommends larger studies before reliable conclusions.
requirements: Larger user studies with more participants and questions to reliably assess the statistical significance of chatbot-output effects, as the article states.
constraints: The article states findings are limited by its dataset and the small group of participants; the quantitative effect of GPT-generated output was not statistically significant under LRT.
target_learning_goals: Answering domain-specific multiple-choice questions in computer science topics such as interactive visual data analysis and computer vision
examples: In the user study, participants were randomly assigned to three groups completing two test attempts with or without GPT-4o output in IVDA and CV lectures.
key_sources: Markos Stamatakis, Omkar Gavali, Joshua Berger, Christian Wartena, Anett Hoppe, and Ralph Ewerth. (2026). Are LLM-based Chatbots Good Enough to Support Computer Science Students in Multiple-Choice Exercises? https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15919

article_title: Cognitive Agent Compilation for Explicit Problem Solver Modeling
citation: Hyeongdon Moon, Carolyn Rosé, and John Stamper. (2026). Cognitive Agent Compilation for Explicit Problem Solver Modeling. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07040
title: SLM prototype Cognitive Agent with QKV-style retrieval over a natural-language Knowledge Base
description: The prototype Cognitive Agent uses Qwen2.5-2B as its core SLM, embedding-gemma (300M parameters) for similarity-based retrieval, and a locally run 4-bit quantized gemma-3-27b-it Teacher LLM, all under zero-shot prompting. Knowledge is stored in natural language across three fields: a description, the applicable Goal state, and the applicable Working Memory state. At each step the SLM deterministically selects one of three actions: set a subgoal, update working memory, or produce a final answer.
requirements: The SLM must reliably follow the structured output format; the Teacher needs carefully specified prompts and three MCP tools for KB inference, similarity scoring, and DM submission
constraints: The authors note the SLM executor retains 'a residual black-box component whose internal prior knowledge cannot be fully inspected'
target_learners: modeled biology students in the OLI_Biology dataset context
target_learning_goals: declarative knowledge retrieval and multi-step problem solving
examples: Experiment code released at a public GitHub repository and a demo with detailed experiment output samples
key_sources: Hyeongdon Moon, Carolyn Rosé, and John Stamper. (2026). Cognitive Agent Compilation for Explicit Problem Solver Modeling. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07040

article_title: When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041
title: Capacity dissolution: erosion of the practices that keep delegated work answerable, distinct from deskilling
description: Capacity dissolution is the article's name for the central risk of AI delegation: a breakdown in the relation among an output, the person or institution that claims or relies on it, and the practice that makes that claim answerable. The article defines it as "a breakdown in the relation among an output, the person or institution that claims or relies on it, and the practice that makes that claim answerable". It is distinguished from deskilling, automation complacency, and diminished contestability: its object is the institutional relation that keeps delegated work answerable, and it can arise while specialists retain skill, performance stays high, and a formal appeal route exists. Its warning sign is successful output production alongside erosion of the learning practices that sustain accountability.
requirements: Recurring occasions for use and institutions that make capacity use consequential, since capacity is sustained by practice rather than stored privately
constraints: Distinct from ordinary deskilling: a person may stop a routine calculation without losing meaningful agency; dissolution concerns the practices that make delegated work answerable
target_learning_goals: maintaining the judgment needed to set ends, use reasons, and make challenge consequential
key_sources: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041

article_title: When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041
title: Lightweight capacity impact statement: a five-judgment deliberative record for AI deployment review
description: A capacity impact statement is a governance artifact the article proposes to make deployment review concrete. It records five judgments: the changed practice and responsible roles; the capacity the prior practice formed or evidenced; who needs that capacity or relies on its certification; how the new workflow preserves an opportunity to exercise it and what evidence makes that opportunity credible; and an observable trigger for review or repair. The article describes it as "a deliberative record, not a validated scale or universal score", whose purpose is to make the institution's reasons inspectable and revisable. It can be incorporated into course approval, assessment moderation, procurement, or periodic review, with depth and review interval scaled to stakes and reversibility.
requirements: An observable trigger for review or repair, and credible evidence that the workflow preserves an opportunity to exercise the capacity
constraints: It is a deliberative record, not a validated scale or universal score; depth and review interval should scale with the stakes and reversibility of the workflow
target_learning_goals: maintaining institutional capacity to understand, challenge, and revise AI-mediated practices over time
examples: The article's example: an AI-supported research essay where repeated inability of students to defend source selection or revise arguments meets the review trigger, prompting task revision or restored guided practice
key_sources: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041

article_title: The impact of risk perception on perceived benefits of generative artificial intelligence users—an empirical study based on university students
citation: Du W, Ning S, Shi Y and Chen Y. (2026). The impact of risk perception on perceived benefits of generative artificial intelligence users—an empirical study based on university students. Front. Psychol. 17:1866428. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1866428
title: Integrated CAT–PMT–TAM/UTAUT2 risk–benefit framework for Gen AI use
description: The article integrates Cognitive Appraisal Theory, Protection Motivation Theory, and TAM/UTAUT2 into a unified framework explaining how risk perception dimensions relate to perceived benefits. Risk dimensions serve as primary appraisals of threat; students then conduct secondary appraisal of controllability and coping resources. Per PMT, high coping appraisal triggers adaptive, problem-focused coping associated with higher perceived benefits, while low coping appraisal triggers maladaptive coping. The framework predicts the risk–benefit relationship is "non-linear and dimension-speciﬁc".
requirements: Risk perception must be measured as multiple distinct dimensions rather than a unitary construct
The framework assumes students' coping self-efficacy and perceived controllability vary across risk types
constraints: The article states the relationship between risk perception and perceived benefit is non-linear and dimension-specific, so linear uniform-risk assumptions do not apply
target_learning_goals: understanding and managing AI-related risks
responsible and effective Gen AI use in academic and daily contexts
examples: The study operationalized five risk dimensions (information, security, technical, ethical, legal) and five benefit dimensions and tested the framework via hierarchical and threshold regression on 814 valid questionnaires
key_sources: Du W, Ning S, Shi Y and Chen Y. (2026). The impact of risk perception on perceived benefits of generative artificial intelligence users—an empirical study based on university students. Front. Psychol. 17:1866428. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1866428

article_title: A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support
citation: Abhishek Jaiswal, Zoe Falomir. (2026). A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20349
title: Camelot Jr. recursive backtracking solver agent
description: A game-playing agent for Camelot Jr. implemented as 'a recursive backtracking protocol' that searches the permutation space of the block inventory for arrangements satisfying two independent criteria: Static Stability and Path Connectivity. Mirroring a human player, it places blocks one after another, evaluates structural validity once the inventory is fully deployed, and then evaluates path connectivity. It also 'implements geometric pruning strategies to cut off impractical search branches that cannot connect the start and the end points with the remaining inventory'.
requirements: A limited block inventory and grid layout defining the challenge
Support-footprint validation before committing to each placement
Backtracking with state reversion when stability or path criteria fail
constraints: Stability is checked only after all blocks are placed, since counterweights can stabilize an initially unstable arrangement
target_learners: players of the Camelot Jr. puzzle game
target_learning_goals: block placement under stability constraints
pathfinding from start to goal
examples: Algorithm 1 recursively selects unused blocks, tests orientations and positions, prunes placements without valid support, and reverts state on failure
key_sources: Abhishek Jaiswal, Zoe Falomir. (2026). A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20349

article_title: Student-AI Interaction in Computer-Assisted Consecutive Interpreting: Patterns and Performance
citation: Kuang H, Li J and Weng Y (2026) Student-AI interaction in computer-assisted consecutive interpreting: patterns and performance. Front. Psychol. 17:1890808. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1890808
title: Structure AI-training to foster stable, balanced student-AI interaction rather than prescribing workflows
description: The article's training course emphasized "exploratory engagement and critical reflections rather than prescribing specific interpreting workflows," and trained students showed higher cross-stage pattern consistency (66.7% vs 50.0%) and more AI-oriented profiles. The authors present this as evidence that formal training shapes predictable AI interaction strategies, informing interpreter education where effective AI integration hinges on rapid, selective, accountable AI use.
requirements: Formal training of meaningful duration (the studied course ran 16 weeks) with practice opportunities using varied AI tools
constraints: The article's instruction emphasized exploratory engagement rather than prescribed workflows; findings come from a quasi-experimental group comparison of 22 trainees
target_learners: interpreting trainees (Master of Translation and Interpreting students)
target_learning_goals: effective and stable interaction with AI support (ASR/MT) during complex bilingual tasks
examples: A 16-week compulsory CACI course introducing core AI-assisted interpreting concepts with practice across various AI tools was associated with more stable, AI-oriented interaction patterns
key_sources: Kuang H, Li J and Weng Y (2026) Student-AI interaction in computer-assisted consecutive interpreting: patterns and performance. Front. Psychol. 17:1890808. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1890808

article_title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
citation: Nataliya Kosmyna, Eugene Hauptmann, Ye Tong Yuan, Jessica Situ, Xian-Hao Liao, Ashly Vivian Beresnitzky, Iris Braunstein, Pattie Maes. (2009). Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task. Preprint, under review. https://www.brainonllm.com/
title: Treat LLM assistance in essay-writing instruction cautiously, since sustained reliance was associated with reduced neural engagement, ownership, and recall
description: The article recommends that educators treat LLM use in writing tasks as carrying measurable cognitive costs: over four sessions, LLM users showed the weakest neural coupling, low essay ownership, and reduced ability to quote their own essays, and the authors argue this demonstrates "a likely decrease in learning skills". The principle is to preserve AI-free writing experiences so learners retain strong engagement, rather than defaulting to LLM assistance.
requirements: Learners need opportunities for tool-free essay writing to maintain strong neural engagement, ownership, and quoting ability as observed in the Brain-only group.
constraints: The authors offer the study as a preliminary guide; the Search Engine group had no session 4, and only 18 of 54 participants completed session 4.
target_learners: students writing essays in educational contexts
target_learning_goals: essay writing
memory encoding of one's own text
sense of ownership over produced work
examples: Participants in the Brain-to-LLM condition, who had prior AI-free writing experience, showed higher memory recall and re-engagement of occipito-parietal and prefrontal nodes when later using the LLM.
key_sources: Nataliya Kosmyna, Eugene Hauptmann, Ye Tong Yuan, Jessica Situ, Xian-Hao Liao, Ashly Vivian Beresnitzky, Iris Braunstein, Pattie Maes. (2009). Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task. Preprint, under review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08872

article_title: Turn to chatbots for sharing feelings or seeking solutions? Differential associations of preferences for chatbot-mediated self-disclosure and instrumental help-seeking with adolescent interpersonal behaviors in the United States and Hong Kong
citation: Huinan Hu, Mojtaba Habibi Asgarabad, Enyi Jen, H. N. Cheung. (2026). Turn to chatbots for sharing feelings or seeking solutions? Differential associations of preferences for chatbot-mediated self-disclosure and instrumental help-seeking with adolescent interpersonal behaviors in the United States and Hong Kong. https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/qm6bg_v1
title: Culturally situated extension of the CASA paradigm: anthropomorphism and cultural foundations of human-computer relationships condition the outcomes of chatbot-mediated self-disclosure
description: The article builds on the computers-are-social-actors (CASA) paradigm, in which "individuals may mindlessly apply social heuristics (e.g., reciprocity, politeness, loyalty) to computers that exhibit social presence cues", and argues it must incorporate cultural context. East Asian animistic traditions and Confucian self-reflection norms foster anthropomorphizing chatbots, making self-disclosure adaptive, while Western human exceptionalism may leave US adolescents feeling emotionally disregarded. The authors state that "cultural foundations (e.g., differences in anthropomorphizing technology) should be integrated into the CASA diagram".
requirements: The account presupposes that conversation preferences translate into actual chatbot interactions, which the study did not measure
constraints: The authors label the proposed mechanisms tentative explanations to be verified in future interaction-based research
Direct evidence for CASA processes in adolescents remains limited, as the paradigm and its supporting evidence derive from general (mostly adult) populations
target_learners: adolescents in the US and Hong Kong
target_learning_goals: social and emotional development through human-AI interaction
adaptive coping and interpersonal behavior
examples: HK adolescents' self-disclosure preference related to adaptive coping and positive behaviors, whereas US adolescents' related to maladaptive coping and more bullying
key_sources: Huinan Hu, Mojtaba Habibi Asgarabad, Enyi Jen, H. N. Cheung. (2026). Turn to chatbots for sharing feelings or seeking solutions? Differential associations of preferences for chatbot-mediated self-disclosure and instrumental help-seeking with adolescent interpersonal behaviors in the United States and Hong Kong. https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/qm6bg_v1

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritize Learning over Performance
