citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: Four-stage adaptive cycle: Capture, Model, Adapt, Evolve
description: The adaptive foundation organises adaptivity into "a four-stage adaptive cycle, Capture, Model, Adapt, and Evolve, that enables AI companions to transform raw learner interactions into personalised and pedagogically grounded support". Capture records digital footprints including LLM dialogue traces; Model builds multi-dimensional learner models combining LLM interpretation with knowledge tracing and memory algorithms; Adapt harmonises personalised guidance with socially shared regulation via outer and inner loops; Evolve treats instructional decisions as hypotheses tested through controlled experiments, bandit algorithms, and simulated learners.
requirements: Sustained adaptation requires overcoming the statelessness of most current LLM applications, where each interaction begins without memory of the last
constraints: The paper warns that fully automated adaptivity can make students passive recipients who offload metacognitive control, motivating shared regulation designs
target_learning_goals: personalised feedback
self-regulated learning
continuous system improvement
key_sources: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816

article_title: The care-full craft of feedback in an age of generative AI
citation: Winstone, N. E., Gravett, K., Bearman, M., Noble, C., Jensen, L. X., Jones, A., & Nicola-Richmond, K. (2026). The care-full craft of feedback in an age of generative AI. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 51(5), 911-927. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2643333
title: A care-full framework for feedback in the age of GenAI built on four core values
description: Drawing on scholarship on matters of care, the authors propose that feedback encounters should be crafted as practices of care within a multimodal, human and non-human feedback landscape. "These core principles include recognising feedback encounters as more than comments; feedback as relational encounters; understanding the role of trust in feedback encounters; and recognising the professional craft of feedback." The framework resists reducing students to instrumentalist motivations and treats feedback labour as valuable rather than solely a cost to minimise.
requirements: Feedback processes must uphold meaning-making, educative relationships, trustworthiness, and professional craft as values guiding GenAI integration
constraints: The authors state these values and the manifesto principles are not exhaustive
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning through feedback encounters
examples: The paper stems in part from producing a Manifesto for Feedback in the Age of GenAI, from which the four core values were identified
key_sources: Winstone, N. E., Gravett, K., Bearman, M., Noble, C., Jensen, L. X., Jones, A., & Nicola-Richmond, K. (2026). The care-full craft of feedback in an age of generative AI. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 51(5), 911-927. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2643333

article_title: Professional Learning Communities: A Review of the Literature
citation: Stoll, L., Bolam, R., McMahon, A., Wallace, M., & Thomas, S. (2006). Professional Learning Communities: A Review of the Literature. Journal of Educational Change. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10833-006-0001-8
title: Capacity as a blend of motivation, skill, positive learning, organisational conditions and culture, and infrastructure of support
description: The review defines capacity as a composite construct: "Capacity is a complex blend of motivation, skill, positive learning, organisational conditions and culture, and infrastructure of support." Together these components give individuals, groups, whole school communities and school systems "the power to get involved in and sustain learning over time." The framework spans individual and collective levels, from single teachers to whole school systems, and underpins the review's argument that building capacity is critical for sustainable improvement.
requirements: Building capacity requires attention to all components of the blend, not only individual teacher skill
target_learning_goals: sustaining learning and improvement over time
promoting pupils' learning
key_sources: Stoll, L., Bolam, R., McMahon, A., Wallace, M., & Thomas, S. (2006). Professional Learning Communities: A Review of the Literature. Journal of Educational Change. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10833-006-0001-8

article_title: Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1)
citation: Kearney CA, Gonzálvez C, Graczyk PA and Fornander MJ (2019) Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1). Front. Psychol. 10:2222. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02222
title: Taxonomy of categorical terms for school attendance problems
description: The review organizes the field's historical categorical vocabulary: school attendance as "a student's complete in-class physical presence during an academic day" and absenteeism as its absence, sometimes excused or unexcused. It defines truancy (illegal, unexcused absenteeism used to trigger legal consequences), school refusal (absence due to emotional difficulties), school withdrawal (parent-initiated absence), and school exclusion (school-initiated absence), noting these terms vary across disciplines and jurisdictions.
requirements: Terms must be defined within a jurisdiction or discipline because definitions vary across contexts
constraints: Considerable controversy and heterogeneity remain even with respect to these characterizations
target_learners: children and adolescents in primary and secondary school
target_learning_goals: promoting school attendance and reducing absenteeism
examples: School districts use truancy thresholds such as 10 unexcused absences in a semester to trigger legal or administrative consequences
key_sources: Kearney CA, Gonzálvez C, Graczyk PA and Fornander MJ (2019) Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1). Front. Psychol. 10:2222. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02222

article_title: Depressive effects of underlining and adjunct questions on children's recall of text
citation: Rickards, J.P., Denner, P.R. (1979). Depressive effects of underlining and adjunct questions on children's recall of text. Instructional Science, 8, 81–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00054983
title: Exercise caution when adding underlining and adjunct postquestions to text for young readers, since they may depress rather than support recall
description: This principle captures the article's cautionary conclusion for instructional design: the study's results suggested that "underlining and adjunct questions may hinder rather than help recall performance in young readers". It applies to designers of text materials for children who would otherwise assume these common study aids are beneficial. The evidence base is a single experiment with ten-year-olds, so the caution is scoped to young readers rather than learners generally.
requirements: Applies when designing text-based materials for young (around ten-year-old) readers who are expected to study and recall passage content.
constraints: Based on one experiment with ten-year-old children; the article frames the effect with hedging ("may hinder rather than help"), so it is a caution, not a demonstrated optimum or prohibition.
target_learning_goals: Recall of prose passage content, including superordinate conceptual material and subordinate passage details
examples: In the experiment, children given both underlining and conceptual postquestions after every paragraph showed the most depressed recall of passage details.
key_sources: Rickards, J.P., Denner, P.R. (1979). Depressive effects of underlining and adjunct questions on children's recall of text. Instructional Science, 8, 81–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00054983

article_title: Student Diversity Representation and Reporting in Universal School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Programs: Implications for Generalizability
citation: Rowe, H. L., & Trickett, E. J. (2018). Student Diversity Representation and Reporting in Universal School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Programs: Implications for Generalizability. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9425-3
title: Exercise caution when generalizing universal SEL program effects across diverse student groups
description: Because the reviewed evaluations reported diversity characteristics inconsistently and rarely tested moderation with adequate justification, the review "suggests caution about the generalizability of the reviewed SEL programs across diverse groups of children and adolescents." Evaluators and program adopters should not assume universal SEL effects hold uniformly across gender, race/ethnicity, SES, disability status, and sexual orientation/gender identity without subgroup-relevant evidence.
requirements: Evaluations should report demographic characteristics and test or justify moderation analyses before generalizability claims are made
constraints: The caution applies to the reviewed universal school-based SEL programs, not to targeted or indicated interventions
target_learners: children and adolescents in universal school-based SEL programs
target_learning_goals: social and emotional learning outcomes
examples: The review's analysis of published SEL evaluations found inconsistent demographic reporting and few, weakly justified moderation tests, grounding the generalizability caution
key_sources: Rowe, H. L., & Trickett, E. J. (2018). Student Diversity Representation and Reporting in Universal School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Programs: Implications for Generalizability. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9425-3

article_title: Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion
citation: Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2011). Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9080-x
title: Treat off-line self-report assessments of strategy use as prone to memory-reconstruction and prompting threats, and pursue more validation work
description: The article's concluding recommendation: designers and users of strategy-use assessments should remain aware that "off-line methods might suffer from memory-reconstruction and prompting problems that produce flawed answers to retrospective questions." Prompting prior or concurrent to task performance restricts assessment scope to availability deficiencies. Despite inventive new instruments, more validation work is needed against the three validity criteria.
requirements: New assessment methods require thorough examination to gain understanding of what these methods precisely are measuring
constraints: Memory-reconstruction and prompting problems cannot be entirely resolved by minimizing delay or task-specific wording; they only mitigate the problem
target_learners: learners whose strategy use is assessed with self-report instruments
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of reading strategy use
examples: The discussion reviews the five special-issue instruments under the three validity criteria and concludes not all of them passed the test
key_sources: Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2011). Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9080-x

article_title: Collaborative learning through augmented reality role playing
citation: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://education.mit.edu
title: Calibrate role overlap in collaborative AR games: enough common ground to discuss, enough asymmetry to preserve interdependence
description: The article identifies role overlap as a key design consideration for collaborative AR games. Too much overlap between roles "will remove the positive interdependence and individual accountability that encourage collaboration," while too little overlap "does not give the students enough common ground to discuss the problem space." Shared information serves as promotive interaction, reinforcing students and giving them a starting point for discussion around common pieces before working toward unique contributions.
requirements: Roles must be designed with partial overlap: shared information for common ground, unique information for interdependence and accountability
constraints: The article states the effect of varying overlap on learning outcomes has not yet been studied; the authors plan to study how increasing and decreasing overlap affects learning outcomes in future phases
target_learning_goals: collaboration
collaborative problem solving
examples: In CRC, all students learned that West Nile Virus was a serious mosquito-borne disease, but only certain roles were privy to the seasonality, the current levels, or the symptoms
key_sources: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://doi.org/10.3115/1149293.1149333

article_title: A Breakthrough for Josh: How Use of an iPad Facilitated Reading Improvement
citation: McClanahan, B., Williams, K., Kennedy, E., & Tate, S. (2012). A Breakthrough for Josh: How Use of an iPad Facilitated Reading Improvement. TechTrends, 56(3). https://link.springer.com/journal/11528
title: Computer-aided instruction for students with ADHD should present tasks in multiple modalities, chunked, with repeated trials and immediate feedback
description: Drawing on the Raggi and Chronis review, the article identifies characteristics of computer-aided instruction that may promote sustained attention and improved work performance for students with ADHD: "presentation of learning tasks in multiple modalities, the capability of chunking tasks into more manageable pieces, and repeated trials with immediate feedback." CAI also offers one-on-one, self-paced, individualized instruction, often with the novelty of game formatting that promotes engagement and attention. The article states these characteristics directly address the core symptoms of ADHD.
requirements: One-on-one tailored, self-paced delivery
game-like formatting or novelty to promote engagement
constraints: The article notes the research on CAI is often flawed or conflicting; the review found most studies had significant design flaws or small samples
target_learners: Students with ADHD in general education classrooms
target_learning_goals: Sustained attention during academic tasks
Improved academic work performance
examples: The iPad tutoring sessions embodied these characteristics: game-formatted apps such as Compound Boogie gave repeated trials with immediate feedback, and the touch screen engaged visual and tactile/kinesthetic modalities.
key_sources: McClanahan, B., Williams, K., Kennedy, E., & Tate, S. (2012). A Breakthrough for Josh: How Use of an iPad Facilitated Reading Improvement. TechTrends, 56(3). https://link.springer.com/journal/11528

article_title: Knowledge is power: How conceptual knowledge transforms visual cognition
citation: Collins, Jessica A., & Olson, Ingrid R. (2014). Knowledge is Power: How Conceptual Knowledge Transforms Visual Cognition. Psychonomic bulletin & review. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-013-0564-3
title: Categorical perception: category knowledge warps perceptual representations along category boundaries
description: Categorical perception is the phenomenon whereby continuous perceptual variation is experienced as discrete qualitative changes organized by learned category boundaries. The review presents it as the most robust evidence that conceptual knowledge penetrates visual analysis: category knowledge abstracts over within-class differences and highlights between-class differences, observed for color, faces, and trained novel objects. It functions as an information-compression mechanism that lets perceivers efficiently process features relevant to behavior.
requirements: Category knowledge or labels relevant to the stimulus dimension must be available to the perceiver
constraints: Within-category differences are attenuated relative to between-category differences, not eliminated; the review notes individuals remain sensitive to within-category phonetic differences
target_learning_goals: learning category structures that organize perceptual dimensions
examples: The rainbow is perceived as seven distinct color bands despite a continuous range of light frequencies; color perception remains categorical even in psychophysically balanced color spaces
key_sources: Collins, Jessica A., & Olson, Ingrid R. (2014). Knowledge is Power: How Conceptual Knowledge Transforms Visual Cognition. Psychonomic bulletin & review. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-013-0564-3

article_title: The structure of working memory in young children and its relation to intelligence
citation: Gray Shelley, Green Samuel, Alt Mary, Hogan Tiffany P., Kuo Trudy, Brinkley Shara, Cowan Nelson. (2016). The Structure of Working Memory in Young Children and Its Relation to Intelligence. Journal of Memory and Language. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5157932/
title: Comprehensive Assessment Battery for Children - Working Memory (CABC-WM): 13 computer-based tasks in a pirate-themed game
description: The Comprehensive Assessment Battery for Children - Working Memory is a computer-based battery of 13 experimental working memory tasks presented "in a computer-based, pirate-themed game that took six to seven 2-hour sessions to complete over a period of approximately two weeks." Tasks span central executive (n-back auditory and visual, number updating), short-term phonological (digit span, digit span running, nonword repetition), short-term visuospatial (location span, location span running, visual span, visual span running), and binding (phonological, visuospatial, cross-modal) domains. A guide pirate delivered instructions and demonstrations, and children earned virtual rocks and gold coins for motivation. Most task reliabilities were moderate to high.
requirements: Children must pass training trials to proceed to each game; tasks are administered individually with children seated 52 cm from a touchscreen monitor
constraints: Children did not know whether individual responses were correct or incorrect during the games; feedback was limited to end-of-session virtual rewards
target_learners: second-grade children ages 7;0-9;1 with typical development
target_learning_goals: measuring central executive, phonological storage, visuospatial storage, attention, and binding components of working memory in children
examples: Nonword repetition included 16 nonwords at 2- to 5-syllable lengths with inter-rater transcription reliability of 87%; phonological binding scoring reliability was 94%
key_sources: Gray Shelley, Green Samuel, Alt Mary, Hogan Tiffany P., Kuo Trudy, Brinkley Shara, Cowan Nelson. (2016). The Structure of Working Memory in Young Children and Its Relation to Intelligence. Journal of Memory and Language. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5157932/

article_title: Maternal emotional support but not cognitive support during problem-solving predicts increases in cognitive flexibility in early childhood
citation: Zeytinoglu, S., Calkins, S. D., & Leerkes, E. M. (2019). Maternal emotional support but not cognitive support during problem-solving predicts increases in cognitive flexibility in early childhood. International Journal of Behavioral Development, 43(1), 12-23. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025418757706
title: Interventions for caregivers of young children should target emotional responsiveness and reduce negative and intrusive behaviors to support cognitive flexibility
description: Based on the finding that emotional but not cognitive support predicted growth in cognitive flexibility, the article recommends that "prevention and intervention work aimed towards improving caregivers’ emotional responsiveness and reducing negative and intrusive behaviors may potentially lead to improvements in children’s cognitive flexibility and executive functioning in early childhood." The recommendation is framed as potential, resting on the longitudinal predictive associations rather than a tested intervention.
requirements: Intervention should focus on the emotional dimension of caregiving (responsiveness, non-intrusiveness, low negativity) rather than instructional or cognitive support alone
constraints: The article states the recommendation only "may potentially" lead to improvements; no intervention was tested in this study
target_learners: children in early childhood (preschool to first grade)
target_learning_goals: cognitive flexibility and executive functioning
examples: The three-wave study identified emotional support as the specific caregiving dimension predicting flexibility gains while cognitive support did not, motivating the intervention target
key_sources: Zeytinoglu, S., Calkins, S. D., & Leerkes, E. M. (2019). Maternal emotional support but not cognitive support during problem-solving predicts increases in cognitive flexibility in early childhood. International Journal of Behavioral Development, 43(1), 12-23. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025418757706

article_title: Physical fitness and academic performance in primary school children with and without a social disadvantage
citation: de Greeff, J. W.; Hartman, E.; Mullender-Wijnsma, M. J.; Bosker, R. J.; Doolaard, S.; & Visscher, C. (2014). Physical fitness and academic performance in primary school children with and without a social disadvantage. Health Education Research, 29(5), 853-860. https://doi.org/10.1093/her/cyu043
title: Support cardiovascular fitness development in primary school children as a lever for mathematics and spelling performance
description: The article's findings support attending to children's cardiovascular fitness in primary education, because cardiovascular fitness showed positive associations with mathematics (beta = 0.23) and spelling (beta = 0.16), while muscular fitness showed none. The authors conclude there is "a specific link between cardiovascular fitness and mathematics, regardless of socioeconomic status". This suggests fitness-promoting activity in schools may accompany, though not causally demonstrate, academic benefit.
requirements: Cardiovascular fitness must be measured or developed specifically; muscular fitness alone does not show the association.
constraints: The study is cross-sectional and reports associations, not causal effects of fitness training on achievement.
The fitness-spelling association is moderated by social disadvantage status.
target_learners: primary school children (mean age 8.0), including socially disadvantaged children
target_learning_goals: mathematics performance
spelling performance
examples: The study measured cardiovascular and muscular fitness with fitness tests and related them to mathematics, spelling and reading scores of 544 children via multilevel analysis.
key_sources: de Greeff, J. W.; Hartman, E.; Mullender-Wijnsma, M. J.; Bosker, R. J.; Doolaard, S.; & Visscher, C. (2014). Physical fitness and academic performance in primary school children with and without a social disadvantage. Health Education Research, 29(5), 853-860. https://doi.org/10.1093/her/cyu043

article_title: Reconstructing constructivism: Causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms, and the theory theory.
citation: Gopnik, A., & Wellman, H. M. (2012). Reconstructing constructivism: Causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory. Psychological Bulletin, 138(6), 1085-1108. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0028044
title: Causal Bayes nets with an interventionist account of causation as a model of intuitive theories
description: Causal Bayes nets represent causal hypotheses as directed graphs whose variables and edges generate patterns of evidence, supporting prediction, intervention and counterfactual inference. The article pairs them with Woodward's interventionist account: 'if there is a direct causal relation between A and B, then, other things equal, intervening to change the probability of A will change the probability of B'. Interventions alter the graph ('graph surgery'), letting learners infer structure from observations and from the outcomes of experiments.
requirements: Assumptions about the parameterization of the graph (e.g., whether causes independently raise effect probability, whether evidence is a random sample) to constrain inferences
constraints: The article notes many hypotheses may be compatible with any evidence pattern (underdetermination), so Bayesian methods rank hypotheses by probability rather than deciding truth outright
target_learners: children and adults learning causal structure
target_learning_goals: causal inference, prediction, intervention planning and counterfactual reasoning
examples: The wine-insomnia example shows how distinguishing a causal chain from a common-cause graph predicts different consequences of intervening on drinking versus partying
key_sources: Gopnik, A., & Wellman, H. M. (2012). Reconstructing constructivism: Causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory. Psychological Bulletin, 138(6), 1085-1108. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0028044

article_title: Developmental Changes in the Profiles of Dyscalculia: An Explanation Based on a Double Exact-and-Approximate Number Representation Model
citation: Noël M-P and Rousselle L (2011) Developmental changes in the profiles of dyscalculia: an explanation based on a double exact-and-approximate number representation model. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 5:165. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2011.00165
title: Carey's developmental account: exact number concepts built via parallel individuation and the successor function, then mapped onto the ANS
description: The article describes Carey's (2001, 2004, 2009) model as illustrating the standpoint that symbolic number meaning is not gained by simple mapping onto the ANS. Representations of natural numbers are first built on a "parallel individuation" system that keeps track of items in small sets through mental models, providing an exact though implicit representation of small numerosities. The child then must "discover that the cardinal value of a number word is determined by its order on the list, and that successive numbers are related by the function '+1'" — the successor function, worked out by induction. Only after creating this exact representation does the child start to map it with the ANS.
requirements: Discovery of the successor function by induction on knowledge of the cardinal meaning of one through four
A two-stage process in which children first understand that adding one item leads to a cardinal labeled by a word further along the counting list, then that it is labeled by the word just after
constraints: The parallel individuation system is very limited and only allows the child to track 3 or 4 items in parallel
target_learners: preschool and early primary children learning counting and number words
target_learning_goals: acquiring the cardinal meaning of number words
mastering the successor function
examples: Sarnecka and Carey (2008) showed the conceptual jump to the successor function is at least a two-stage process, as the article reports
key_sources: Noël M-P and Rousselle L (2011) Developmental changes in the profiles of dyscalculia: an explanation based on a double exact-and-approximate number representation model. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 5:165. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2011.00165

article_title: Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference
citation: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287
title: Computer-assisted reading lessons for relativization instruction (MOG, ROG, and COG treatments)
description: Ten daily computer-assisted reading lessons delivered the treatments to all three groups in a common format: "a text that appeared on the screen in three sequential reading-skills formats—a skimming format, an in-depth reading format, and a scanning format—followed by the two measures of comprehension". The experimental manipulation occurred during Reading for Understanding: the meaning-oriented group received lexical rephrasings and sentence clarification, the rule-oriented group viewed Animated Grammar decomposition and recombination, and controls viewed only the text sentences. Daily comprehension tests and L1 recall summaries were built in.
requirements: Computer laboratory access and daily one-lesson assignments on individual diskettes
Researcher presence to ensure subjects viewed only assigned lessons
constraints: Instruction was limited to restrictive OBJECT OF A PREPOSITION relative clauses within three created stories
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and acquisition of English relative clauses
examples: The computer format was chosen for convenient, controlled administration of treatments and permanent availability of the instruction for future analysis
key_sources: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287

article_title: Advocating for group interaction in the age of COVID-19
citation: Sanna Järvelä & Carolyn P. Rosé. (2020). Advocating for group interaction in the age of COVID-19. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09324-4
title: Collaborative learning requires careful design rather than occurring spontaneously
description: The editorial states as field consensus that collaborative learning "is not best conducted in a spontaneous fashion, but careful design of collaborative learning will contribute to effective computer-supported collaborative learning." It notes a decade of work scripting, prompting and structuring collaboration and supporting roles and participation, and identifies evaluating complete designs and their instructional alignment as an open problem. Design-centered research is presented as one emerging methodology addressing it.
requirements: Evaluation must address alignment between the design and its engagement to extract insights for later iterations, as the editorial frames the still-unmet attention.
constraints: The editorial states that how to evaluate the complete designs and their instructional alignment had not yet received attention.
target_learners: students in computer-supported collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: productive collaboration and effective computer-supported collaborative learning
examples: The editorial cites scripting, prompting and structuring the collaboration process and supporting roles and participation as developed approaches over the past decade.
key_sources: Sanna Järvelä & Carolyn P. Rosé. (2020). Advocating for group interaction in the age of COVID-19. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09324-4

article_title: Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning
citation: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7
title: CAVA360VR — a software platform for within-VR collaborative analysis of 360-degree video
description: CAVA360VR is a software solution that allows learners within IVR to engage and collaborate with 360-degree video recordings (Davidsen & McIlvenny, 2022). Learners have access to tools such as "pause, rewind, annotation and spatialised audio", supporting multi-layered analysis, discussion and debate within the recording. In the mentoring case it additionally allows warping between different camera positions, and using a laser to pinpoint actions and moments in the recorded interaction.
requirements: 360-degree video recordings of relevant activities and HMD hardware; the software layer distinguishing environment content from the interactive layer
constraints: Recordings cannot be manipulated during playback owing to the reduced interactivity of 360VR
target_learners: teachers and mentors in professional development
target_learning_goals: collaborative video analysis
annotation of key moments in recorded interaction
examples: Used in both empirical cases: medical students immersed in CAVA360VR analysing knee examination footage, and teacher–mentor mentoring sessions
key_sources: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7

article_title: Is it distracting? A further exploration of non-gameplay social interaction during collaborative digital game-based learning
citation: Jiqing Sun, Andrew Skourdoumbis. (2026). Is it distracting? A further exploration of non-gameplay social interaction during collaborative digital game-based learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09476-9
title: An online card-matching game for early algebra designed under Realistic Mathematics Education principles
description: The research team designed an online card-matching game in which students match equivalent mathematical structures presented in different forms, supporting understanding of algebraic symbols and expressions. It comprised "four levels of increasing challenge, with tasks progressing from arithmetic expressions to formal algebraic expressions." Students played in dyads in 2-versus-2 team competition, justifying their reasoning when matching cards to minimise random guessing.
requirements: Students must justify their reasoning when matching cards; teacher facilitates by circulating among groups
constraints: Designed for a single 57-min lesson in dyad competition; teams sat at the same table face-to-face
target_learning_goals: Understanding pronumerals and combining like terms
examples: The game was implemented with four students in two dyads seated with their opponents, with gameplay video/audio recorded
key_sources: Jiqing Sun, Andrew Skourdoumbis. (2026). Is it distracting? A further exploration of non-gameplay social interaction during collaborative digital game-based learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09476-9

article_title: Mountain rescuers’ experiences with video-assisted and verbal debriefings: a qualitative study
citation: Stefan A. Schreder, Helen Jossberger, Hans Gruber. (2025). Mountain rescuers' experiences with video-assisted and verbal debriefings: a qualitative study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09716-9
title: Implement video-assisted debriefing with careful facilitation that balances positive and negative feedback to protect psychological safety
description: The article concludes that VAD can have advantages over verbal debriefing but requires deliberate facilitator implementation. Because displayed mistakes can intimidate participants, facilitators should balance critical comments with positive visualised situations, use disclaimers ensuring confidentiality, and state that "If you use the video in the wrong way, you can hurt people." This maintains psychological safety and motivation during debriefing.
requirements: Facilitator training in VAD technology and in maintaining psychological safety
Balanced feedback including positive as well as negative video segments
constraints: Breaches of psychological safety can occur even with facilitator safeguards
Equipment unsuited to some simulation conditions (e.g., not operable inside the cooling chamber)
target_learners: volunteer rescue and healthcare professionals in simulation-based training
target_learning_goals: reflecting on team and individual performance after simulation
accepting and benefiting from feedback
examples: Facilitators added pre-debriefing disclaimers that the video was "an aid and not a tool to keep you under surveillance" and deliberately showed positive interactions alongside mistakes to avoid an overly negative impression.
key_sources: Stefan A. Schreder, Helen Jossberger, Hans Gruber. (2025). Mountain rescuers' experiences with video-assisted and verbal debriefings: a qualitative study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09716-9

article_title: When is observing failure productive? Investigating the role of solution diversity in vicarious failure
citation: Thomas C. Braas, Christian Hartmann, Vincent Hoogerheide, Nikol Rummel, Tamara van Gog. (2025). When is observing failure productive? Investigating the role of solution diversity in vicarious failure. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09706-x
title: Solution diversity defined as the number of canonical solution components present in solution attempts
description: The article proposes measuring solution diversity by counting how many of the four canonical components of the target solution (using all numbers, absolute deviations, mean as fixed reference point, division by total data points) appear in solution attempts, rather than by quantity or quality of solutions. The authors argue "utilizing the number of canonical components as measure of diversity seems more sensible", because quantity can be high with no canonical component present and quality can repeat the same components. This definition also permits experimental control in VF modeling examples.
requirements: Requires specifying the canonical solution and decomposing it into its constituent components before designing or coding solution attempts.
constraints: The article notes prior correlational evidence on RSM-diversity and conceptual knowledge has been mixed and exclusively correlational; this study's own range-based measure did not correlate with outcomes.
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of statistical variability (mean absolute deviation)
examples: VF-high videos presented solutions covering all four canonical components, while VF-low videos presented only two, with total solution quality held equal across conditions.
key_sources: Thomas C. Braas, Christian Hartmann, Vincent Hoogerheide, Nikol Rummel, Tamara van Gog. (2025). When is observing failure productive? Investigating the role of solution diversity in vicarious failure. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09706-x

article_title: Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Loyens, S. M. M., Magda, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2008). Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9082-7
title: Candy's four-dimension model of self-directed learning
description: Candy's framework, drawn from adult education and frequently used to study SDL in PBL, treats SDL as both a goal and a process and "defines four dimensions of SDL: personal autonomy, self-management in learning, the independent pursuit of learning, and the learner control of instruction". Personal autonomy is a dispositional attribute; self-management is its exercise in learning; learner control concerns the instructional situation; independent pursuit concerns autodidaxy outside formal settings. Blumberg applied it to PBL learning processes, strategies, and outcomes.
requirements: The framework is applied by analyzing the learning process, learning strategies, and performance outcomes separately, as Blumberg did for PBL
constraints: Stems from adult education, so its independent-pursuit dimension concerns learning outside formal educational settings
target_learners: higher education and medical students in PBL
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning skills
deep-level processing strategies
examples: Blumberg (2000) used the model to evaluate whether problem-based learners are self-directed learners, organized along learning process, strategies, and outcomes
key_sources: Loyens, S. M. M., Magda, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2008). Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9082-7

article_title: Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review
citation: Sofie M. M. Loyens, Julianne E. van Meerten, Lydia Schaap, Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09757-x
title: Critical-analytic thinking as evidence-weighing across four consecutive steps
description: The review defines CAT as the processes used "when we question or at least do not simply passively accept the accuracy of claims as givens," distinguishing it from CT by its focus on justification and on whether credible evidence supports a claim. It reports that "Alexander (2014) describes the process of CAT in four consecutive steps": starting with a claim or task for which one collects data or evidence, evaluating or judging that evidence, and integrating it with one's knowledge and beliefs. Unlike CT, the CAT literature does not consider dispositions, though prior knowledge and goals can act as moderators.
requirements: Instructionally, students should pose unanswered questions requiring data collection, gather evidence with appropriate methodologies, and discuss or debate how anticipated, unanticipated, and missing evidence should be interpreted
constraints: Dispositions are not considered in the CAT literature the review describes, although individual differences such as prior knowledge and goals can act as moderators
target_learning_goals: Weighing evidence and justifying claims rather than passively accepting them
examples: The review draws parallels between these CAT-facilitating approaches and PBL and PjBL, in which a problem or question is the starting point for learning activities
key_sources: Sofie M. M. Loyens, Julianne E. van Meerten, Lydia Schaap, Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09757-x

article_title: The Threads of Campus Life: A Review of the Literature on the Use of Social Network Analysis in Research Articles on Undergraduate Students
citation: Michael Brown, Rachel Smith, Jennifer Tipton, Gabrielle Leitner. (2026). The Threads of Campus Life: A Review of the Literature on the Use of Social Network Analysis in Research Articles on Undergraduate Students. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543261438444
title: Campus Ecological Networks Model with bonding and exploring mechanisms for campus community formation
description: The review organizes its analysis with the Campus Ecological Networks Model (M. G. Brown & Smith, 2024), which builds on Renn and Arnold's campus ecological perspective to connect students' individual characteristics, interaction contents, institutional social structure, and educational outcomes. It incorporates Smith and Vonhoff's (2019) mechanisms: "social mechanisms that help students bond with one another, such as balance, exchange, homophily, and proximity, as well as those that help students explore broadly, such as self-interest and contagion" (Table 1). The framework hypothesizes mechanisms may compete in shaping community structure and that networks can have negative as well as beneficial educational outcomes.
requirements: Institutional personnel should intentionally choose which theoretical mechanism(s) to draw on to help students form community, make program and policy decisions accordingly, and then measure resulting networks and outcomes
constraints: The review observes the field lacks a theory for how relational structure emerges, is maintained, or abandoned on campus, in classrooms, and across a student's academic career
target_learning_goals: understanding how campus community structures form, persist, and dissolve and how they relate to learning, development, and persistence
examples: Table 1 maps each mechanism to measures: homophily to shared characteristics predicting ties, proximity to physical closeness, self-interest to betweenness centrality, contagion to longitudinal tracking of behavior spread
key_sources: Michael Brown, Rachel Smith, Jennifer Tipton, Gabrielle Leitner. (2026). The Threads of Campus Life: A Review of the Literature on the Use of Social Network Analysis in Research Articles on Undergraduate Students. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543261438444

article_title: A systematic review of the association between social and emotional competencies and student engagement in youth
citation: Anabela Caetano Santos, Celeste Simões, Márcia H.S. Melo, Margarida F. Santos, Iara Freitas, Cátia Branquinho, Carmel Cefai, Patrícia Arriaga. (2023). A systematic review of the association between social and emotional competencies and student engagement in youth. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100535
title: CASEL 5 framework of social and emotional competencies
description: The review organises social and emotional competencies using the CASEL (Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning) 5 framework, "which includes five broad and interrelated areas of competence: i) self-awareness; ii) self-management; iii) social awareness; iv) relationship skills; and v) responsible decision-making". The model holds that changing these five areas positively impacts proximal outcomes and contexts, and thereby more distal outcomes: SECs directly affect school achievement and indirectly increase student engagement and decrease mental health difficulties. The review uses these five domains as its coding categories for SEC variables across the 91 studies.
requirements: SEC measures must address broad CASEL-defined competencies rather than context-specific competencies such as academic or familial context
constraints: The framework's five domains were unevenly represented in the reviewed literature, with social awareness studied in only 7 of 91 studies
target_learners: youth students aged 10–25 in middle school, high school and university
target_learning_goals: social and emotional competencies
student engagement
key_sources: Anabela Caetano Santos, Celeste Simões, Márcia H.S. Melo, Margarida F. Santos, Iara Freitas, Cátia Branquinho, Carmel Cefai, Patrícia Arriaga. (2023). A systematic review of the association between social and emotional competencies and student engagement in youth. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100535

article_title: Placebo or Assistant? Generative AI Between Externalization and Anthropomorphization
citation: Skulmowski, A. (2024). Placebo or Assistant? Generative AI Between Externalization and Anthropomorphization. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 58. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09894-x
title: Computers as Social Actors (CASA) framework
description: The CASA framework holds that "humans expect computers to function in alignment with certain social rules, leading them to perceive technology as a human-like partner". The essay extends this account to AI systems, smartphones, and smartwatches, and uses it to organize findings on anthropomorphization triggers, such as humanized chatbot elements increasing social presence and thereby trust, empathy, and satisfaction. It serves as the essay's explanatory backdrop for why users might be expected to credit AI contributions, and highlights a research gap regarding relationships with AI collaborators in education.
requirements: The framework applies to human-technology interaction in which social-rule expectations can be triggered by design factors.
constraints: The essay notes most studies in this section predate the 2023 widespread adoption of generative AI, and that little is known about these relationships with AI collaborators in educational contexts.
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring and attribution of one's own versus AI contributions to learning tasks
examples: The essay applies CASA to interpret why users might treat chatbots as partners, and to frame the conflict between liking AI output quality and taking credit for it.
key_sources: Skulmowski, A. (2024). Placebo or Assistant? Generative AI Between Externalization and Anthropomorphization. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 58. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09894-x

article_title: Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement’s Directional Ordering
citation: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w
title: Taxonomy of causality theories: sequential, simultaneous, and reciprocal
description: The article organizes philosophical, theological, and scientific perspectives on causation into three families relevant to interpreting cross-lagged panel models. "Sequential theories of causation posit that causes and effects are temporally distinct, with causes preceding effects" — the traditional Western view from Aristotle onward and the default in psychological research. Simultaneous theories (from Nagarjuna and Dogen to Descartes, Kant, and Cramer's transactional interpretation) allow cause and effect to co-occur. "Reciprocal causation occurs when two or more variables mutually influence each other, forming a causal loop", combining bidirectionality with temporal ordering. The article uses this taxonomy to motivate testing lag0 alongside lag1 and lag2 paths.
requirements: Testing reciprocal directional ordering requires both constructs measured across at least two, preferably three or more, waves of data
constraints: The article adheres to a Granger predictive-causality perspective, under which truly instantaneous lag0 effects might not fit as prospective effects
target_learning_goals: understanding directional ordering of academic self-concept and achievement
examples: The article illustrates time-interval dependence with Gollob and Reichardt's aspirin example: no effect in 2 minutes, maximum effect after several hours, little effect after 24 hours
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w

article_title: The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis
citation: Achraf Ammar, Khaled Trabelsi, Mohamed Ali Boujelbane, Atef Salem, Omar Boukhris, Jordan M. Glenn, Piotr Zmijewski, Haitham A. Jahrami, Hamdi Chtourou, Wolfgang I. Schöllhorn. (2024). The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09892-z
title: Do not assume high contextual interference (random) practice guarantees a longer-term performance advantage in PE and sports
description: The meta-analysis finds "very limited evidence supporting the recommendation to employ high CI practices to gain a longer-term performance advantage, calling into question the generalization of the CI model to PE and sports practices." Practitioners should therefore not schedule random/serial practice on the expectation of guaranteed retention benefits over blocked practice; gains differences were negligible acutely and non-significant long-term. The authors instead call for "High-quality follow-up research evaluating alternative motor-learning models."
requirements: Decisions about practice schedules should rest on outcome gains (Δ pre-post, Δ post-retention, Δ pre-retention) rather than on post-test group comparisons alone, as the article argues prior conclusions lacked gain analyses.
constraints: Evidence base is gross motor skills in healthy populations in PE and sports contexts; studies on cognitive performance, fine motor skills, and populations with physical or mental disability were excluded.
target_learners: sports participants across age groups from children to older adults
target_learning_goals: acquisition and retention of gross motor and sports skills
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 183 outcomes from 36 studies and found only 20% agreed with the paradoxical CI prediction.
key_sources: Achraf Ammar, Khaled Trabelsi, Mohamed Ali Boujelbane, Atef Salem, Omar Boukhris, Jordan M. Glenn, Piotr Zmijewski, Haitham A. Jahrami, Hamdi Chtourou, Wolfgang I. Schöllhorn. (2024). The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09892-z

article_title: Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods
citation: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5
title: CAPERS: a prospective mixed-methods framework integrating community participatory methods into research synthesis
description: CAPERS (Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis) is a mixed-methods framework that engages community partners prospectively in research synthesis rather than post hoc. The article describes it as "a novel mixed-methods synthesis framework" that shifts community engagement "from a post hoc interpretive activity/responsibility to a prospectively planned component of the research synthesis design." It applies across synthesis types including meta-analyses, scoping reviews, and qualitative meta-syntheses.
requirements: Requires identifying community members "aligned with the goals of the synthesis" who have relevant practical perspectives on feasibility, adoptability, and sustainability
constraints: The article presents it as a proposal to "stimulate dialogue and provide a guidance" rather than a validated method with empirical evidence of effectiveness
target_learners: Practitioners and policymakers using synthesis evidence
target_learning_goals: Improve relevance, usability, and implementation readiness of research syntheses for practice
examples: Integrating meta-analytic findings with practitioner and student perspectives to identify contextually-grounded mechanisms of change in school-based interventions
key_sources: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5

article_title: Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods
citation: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5
title: Five mixed-methods integration functions organize CAPERS: convergence, complementarity, development, expansion, and sampling
description: CAPERS organizes the integration of participatory and synthesis methods through "five mixed-methods functions (Palinkas et al. 2011a, b) that are tailored to the research synthesis workstream": Convergence (same question, both methods), Complementarity (related questions, elaboration), Expansion (one method extends the other), Development (one method informs the design or coding of the other), and Sampling (one method guides selection for the other). Each function is defined with rationale, an extant-literature example, and an educational psychology application.
requirements: Researchers must decide which function(s) fit their synthesis purpose; the article notes "it is possible to integrate PAR and RS methods in more than one way in each study"
constraints: Adapted from Palinkas et al. (2011a, b); the taxonomy is borrowed rather than newly validated in this article
target_learning_goals: Structure intentional integration of qualitative participatory data with research synthesis
examples: Complementarity: a scoping review of Tier 2 mathematics tutoring implementation strategies followed by school-team implementation blueprinting
key_sources: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5

article_title: Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods
citation: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5
title: Eight-stage synthesis process with participatory integration actions at each stage
description: The article maps community integration onto eight synthesis stages: planning and protocol development, literature search, study identification, coding and data extraction, data analysis, results interpretation, reporting, and dissemination. Each stage carries actionable steps and integration examples, e.g., at coding, "Coding expands beyond effect sizes to include implementation features, participation outcomes, equity relevant variables." The pattern transforms a review "from a retrospective aggregation of effects into a mechanism- and context-informed synthesis."
requirements: A synthesis protocol with planned participatory integration developed at stage 1, including registered goals and equity checkpoints
constraints: Depth of integration varies "depending on the research, practice, and policy goals of the synthesis"
target_learners: Researchers conducting systematic reviews or meta-analyses in education
target_learning_goals: Produce community-aligned, implementation-ready synthesis findings
examples: Table 3 maps a teacher professional development review onto the stages, with shareholders co-defining priorities and co-interpreting findings through structured sensemaking
key_sources: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5

article_title: Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework
citation: Klingenberg, S., Bosse, R., Mayer, R. E., & Makransky, G. (2024). Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09956-0
title: Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL) pathways for embodiment and cognitive load
description: CAMIL is described as "an evidence-based theoretical framework that explains how highly immersive learning environments, such as VR, can influence learning outcomes." It proposes six cognitive-affective pathways through which presence and agency influence knowledge acquisition and transfer. The article draws on two: a pathway in which "higher levels of presence and agency lead to more embodied learning experiences, which should result in better procedural learning outcomes," and a pathway in which immersion and interactivity raise extraneous cognitive load, which can impair learning and transfer. The study tests the embodiment pathway against the cognitive-load pathway.
requirements: Measures of presence, agency, embodiment, cognitive load, and learning outcomes to test the proposed pathways
constraints: The article notes existing evidence does not clarify how the goals of increased embodiment and reduced extraneous cognitive load are congruent
target_learners: learners in immersive virtual learning environments, here high school students
target_learning_goals: procedural learning outcomes and transfer in immersive VR
examples: The study's hypotheses H1-H5 were derived from CAMIL's embodiment and cognitive-load pathways
key_sources: Klingenberg, S., Bosse, R., Mayer, R. E., & Makransky, G. (2024). Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09956-0

article_title: Does Touching Real Objects Affect Learning?
citation: Magdalena Novak & Stephan Schwan. (2021). Does Touching Real Objects Affect Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09551-z
title: Cognitive-Affective Theory of Learning with Media (CATLM) as a framework for haptic learning
description: CATLM extends multimedia learning theory by adopting two-channel processing, limited working memory, and active construction, and supplementing them with assumptions about episodic memory, motivation and affect, metacognition, and learner differences. The article uses CATLM to organize empirical findings on haptics along situational interest, attention and information selection, working memory processing, long-term memory storage, and affect. It "also considers tactile, olfactory, and gustatory sensory input as additional information sources that may affect the learning process."
requirements: Learning with haptic input occurs in concert with other learning materials such as verbal explanations, texts, or illustrations
constraints: The article notes systematic research on affective effects of haptic exploration in educational contexts is virtually absent
target_learners: adult learners in informal and museum settings
target_learning_goals: multimodal integration of sensory input with verbal content
knowledge acquisition about real objects and artifacts
key_sources: Magdalena Novak & Stephan Schwan. (2021). Does Touching Real Objects Affect Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09551-z

article_title: Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions
citation: Tina Seufert. (2026). Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10119-6
title: CAMM framework and its proposed CAMMS extension adding social and somatic dimensions
description: CAMM is a conceptual taxonomy differentiating the cognitive, metacognitive, affective, and motivational components of SRL, aligned with current SRL models describing their interrelatedness. The paper argues the Moreno et al. study "introduces an additional dimension: social processes and dynamics in socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL)," suggesting expansion into a CAMMS model. An expanded CAMMS model may better reflect the embodied and distributed nature of regulation in complex learning environments, particularly collaborative or high-stakes settings.
requirements: Integrated approaches that examine the dynamic interplay of the four components over time, which the paper says would strengthen theoretical development.
constraints: The paper reports motivational and affective components are frequently neglected in reviewed studies, and Törmänen et al. focus on motivation without connecting it to other CAMM domains.
target_learners: Learners in collaborative and high-stakes learning environments studied with multimodal data
target_learning_goals: Understanding self-regulated learning as interrelated cognitive, metacognitive, affective, motivational, social, and somatic processes
examples: Moreno et al. modeled collective regulatory dynamics in medical simulation, which the paper treats as evidence for extending CAMM toward CAMMS.
key_sources: Tina Seufert. (2026). Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10119-6

article_title: The Effect of Playback Speed and Distractions on the Comprehension of Audio and Audio-Visual Materials
citation: Ashley Chen, Suchita E. Kumar, Rhea Varkhedi, Dillon H. Murphy. (2024). The Effect of Playback Speed and Distractions on the Comprehension of Audio and Audio-Visual Materials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09917-7
title: Advise learners not to exceed 2x playback speed, and pair accelerated narration with visual content to protect comprehension
description: The article recommends two practices for speeded lecture consumption: keep acceleration at or below 2x, and prefer audio-visual over audio-only formats when learning at faster speeds. The authors write "we still do not advise exceeding 2x speed since performance tends to quickly decline beyond that point," and conclude that viewing information in dual modalities "may thus be preferable when learning at faster speeds." The recommendation rests on their own experiments showing a near-significant 1x-to-2.5x decline and a significant multimedia advantage.
requirements: Pre-recorded audio or audio-visual lectures with user-controlled playback speed
Visual components (slides, text, or images) available to accompany narration
constraints: The speed caution is based on a 6% difference between 1x and 2.5x groups that only approached significance (ptukey = 0.051); distraction findings apply to passive, non-interactive notifications
target_learners: undergraduate and other students watching pre-recorded lectures, including MOOC learners
target_learning_goals: preserving comprehension while accelerating lecture playback
examples: Experiment 1 assigned listeners across 1x, 1.5x, 2x, and 2.5x speeds; Experiment 2's 2x audio-only group scored about 12% lower than the 1x audio-visual group
key_sources: Ashley Chen, Suchita E. Kumar, Rhea Varkhedi, Dillon H. Murphy. (2024). The Effect of Playback Speed and Distractions on the Comprehension of Audio and Audio-Visual Materials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09917-7

article_title: How Learners’ Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments
citation: Birgit Brucker, Georg Pardi, Fabienne Uehlin, Laura Moosmann, Martin Lachmair, Marc Halfmann, Peter Gerjets. (2024). How Learners' Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09895-w
title: Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL): presence and agency as key benefits of immersive VR
description: The article describes CAMIL, introduced by Makransky and Petersen (2021), as a model that "highlights presence and agency as the key benefits of immersive VR", because these aspects are facilitated by immersion, interactive control, and representational fidelity. CAMIL identifies six factors influencing learning that can be enhanced by presence and agency: interest, motivation, self-efficacy, embodiment, cognitive load, and self-regulation. The article uses CAMIL to frame why embodiment and agency in immersive VR may affect learning outcomes.
requirements: Presence and agency are assumed to be facilitated by immersion, interactive control, and representational fidelity
constraints: The article cites CAMIL as background theory; it does not test CAMIL itself in the reported studies
target_learning_goals: learning about dynamic movements with 3D-models
examples: The article invokes CAMIL alongside Dalgarno and Lee (2010) when motivating the comparison of interaction formats across Desktop-VR and immersive VR
key_sources: Birgit Brucker, Georg Pardi, Fabienne Uehlin, Laura Moosmann, Martin Lachmair, Marc Halfmann, Peter Gerjets. (2024). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09895-w

article_title: Self-regulated Learning in the Digitally Enhanced Science Classroom: Toward an Early Warning System
citation: Kubsch, M., Strauß, S., Grimm, A., Gombert, S., Drachsler, H., Neumann, K., & Rummel, N. (2025). Self-regulated Learning in the Digitally Enhanced Science Classroom: Toward an Early Warning System. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10011-9
title: CAMM framework of self-regulated learning processes in technology-enhanced classrooms
description: The article organizes self-regulated learning around four components—"cognition, affect, metacognition, and motivation"—referred to as CAMM processes, drawing on Winne and Perry's COPES model and cyclical SRL accounts. Learners set goals, monitor progress, and regulate their cognitions, affects, metacognition, and motivation; the cycle is recursive rather than strictly linear. The study operationalizes the cognitive, affective, and metacognitive dimensions (motivation data was unavailable) as data streams for predicting learning productivity in inquiry classrooms.
requirements: Data streams capturing cognitive, affective, and metacognitive processes must be collectable unobtrusively, validly, economically, and within legal and ethical bounds in real classrooms
constraints: The dataset did not include data on students' motivation during learning, so the motivational component was not modeled
target_learners: middle school students in grades 7 and 8
target_learning_goals: physics energy concept understanding
self-regulated learning during inquiry
examples: The study scored 36 workbook tasks into 107 cognitive scores per student and assessed epistemic emotions and metacognitive judgments after each of five unit parts
key_sources: Kubsch, M., Strauß, S., Grimm, A., Gombert, S., Drachsler, H., Neumann, K., & Rummel, N. (2025). Self-regulated Learning in the Digitally Enhanced Science Classroom: Toward an Early Warning System. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10011-9

article_title: The Cognitive-Affective-Social Theory of Learning in digital Environments (CASTLE)
citation: Sascha Schneider, Maik Beege, Steve Nebel, Lenka Schnaubert, Günter Daniel Rey. (2021). The Cognitive-Affective-Social Theory of Learning in digital Environments (CASTLE). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09626-5
title: CASTLE: social processes triggered by social cues mediate cognitive processing in individual digital learning
description: CASTLE extends the CTML and CATLM by adding a basic assumption: "Social processes triggered by social cues mediate the cognitive processing of information when learning with digital materials." Social cues activate social schemata in long-term memory, leading to enhanced (para-)social, motivational, emotional, and metacognitive processes that influence selection, organization, integration, and retrieval. The theory applies to individual learners interacting with digital material and excludes truly collaborative scenarios. It is illustrated in Fig. 1 of the article as an extension of the CATLM according to Moreno (2006).
requirements: Social cues must be present in the digital learning material to raise the probability of activating the social potential of human–technology interaction
constraints: The theory "only refer[s] to an instructional interaction that is designed as learning or retrieving task for one learner, therefore excluding truly collaborative learning scenarios involving direct interaction of more than one learner"
target_learners: individual learners with digital learning materials
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction and learning outcomes with digital multimedia materials
key_sources: Sascha Schneider, Maik Beege, Steve Nebel, Lenka Schnaubert, Günter Daniel Rey. (2021). The Cognitive-Affective-Social Theory of Learning in digital Environments (CASTLE). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09626-5

article_title: Relations between Teachers’ and Students’ Social-emotional Competence: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis
citation: Nguyen, T.-A., Hidajat, T., Zhou, T., Ma, T., Hoang, A., Poed, S., & Edwards, E. J. (2026). Relations between Teachers' and Students' Social-emotional Competence: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10218-4
title: CASEL five-domain framework of social-emotional competence as the review's organizing taxonomy
description: The review adopts the CASEL framework as its multidimensional conceptual model for classifying teachers' and students' SEC. The article states that "The CASEL framework conceptualises SEC as five distinct yet interrelated domains (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making; CASEL, 2020)." Constructs were coded as domain-specific or broad/mixed SEC based on definitions and measurement content rather than authors' labels, with interrater reliability of κ = 0.87 for teacher codes and κ = 0.85 for student codes. The framework enabled domain-specific meta-analytic models of teacher-student SEC associations.

citation: Geary David C., vanMarle Kristy, Chu Felicia W., Hoard Mary K., Nugent Lara. (2019). Predicting Age of Becoming a Cardinal Principle Knower. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000277
title: Carey's bootstrapping model of cardinality learning via analogical reasoning and enumeration
description: The article invokes Carey's (2004) bootstrapping model as a theoretical account of how children learn cardinal value. On this view, children learn the cardinality of the first few number words through "analogical reasoning and inductive inference to form a conceptual link between count words and the number of objects" in focus of visual attention. Enumeration of collections of three or four items is critical to initial insights about cardinal value, with diminishing returns beyond that. The study's findings on early and delayed CPK status are interpreted through this framework.

constraints: The ability to enumerate up to three or four is critical, with diminishing returns for enumeration of larger collections
target_learning_goals: understanding the cardinal value of number words
examples: The article interprets delayed CPKs' enumeration deficit (averaging up to about four) as consistent with Carey's proposal that enumerating three or four items is critical to initial cardinal value insights

citation: Youngwoo Bryan Yoon & Wi Hoon Jung. (2025). Impact of impulsivity on the relationship of the brain structures with school performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00344-z
title: Opposing caudate and cerebellar pathways to academic performance via impulsivity and self-regulation
description: The article proposes an explanatory account in which two brain structures influence school performance through distinct, opposing routes tied to impulsivity. A larger caudate nucleus volume is associated with "heightened sensitivity to immediate rewards, making students more susceptible to distractions and less able to defer gratification for long-term academic goals", raising impulsivity and lowering GPA. A larger cerebellum supports executive functions such as working memory and attention through extensive prefrontal connections, lowering impulsivity and supporting better GPA. Impulsivity serves as the key mediator connecting structural differences to academic outcomes.
requirements: Structural differences in the caudate and cerebellum are assumed to translate to functional differences in self-regulation and decision-making, an assumption the article flags as not directly tested.
constraints: The account rests on cross-sectional correlational data; causal relationships and temporal precedence were not established.
Interpretation assumes structure-function correspondence, which the article notes is complex and not always direct.

impulse control
examples: The mediation analyses showed left cerebellar GMV exerting a positive indirect effect on GPA through lower impulsivity, and right caudate GMV a negative indirect effect through higher impulsivity.
