description: Across its three domains the article varies abstraction by grade level: high school kinematics uses kinematic equations, middle school Marine Biology first expresses relations qualitatively then quantitatively, and Earth Science "represents the highest level of domain and computational abstraction". The authors state the DSML process "needs to systematically create abstractions that simplify the coral's behavioral processes ... but still retain the pertinent science knowledge". Designers should match blocks and simulation semantics to students' mathematical background.
requirements: Domain analysis must identify the target audience grade level, curricular objectives, and known difficulties before selecting the abstraction level
constraints: Over-constraining DSMLs risks taking away learning opportunities from students, per the authors; teacher input shaped abstraction choices (e.g., the Marine Biology teacher requested incremental treatment of rates)
target_learners: upper elementary, middle, and high school science students
target_learning_goals: modeling domain processes at a mathematically accessible level of abstraction
incremental development of quantitative reasoning such as rates
examples: The Earth Science DSML abstracts away rate and step-by-step execution: students update total rainfall by a fixed hourly amount times duration and apply an absorption limit per surface material.

citation: Sowmya Vajjala. (2016). Automated assessment of non-native learner essays: Investigating the role of linguistic features. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.00729
title: CAF-based six-group taxonomy of linguistic features for L2 essay scoring
description: The article organizes its automatically extractable features around the SLA notions of Complexity, Accuracy and Fluency (CAF), stating that "L2 writing proﬁciency in SLA research has been discussed in the context of the notions of Complexity, Accuracy and Fluency (CAF)". Concretely, "the features are classiﬁed into 6 groups: word level, parts of speech, syntactic characteristics, discourse properties, errors, and others", with lexical richness and syntactic complexity encoding complexity, error features encoding accuracy, and discourse coherence features encoding fluency. All representations are computed with open-source NLP tools (Stanford Parser/CoreNLP, LanguageTool).
requirements: Automatically extractable features computed from learner text using NLP preprocessing (tagging, parsing, coreference)
constraints: Prompt is used only as a categorical feature without prompt-specific vocabulary features
Ngram features were deliberately excluded as sparse, hard to interpret, and topic-specific
target_learners: non-native English speakers writing exam essays
target_learning_goals: second language writing proficiency assessment
examples: Feature extraction code was hosted at bitbucket for the paper; features were computed with Stanford Parser, Stanford CoreNLP, and LanguageTool

article_title: Care - Making the Affective Leap: More Than a Concerned Interest in a Learner's Cognitive Abilities
citation: Bridget Cooper. (2003). Care - Making the Affective Leap: More Than a Concerned Interest in a Learner's Cognitive Abilities. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.3-9. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197311
title: An elaborate definition of 'care' in intelligent learning systems that includes the affective aspects of learning
description: The commentary develops a definition of 'care' for intelligent learning systems that goes beyond a merely cognitive concern for learners. It explicitly 'elaborat[es] and extend[s] the definition to include recent research from neuroscience and education on the affective aspects of learning'. Care is treated as tied to profound empathy rather than as detached monitoring of cognitive ability, and the article argues that current systems fall short of this elaborate definition, which limits their capacity to reproduce care.
requirements: The definition must incorporate affective-aspect research from neuroscience and education, not only learner cognition
constraints: The commentary itself concludes existing systems 'tend to focus more heavily on the cognitive rather than the affective nature of care'
target_learning_goals: affective as well as cognitive dimensions of learning
examples: The commentary evaluates the systems described in the same journal issue against this extended definition of care and profound empathy

constraints: Without that definition, the article argues, a system's 'ability to reproduce it is limited'

title: Cap Cloze questions per key sentence at the three highest-probability candidate words to reduce manual evaluation burden
description: The article limits blank selection to the top-ranked words from the Naive Bayes probability list, because generating every candidate would make human evaluation prohibitive: "the number of Cloze questions generated from each key sentence is limited by choosing only the first three words from the Word_prd list." This keeps expert evaluation of usefulness tractable while retaining the highest-probability blanks.

constraints: The article presents this cap as an evaluation-burden trade-off; it does not report testing whether three blanks per sentence is optimal

citation: Okada, A., Sherborne, T., Panselinas, G., & Kolionis, G. (2024). AI in Education: A Cross-National Study of Open Schooling Using the CARE-KNOW-DO Framework for Sustainable Development Goals. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-3960164/v1
title: CARE-KNOW-DO framework for open schooling
description: The CARE-KNOW-DO framework integrates real-life problems into learning through a structured three-phase approach: students "engage (CARE) with signicant issues, understand (KNOW) them through curriculum-based knowledge, and take action (DO) through their insights into sustainable solutions". CARE fosters emotional intelligence and ethical understanding, KNOW develops critical thinking and problem-solving, and DO translates empathy and knowledge into practical action. The framework underpins the study's AI-based open schooling activities and its self-report instrument.

citation: Behera, A., Matthew, P., Keidel, A., Vangorp, P., Fang, H., & Canning, S. (2020). Associating Facial Expressions and Upper-Body Gestures with Learning Tasks for Enhancing Intelligent Tutoring Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00195-2
title: A data-driven cause-effect framework links learning context to nonverbal behavior via hidden affective states.
description: The authors propose a framework in which task difficulty (cause) influences hidden affective or mental states, which in turn produce observable nonverbal behaviors such as gestures and movements (effect). They "propose a data-driven cause-effect approach (difficulty → affect → gestures)" that capitalizes on digital learning environments and advances in computer vision. By varying the cause and measuring the effect, the relationship between learning context and behavior can be established without directly measuring affect, enabling inference of learner states from observable behavior.
requirements: Observable and measurable learning context (task type and difficulty) and observable gestures or body movements.
constraints: Hidden affective or mental states are not explicitly measured; the approach is speculative and context-specific.
target_learning_goals: inferring learner engagement and affective states from nonverbal behavior

article_title: Modelling and Optimizing Mathematics Learning in Children
citation: Käser, T., Busetto, A.G., Solenthaler, B., Baschera, G.-M., Kohn, J., Kucian, K., von Aster, M., Gross, M. (2013). Modelling and Optimizing Mathematics Learning in Children. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0003-7
title: Calcularis adaptive computer-based training system for numerical cognition
description: Calcularis is a computer-based training system for enhancing numerical cognition in children with developmental dyscalculia or mathematics difficulties, composed of multiple games in a hierarchical structure grouped into Part A (number representations and understanding, e.g. the LANDING game) and Part B (cognitive operations and procedures with numbers, e.g. the PLUS-MINUS game). The article states it provides "a fully adaptive learning environment" in which the student model and controlling algorithm optimize learning by providing an ideal level of cognitive stimulation. Its curriculum is structured on the natural, hierarchical development of number processing, with specific numerical stimulus design and training of operations and procedures.
requirements: Children trained with the program for a period of 6 weeks with a frequency of five times per week, during sessions of 20 min
constraints: The article notes existing computer-based approaches for children with mathematics difficulties lack user adaptation, which this system addresses; analyses included only children with at least 24 complete training sessions
target_learners: Children with developmental dyscalculia or difficulties in learning mathematics in grades 2–5 of public elementary schools
target_learning_goals: Number understanding across representations (verbal, Arabic, concrete, number line)
Automation of addition and subtraction procedures
examples: In the LANDING game children indicate the position of a displayed number on a number line by steering a falling cone with a joystick; in the PLUS-MINUS game children solve addition and subtraction tasks using blocks of tens and ones

article_title: The impact of high-immersion virtual reality on anatomy learning, enjoyment, presence, and cognitive load
citation: Kaplan-Rakowski, R., Norton, S., & Wojdynski, T. (2026). The impact of high-immersion virtual reality on anatomy learning, enjoyment, presence, and cognitive load. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10676-1
title: Cognitive affective model of immersive learning (CAMIL)
description: CAMIL is a theoretical framework describing affective and cognitive factors influencing learning within VR, with constructivist foundations. The article states that "CAMIL states that the instructional methods, specifically effective interaction and immersion, enrich the learning experience, thus increasing academic gains rather than the medium of VR." It explains how technological factors such as immersion, control dimensions, and representational fidelity impact presence and agency, subsequently influencing interest, motivation, self-efficacy, embodiment, cognitive load, and self-regulation. The study uses CAMIL to interpret why presence and enjoyment rose while learning fell.
requirements: Instructional methods must channel immersion toward productive cognitive activity for proximal affective benefits to translate into learning
constraints: The article notes that in the absence of carefully aligned instructional methods, proximal benefits may not translate into superior performance on factual knowledge tests
target_learning_goals: factual and spatial knowledge of anatomy and other STEM content
examples: The study used CAMIL to interpret that higher immersion and presence do not guarantee improved learning when the instructional goal is primarily factual and spatial recall of anatomical structures

article_title: From avoidance to ownership: preschool teachers learn to teach code—a case study
citation: Avia Ben-Ari, Tess Gavrielle Levinson, Jessica Blake-West, Marina Umaschi Bers, Rinat B. Rosenberg-Kima. (2025). From avoidance to ownership: preschool teachers learn to teach code—a case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10548-0
title: Coding as Another Language (CAL) framework: coding as a literacy acquired through five consecutive stages
description: Coding as Another Language (CAL; Bers, 2019) is a pedagogical approach that "recognizes coding as a form of literacy—as a language like any other", bridging computer science powerful ideas with language arts via the ScratchJr block platform. It stems from three theoretical frameworks: the Curriculum Research Framework, Constructionism, and Positive Technological Development. Bers proposes "five consecutive coding stages"—Emergent, Coding and Decoding, Fluency, New Knowledge, and Purposefulness—corresponding to the accumulative consolidation of traditional literacy, with the Fluency stage marking the shift from learning to read/write/code to using these skills for learning.
requirements: Implementation uses the ScratchJr block-programming platform and the CAL curriculum's 24 lessons combining unplugged and screen-based activities
constraints: The curriculum was originally designed for the U.S. context and aligned to American educational standards, requiring cultural adjustments when implemented outside the U.S.
target_learners: preschool and kindergarten children, including non-writing children
target_learning_goals: basic coding concepts and computational thinking
socio-emotional aspects of learning
creative self-expression
examples: In this study the CAL-ScratchJr curriculum consisted of 45-min long 24 sessions including songs, games, scaffolded coding instruction, exploration and creation, read-aloud story time, and literacy activities, translated into Hebrew

title: CADDIE: Cyclic ADDIE model of instructional design
description: The author proposes CADDIE (Cyclic ADDIE), 'a simplification of Tennyson's 4th generation ISD model that emphasizes the notion that design is essentially a dynamic and iterative process that sometime starts in the middle'. The C stands for cyclic, with 'cycles within a particular aspect of instructional design as well as between various aspects'. The designer is analogous to a golf caddie whose main task is to help the learner have a successful experience.

article_title: Beyond boundaries: leveraging technology for differentiated professional development with lesson study video club
citation: Yuzhu Xia, Adria Patthoff, Liana Balloffet, Marco A. Bravo, Kip Téllez. (2025). Beyond boundaries: leveraging technology for differentiated professional development with lesson study video club. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10524-8
title: Career-span differentiation framework for teacher PD (three experience categories)
description: The study reframes the expert/novice binary into an extended learning progression, grouping teachers by "less than five years, five to ten years, and over ten years" of experience and treating experience differences as assets rather than deficits. Grounded in situated perspectives of learning and communities of practice (Lave & Wenger), it holds that teacher learning unfolds in iterative cycles across the career continuum, so a single PD initiative should differentiate support by career stage. The framework motivated the study's second research question on whether perceived growth differs by career experience group.
requirements: PD structures that center the spectrum of teachers' years of experience and specialized contexts
constraints: The trajectory of teacher learning is recognized as non-linear (Feiman-Nemser)
target_learners: novice, mid-career, and veteran in-service teachers in specialized contexts such as dual language programs
target_learning_goals: differentiated professional growth across career stages
examples: The authors initially framed analysis around an expert/novice distinction and refined it into the three-category career-span grouping used in the survey analysis.

article_title: Look at me! Can a pedagogical agent facilitate orientation and support learning in VR?
citation: Daniela Decker, Martin Merkt. (2025). Look at me! Can a pedagogical agent facilitate orientation and support learning in VR? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10531-9
title: Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL)
description: CAMIL is an explanatory framework for learning in immersive VR, built in part on Cognitive Load Theory's assumption of limited working-memory capacity. The article states that "CAMIL extends this perspective by identifying three key technical factors that shape learning in VR: immersion, control, and representational fidelity". All three factors influence presence, the feeling of being there, which the article treats as a prerequisite for learning in VR; only control factors determine agency. The study uses CAMIL to motivate expectations that cueing could raise presence and that reduced representational fidelity from non-diegetic cues could lower it.
requirements: Presence and agency as psychological prerequisites for learning in VR
constraints: The article notes CAMIL suggests highly immersive VR may be particularly beneficial for procedural knowledge, while this study tested declarative memory
target_learners: adult learners in immersive VR environments
target_learning_goals: declarative factual knowledge
spatial representation of a learning environment
examples: The experiment operationalized CAMIL's factors by comparing a diegetic-style light cue and a human-like agent cue against no cueing in a virtual workshop
key_sources: Daniela Decker, Martin Merkt. (2025). Look at me! Can a pedagogical agent facilitate orientation and support learning in VR? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10531-9

article_title: Look at me! Can a pedagogical agent facilitate orientation and support learning in VR?
citation: Daniela Decker, Martin Merkt. (2025). Look at me! Can a pedagogical agent facilitate orientation and support learning in VR? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10531-9
title: Carefully calibrate a pedagogical agent's level of realism and pre-test its design elements and animations before deployment
description: Because the highly embodied pedagogical agent reduced physical and self-presence in the VR experiment, the article recommends calibrating agent realism carefully. The authors state that "the pedagogical agent reduced physical and self-presence, underscoring the importance of carefully calibrating its level of realism. Pre-testing both the design elements and their animations is therefore advisable." They suggest possible causes include an uncanny valley effect and disruptive repositioning between tasks, and propose more fluid repositioning, such as the agent walking to its new position, in future designs.
requirements: Pre-testing of agent design elements and animations before use
constraints: The agent's negative presence effects were observed in a short (~5 minute) passive-listening laboratory setting
target_learners: adult learners in immersive VR learning environments
target_learning_goals: maintaining presence during VR learning
examples: The agent was designed with Character Creator 3.3 and iClone 7.8, featured conversational gestures, idle positions, breathing movements, and facial expressions, and was pilot-tested for credibility

article_title: Impact of the provision of PowerPoint slides on learning
citation: Samuel P. León, Inmaculada García-Martínez. (2021). Impact of the provision of PowerPoint slides on learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104283
title: Do not assume that providing teacher slides before class benefits learning; provision can harm performance and attendance
description: The article's findings caution against routine pre-class distribution of teacher-made slides. In its within-subject study, "access to slides developed by teachers had a negative impact on student performance and attendance to classes", and the authors suggest the dilemma of whether to provide slides may require a change of focus toward the material itself and students' own note-making.

target_learning_goals: subject-matter exam performance
class attendance
examples: Slides were concise outlines created by the teacher; exam questions were designed so correct responses could not be literally extracted from any of the slides.

citation: Xining Wang, Gareth W. Young, Adéla Plechatá, Conor Mc Guckin, Guido Makransky. (2023). Utilizing virtual reality to assist social competence education and social support for children from under-represented backgrounds. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104815

The article also invokes the immersion principle of multimedia learning, under which people "learn better with VR than with standard media when immersive lessons are designed according to instructional design principles", and Experiential Learning Theory, situating VR exploration as active experimentation.

article_title: Mood-affect congruency. Exploring the relation between learners’ mood and the affective charge of educational videos
citation: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001
title: CASTLM and ICALM frame social and affective processes as providing cognitive resources for learning
description: The thesis presents the cognitive-affective-social theory of learning with media (CASTLM; Schneider, Beege, Nebel, & Rey, 2018b) and the Integrated Cognitive Affective Model of Learning with Multimedia (ICALM; Plass & Kaplan, 2016) as frameworks countering purely cognitive accounts. "According to CASTLM and aCLT, social entities in instructional videos can foster learning." ICALM "postulates a solid connection between emotions and cognition," and holds "emotional experiences during learning influence the learner's ability to self-regulate." These frameworks motivate the thesis's experimental manipulation of social and affective cues.

target_learning_goals: cognitive activation and resource allocation during multimedia learning

article_title: Detecting and preventing “multiple-account” cheating in massive open online courses
citation: Northcutt, C. G., Ho, A. D., & Chuang, I. L. (2015). Detecting and Preventing “Multiple-Account” Cheating in Massive Open Online Courses. https://doi.org/10.1145/2724660.2728663
title: CAMEO: a MOOC cheating strategy using harvester and master accounts
description: CAMEO (Copying Answers using Multiple Existences Online) is a cheating strategy in which a user creates at least two accounts: "harvester" accounts used to acquire correct answers by guessing at test answers and then accessing instructor-provided solutions via a "Show Answer" button, and "master" accounts used to submit these solutions as correct test answers. The strategy is internally sufficient (copying from oneself), exploitable in asynchronous courses for every question, and unrestricted in open-admission settings, making it a course-level threat to certificate validity.
requirements: At least two accounts in a MOOC with a "show answer" option available after submission
constraints: Unique to MOOC-style platforms with immediate solution feedback and open enrollment
target_learning_goals: Course certification of proficiency
examples: The authors illustrate two prototypical CAMEO users, each with two accounts, alternating or clustering harvest-and-submit sequences (Fig. 1).
key_sources: Northcutt, C. G., Ho, A. D., & Chuang, I. L. (2015). Detecting and Preventing “Multiple-Account” Cheating in Massive Open Online Courses. https://doi.org/10.1145/2724660.2728663

article_title: Detecting and preventing “multiple-account” cheating in massive open online courses
citation: Northcutt, C. G., Ho, A. D., & Chuang, I. L. (2015). Detecting and Preventing “Multiple-Account” Cheating in Massive Open Online Courses. https://doi.org/10.1145/2724660.2728663
title: Five-filter CAMEO detection algorithm using clickstream timestamp distributions
description: A detection algorithm that considers all ordered pairs of accounts as candidate harvester–master pairs and applies five conjunctive filters: a Bayesian criterion requiring 90% confidence that the proportion of positive Δt values exceeds 0.9; a 90th-percentile Δt cutoff of 5 minutes; certified master with uncertified harvester; shared IP address via transitive closure of modal IPs and usernames; and exclusion of groups with 10 or more accounts sharing a modal IP. The algorithm "is comprised of five filters with highly conservative cutoffs intended to reduce false positives."
requirements: Clickstream server logs recording "show answer" clicks and correct-answer submissions with timestamps
constraints: Provides a lower-bound estimate; the authors concede no ground-truth validation of individual classifications
target_learning_goals: Valid certification of course completion
examples: Filter 2's 5-minute cutoff sits at an "elbow" in the cumulative distribution of identified CAMEO users (Fig. 3).
key_sources: Northcutt, C. G., Ho, A. D., & Chuang, I. L. (2015). Detecting and Preventing “Multiple-Account” Cheating in Massive Open Online Courses. https://doi.org/10.1145/2724660.2728663

article_title: Immersive procedural training in virtual reality: A systematic literature review
citation: Jongbloed, J., Chaker, R., & Lavoué, E. (2024). Immersive procedural training in virtual reality: A systematic literature review. Computers & Education, 221, 105124. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105124
title: Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL)
description: CAMIL is an adaptation of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning specifically for immersive VR, proposed by Makransky and Petersen (2021) and used in this review as a lens for understanding learning in IVR. The review describes how "CAMIL illustrates how the technological affordances of immersion, control, and representational fidelity result in both a sense of presence and agency that in turn influences affective and cognitive factors that lead to learning in IVR". It positions presence and agency as the central affordances distinguishing IVR from less immersive media.
requirements: Technological affordances of immersion, control, and representational fidelity in the IVR environment
target_learners: Adults in professional procedural training (e.g., medical, industrial, emergency-response trainees)
target_learning_goals: Procedural knowledge and skill acquisition

article_title: Cartoons beyond clipart: A computer tool for storyboarding and storywriting
citation: M. Madden, P.W.H. Chung and C.W. Dawson. (2007). Cartoon beyond clipart: a computer tool for storyboarding and storywriting. Loughborough University. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Prototype storyboarding and storywriting software with enhanced-frontal-orientation character posing
description: A Java prototype computer tool for story visualisation prior to storywriting, implementing an "enhanced-frontal-orientation" approach in which 2D vector characters are mapped to a 3D skeleton so they can be posed and warped. Users create pictures, place them on stage view screens, and enter text for each picture. The tool was trialled with Year 5 children (ages 9-10) in a school-based study.
requirements: Requires pre-supplied characters, as learners could not create their own posable characters in the prototype
constraints: Exhibits the 'constant background effect' where backgrounds are unaffected by zoom, translation or tilt
target_learning_goals: Narrative writing
Visual storytelling
Point-of-view story writing

article_title: The impact of an iPad-supported annotation and sharing technology on university students' learning
citation: Wakefield, J., Frawley, J. K., Tyler, J., & Dyson, L. E. (2018). The impact of an iPad-supported annotation and sharing technology on university students’ learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.013
title: Exercise caution in how instructor tablet use affects the classroom environment and what students learn
description: The article recommends that educators critically examine how tablet technology is implemented, especially in equation-centred subjects. The authors suggest that instructors "may decide to put the tablet aside and discuss the extended responses" after facilitating initial participation, and that care is needed to avoid letting the tablet dominate class time. This principle arises directly from the finding that tablet use benefited procedural learning at the expense of theoretical learning.
requirements: Instructors must monitor which types of questions and learning activities the tablet-supported interaction favours
constraints: The finding arises in a compulsory introductory first-year subject where student motivation and self-regulation may be low
target_learning_goals: procedural and theoretical disciplinary knowledge
key_sources: Wakefield, J., Frawley, J. K., Tyler, J., & Dyson, L. E. (2018). The impact of an iPad-supported annotation and sharing technology on university students’ learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.013

article_title: Validation status of definitive airway management simulators: a systematic review.
citation: McCarthy Roisin, Maher Liam, O'Dea Angela. (2026). Validation status of definitive airway management simulators: a systematic review. BJA: British Journal of Anaesthesia. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2026.01.027
title: Educators should exercise caution when interpreting simulator performance as evidence of clinical competence, and validation evidence should guide simulator selection
description: Because most airway simulators lack robust validation—particularly predictive validity linking simulator performance to clinical outcomes—the review recommends that educators and training institutions treat simulator performance cautiously and let validation evidence drive selection and endorsement of simulators for teaching and assessment. It further urges development of "a unified, transparent validation framework, supported by professional and academic consensus" to improve simulator design, comparability, and clinical relevance.
requirements: Validation evidence should be available and consulted when selecting or endorsing simulators for teaching and assessment
constraints: Current evidence base is limited: most studies were small, cross-sectional, underpowered, with short follow-up intervals restricting conclusions about durable skill transfer
target_learning_goals: tracheal intubation
fibreoptic intubation
front-of-neck access procedures
examples: The review found studies comparing airway devices on static manikin models drew clinical conclusions without verifying anatomical accuracy or transferability, motivating the caution recommendation
key_sources: McCarthy Roisin, Maher Liam, O'Dea Angela. (2026). Validation status of definitive airway management simulators: a systematic review. BJA: British Journal of Anaesthesia. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2026.01.027

article_title: Primary care physicians' knowledge and confidence in providing cancer survivorship care: a systematic review.
citation: Vos Julien A. M., Wollersheim Barbara M., Cooke Adelaide, Ee Carolyn, Chan Raymond J., Nekhlyudov Larissa. (2023). Primary care physicians’ knowledge and confidence in providing cancer survivorship care: a systematic review. Journal of Cancer Survivorship. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11764-023-01397-y
title: Nekhlyudov cancer survivorship care domains framework for characterizing PCP knowledge and confidence
description: The review organizes its outcomes using the five domains of quality cancer survivorship care proposed by Nekhlyudov et al.: prevention and surveillance for recurrences and new cancers; surveillance and management of physical effects; surveillance and management of psychosocial effects; surveillance and management of chronic medical conditions; and health promotion and disease prevention. The review states that quantitative outcomes "were analyzed using the framework method and mapped to the different domains of cancer survivorship care". Mapping outcomes to these domains reveals that confidence and knowledge vary across care domains, with gaps concentrated in physical effects and recurrence surveillance.
requirements: Outcomes must be classifiable into the five survivorship care domains to apply the mapping method
constraints: The review notes it did not address care coordination and communication, a sixth component of the quality framework
target_learners: Primary care physicians (PCPs, GPs, family physicians) providing cancer survivorship care
target_learning_goals: Knowledge and confidence in providing cancer survivorship care across its domains
examples: The review mapped quantitative outcomes from 33 papers to the domains and found most papers described physical effects (n = 19), psychosocial effects (n = 12), and recurrence surveillance (n = 14)
key_sources: Vos Julien A. M., Wollersheim Barbara M., Cooke Adelaide, Ee Carolyn, Chan Raymond J., Nekhlyudov Larissa. (2023). Primary care physicians’ knowledge and confidence in providing cancer survivorship care: a systematic review. Journal of Cancer Survivorship. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11764-023-01397-y

article_title: Comparison of the Informed Health Choices Key Concepts Framework to other frameworks relevant to teaching and learning how to think critically about health claims and choices: a systematic review.
citation: Oxman Andrew D., García Laura Martínez. (2020). Comparison of the Informed Health Choices Key Concepts Framework to other frameworks relevant to teaching and learning how to think critically about health claims and choices: a systematic review. F1000Research 9:164. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.21858.1
title: Catalogue of 22 included frameworks relevant to teaching critical thinking about claims, comparisons, and choices
description: This element is the set of 22 frameworks the systematic review included, spanning critical thinking (e.g. Ennis's taxonomy, Paul's model, Halpern's list, Baron's model of the good thinker), logic and argumentation (logical fallacies, Allen's taxonomy, the evidence based reasoning framework), cognition (cognitive biases, metacognitive frameworks, epistemological models, the AIR model), scientific thinking (PISA scientific literacy, the K-12 science education framework, systems thinking, a model for scientific thinking), and evidence-based health care (health literacy, EBP core competencies, GRADE, Bradford-Hill criteria, critical appraisal, the Cochrane risk of bias tool, and the Catalogue of biases). The review records each framework's purpose, background, and definitions of its core term.
requirements: Each included framework had to have a description of its purpose, a list of its elements, and definitions of key terms
constraints: Frameworks that were modifications of another framework were considered together with the framework that had been modified; 13 assessed frameworks were excluded for not providing a framework for thinking critically about claims, comparisons or choices
target_learning_goals: critical thinking about treatment claims
evaluation of evidence supporting claims
informed choices
examples: Table 6 lists each framework with who developed it, when, its purpose, and background; Table 7 gives the definition of the core term for each included framework

article_title: Is project-based learning effective among kindergarten and elementary students? A systematic review.
citation: Ferrero Marta, Vadillo Miguel A., León Samuel P. (2021). Is project-based learning effective among kindergarten and elementary students? A systematic review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249627
title: Do not assume PjBL results from secondary and higher education transfer directly to kindergarten and primary students without monitoring
description: The review argues that because of considerable differences between senior and novice learners, what is effective in secondary or postsecondary settings may not transfer directly to younger students. It states that "it should not be assumed that novice learners possess the advanced self-regulation skills, prior knowledge, or group work skills" necessary for PjBL, so any attempt to translate this literature to kindergarten and primary students should be properly monitored.
requirements: Any attempt to translate the main results and conclusions of this literature to kindergarten and primary students should be properly monitored
constraints: The studies included in the review do not address how different learning profiles affect PjBL effectiveness, since all populations were students without special needs
target_learning_goals: content knowledge acquisition
examples: The review examined eleven studies with kindergarten to grade 6 students and found mixed results and low methodological quality, supporting caution about firm effectiveness claims
key_sources: Ferrero Marta, Vadillo Miguel A., León Samuel P. (2021). Is project-based learning effective among kindergarten and elementary students? A systematic review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249627

article_title: Using conversation analysis to inform role play and simulated interaction in communications skills training for healthcare professionals: identifying avenues for further development through a scoping review.
citation: Pilnick Alison, Trusson Diane, Beeke Suzanne, O'Brien Rebecca, Goldberg Sarah, Harwood Rowan H. (2018). Using conversation analysis to inform role play and simulated interaction in communications skills training for healthcare professionals: identifying avenues for further development through a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1381-1
title: Conversation Analytic Role-play Method (CARM)
description: CARM is a training method that uses videos of real-life anonymised interactions instead of simulated role play. It "presents both transcribed and recorded conversations in real time", stopping the recording at chosen points so trainees can discuss whether the talk is helping or impeding preferred outcomes. The review presents CARM as a CA-based alternative to role play that overcomes some inauthenticity but removes real-time thinking, feedback on the simulation, and observing others approach the same task.
requirements: Recorded, anonymised naturally-occurring interactions from the relevant institutional setting
A facilitator able to stop recordings at discussion points
constraints: Removes the need to think on one's feet in real time, feedback on the simulation, and watching others approach the same task
Possible uneven contribution across group members
Used extensively in mediation; applicability elsewhere is argued, not demonstrated
target_learning_goals: Communication skills in institutional interactions
Recognising how word choice, pauses and silences affect interaction outcomes
examples: The review describes a one-day neurology training program 'inspired by' CARM that taught senior trainees to open consultations with a neutral enquiry and tolerate silences
key_sources: Pilnick Alison, Trusson Diane, Beeke Suzanne, O'Brien Rebecca, Goldberg Sarah, Harwood Rowan H. (2018). Using conversation analysis to inform role play and simulated interaction in communications skills training for healthcare professionals: identifying avenues for further development through a scoping review. article_title: Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review.
citation: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/
title: The Canadian Safety Competencies Framework's six domains as the content scope for patient safety assessment
description: The review adopts the Canadian Safety Competencies Framework, finalised by the Canadian Patient Safety Institute in 2008, as the content scope for selecting and analysing assessment tools. The framework "consists of six core competency domains: 1. Contributing to a culture of patient safety. 2. Working in teams for patient safety. 3. Communicating effectively for patient safety. 4. Managing safety risks. 5. Optimising human and environmental factors. 6. Recognising, responding to, and disclosing adverse events". Articles were included only if their assessment content covered these domains.
requirements: Assessment content must cover the domains of the Canadian Safety Competencies Framework.
constraints: The review excluded procedural or technical skills, medication safety skills, general clinical skills, diagnostic skills, and open disclosure skills.
target_learners: Physicians, residents, medical students, nurses, and nursing students in hospital settings
target_learning_goals: The six patient safety competency domains of the Canadian Safety Competencies Framework
examples: The review mapped each of the 34 tools to the six domains, finding 'managing safety risks' assessed by 25 tools and 'optimising human and environmental factors' by only four.
key_sources: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/

article_title: Development of Skills for Pharmacy Students in Evaluating Randomized Controlled Trials Using CASP Checklist
citation: Nawanopparatsakul, S., Watana, S., Taesotikul, T., Phuagphong, P., & Chinpaisal, C. (2024). Development of Skills for Pharmacy Students in Evaluating Randomized Controlled Trials Using CASP Checklist. Proceedings of ICRES 2024 -- International Conference on Research in Education and Science. https://www.icres.net
title: Four-stage CASP-based sequence: lecture with worked examples, individual RCT analysis, instructor feedback, then collaborative group evaluation
description: A lesson/unit-level instructional pattern for teaching critical appraisal of clinical trials. The article's abstract describes "four stages: 1) introducing principles and providing example RCT evaluations, 2) assigning individual students the RCT analysis tasks, 3) instructor feedback, and 4) collaborative group assignments for new drug evaluations using CASP." Performance was evaluated with a rubric across individual and group work, and the sequence culminates in teamwork mirroring real-world pharmacy evaluation scenarios.
requirements: Instructors provide constructive feedback on individual work before group tasks
A scoring rubric with defined criteria is devised in the preparation phase
Students re-evaluate new clinical studies individually after feedback
constraints: The article notes that in larger classrooms, instructors would need feedback mechanisms tailored to the class size
target_learning_goals: evaluating randomized controlled trials
critical thinking
problem-solving
applying evidence in medication evaluation
examples: Students were assigned individual RCT assessment tasks, received faculty feedback, re-evaluated new clinical studies with CASP, then collaborated in small teams to present new medications and their assessments
key_sources: Nawanopparatsakul, S., Watana, S., Taesotikul, T., Phuagphong, P., & Chinpaisal, C. (2024). article_title: Card Games and Algebra Tic Tacmatics on Achievement of Junior Secondary II Students in Algebraic Expressions
citation: Okpube Nnaemeka Michael, Anugwo M. N. (2016). Card Games and Algebra Tic Tacmatics on Achievement of Junior Secondary II Students in Algebraic Expressions. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE). http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE
title: Card games and algebra tic-tacmatics for teaching algebraic expressions
description: Card games suitable for teaching algebraic expressions and linear equations, plus algebra tic-tacmatics for algebraic expansions, were developed by the researchers with an accompanying lesson plan and validated by three mathematics specialists and two measurement and evaluation experts. Mathematical games are described as "an enjoyable social activity with goals, rules, and regulational objectives" in which two or more students work together and the winner, loser and spectators all learn the concept being practiced. The package was taught over six weeks in four 40-minute contacts per week.
requirements: Teachers trained by the researchers to control teacher quality
Validated instructional materials and lesson plan
constraints: Used with JS2 intact classes in public secondary schools in Onicha Local Government Area, Ebonyi State, Nigeria
target_learning_goals: Algebraic expressions and related JS2 algebra topics
examples: Experimental group (136 students) taught with games while the control group (104 students) was taught the same units by conventional lecture method

article_title: The Effect of Computer-Assisted Language Learning on Reading Comprehension in an Iranian EFL Context
citation: Mahnaz Saeidi & Mahsa Yusefi. (2012). The Effect of Computer-Assisted Language Learning on Reading Comprehension in an Iranian EFL Context. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. Research-publishing.net. https://research-publishing.net
title: Three multimedia software packages used as the CALL reading treatment (Rosetta Stone, VOA Special English, Learn to Speak English)
description: The experimental treatment consisted of three types of software used for reading instruction. Rosetta Stone presents "texts with pictures" with immediate feedback; VOA Special English provides 40 texts that the software reads aloud, with a Babylon dictionary giving word meanings "just by one left click"; Learn to Speak English presents texts "with motion pictures which can affect comprehension positively". The control group read the same materials on printed pages.
requirements: A computer environment in which learners can read the same texts on screen with multimedia support rather than on printed pages
constraints: The comparison held course aim, scope and teacher constant over ten sessions in an Iranian EFL institute setting
target_learners: Iranian female intermediate EFL learners aged 18-25
target_learning_goals: Second/foreign language reading comprehension
examples: The experimental group read the same texts as the control group from the computer screen using the three software packages across ten treatment sessions
key_sources: Mahnaz Saeidi & Mahsa Yusefi. (2012). The Effect of Computer-Assisted Language Learning on Reading Comprehension in an Iranian EFL Context. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. Research-publishing.net. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED574943

article_title: The Effect of Computer-Assisted Language Learning on Reading Comprehension in an Iranian EFL Context
citation: Mahnaz Saeidi & Mahsa Yusefi. (2012). The Effect of Computer-Assisted Language Learning on Reading Comprehension in an Iranian EFL Context. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. Research-publishing.net. https://research-publishing.net
title: Interactivity account: CALL's advantage in reading comprehension stems from deeper, more interactive reader-text processing
description: The authors propose an explanatory account for why computer-assisted reading instruction outperformed print: the interactive nature of CALL makes language learning more interesting and may encourage readers "to process the meaning of the text more deeply and more actively". On this view the computer "permits deeper and more interactive information between the reader and the text", providing opportunities for managing readers' interaction with text during independent reading.
requirements: Computerized texts that provide reading support, as in the software used in this study
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretation of one quasi-experiment, not a tested mechanism
target_learners: Intermediate EFL learners in foreign language institutes
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension in a second/foreign language
examples: The authors interpret their post-test difference as evidence that interactive computer software encouraged deeper meaning processing

article_title: Efficacy of an Online Resource for Teaching Interpersonal Problem Solving Skills to Women Graduate Students in Engineering
citation: Jennifer M. Bekki, Bianca L. Bernstein, Natalie Fabert, Natalie Gildar, and Amy Way. (2014). Efficacy of an Online Resource for Teaching Interpersonal Problem Solving Skills to Women Graduate Students in Engineering. Advances in Engineering Education. https://careerwise.asu.edu
title: CareerWISE online learning environment for women STEM doctoral students
description: CareerWISE is an online learning environment grounded in research on personal resilience and coping, self-efficacy and social-cognitive career theories, and problem-solving processes and cognitive-behavioral interventions. It offers skill building around four areas of common concern: "handling difficult interactions with an advisor, juggling academic and personal commitments, navigating a climate that can be unfriendly to women and managing delays and setbacks". The program contains "more than 250 content pieces", including over 160 video clips of 3 to 8 minutes and over 50 informational and instructional modules, self-tests, practice exercises, and links to professional resources.
requirements: Learners interact with the online environment; in the RCT participants were asked to spend at least five hours exploring it in an unconstrained manner during a two-week time frame.
constraints: The examples included in the online program are intentionally designed to appeal to female and research-active doctoral students in STEM fields; additional research would be required to determine whether other communities find the content useful.
target_learners: Women in doctoral programs in the physical sciences and engineering
target_learning_goals: Interpersonal problem solving skills
Personal resilience skills
examples: In the RCT, 64 treatment participants explored the environment unconstrained for a mean of 5.39 hours before completing the APSS.
key_sources: Jennifer M. Bekki, Bianca L. Bernstein, Natalie Fabert, Natalie Gildar, and Amy Way. (2014). Efficacy of an Online Resource for Teaching Interpersonal Problem Solving Skills to Women Graduate Students in Engineering. Advances in Engineering Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1076131

article_title: Efficacy of an Online Resource for Teaching Interpersonal Problem Solving Skills to Women Graduate Students in Engineering
citation: Jennifer M. Bekki, Bianca L. Bernstein, Natalie Fabert, Natalie Gildar, and Amy Way. (2014). Efficacy of an Online Resource for Teaching Interpersonal Problem Solving Skills to Women Graduate Students in Engineering. Advances in Engineering Education. https://careerwise.asu.edu
title: CareerWISE four-step interpersonal problem solving model
description: The CareerWISE learning environment teaches a specific model for managing interpersonal problems, shown in Table 1, grounded in problem-solving processes and cognitive-behavioral interventions. The model comprises four steps: "Step 1: Assess the problem", "Step 2: Specify the outcome you want", "Step 3: Strategize", and "Step 4: Execute and evaluate", each with sub-steps such as listing the facts, understanding the context, setting a concrete outcome, weighing strategies, and cycling back to Step 1 if the outcome was not achieved. The environment focuses on developing skills such as considering others' perspectives, managing emotional responses, and appropriately identifying stakeholders needed to apply the model to interpersonal situations.
requirements: Learners must be able to describe and apply the steps and sub-steps; the APSS rubrics were created based on the CareerWISE learning objectives associated with this model.
constraints: There is only a very small amount of specific content on the online program related to Step 4 of the problem solving model, so Step 4 responses were not scored.
target_learning_goals: Applying a problem-solving model to interpersonal situations in graduate school
examples: Table 1 pairs each step with example CareerWISE content, such as a skill module on recognizing stress triggers and video clips on persuading an advisor.

article_title: The Effect of Using Cartoons on Developing Omani Grade 4 Students' Awareness of Water Issues and Their Attitudes towards Using Them in Teaching Social Studies
citation: Al-Rabaani, A. H., & Al-AAmri, I. H. (2017). The Effect of Using Cartoons on Developing Omani Grade 4 Students’ Awareness of Water Issues and their Attitudes towards Using them in Teaching Social Studies. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 8(1), 35-46. https://www.jsser.org
title: Cartoon-based lesson routine: read, interpret, debate, and draw cartoons about a local issue
description: The experimental treatment followed a recurring lesson pattern: students worked in subgroups of 5-6 to read cartoons, explain what they understood, express views on the presented issue, consider why it was presented that way, voice agreement or disagreement with the artist, and relate the issue to their local area. Students then "were asked to draw their own cartoons about water issue", with an award for the best cartoon. This combines interpretation, argumentation and creative production around a controversial topic.

constraints: Applied in a three-week unit on water in the Grade 4 social studies textbook in one Omani school
target_learning_goals: Awareness of water issues
Critical thinking about a controversial issue
Expressing and debating views
examples: Students drew cartoons reflecting local water behavior such as protection of water streams from pollution and rational use of water in irrigation at home or farms.

citation: Al-Rabaani, A. H., & Al-AAmri, I. H. (2017). The Effect of Using Cartoons on Developing Omani Grade 4 Students’ Awareness of Water Issues and their Attitudes towards Using them in Teaching Social Studies. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 8(1), 35-46. https://www.jsser.org

description: The article argues that cartoons suit contested topics because their humor, caricature, irony and symbols attract attention and push students to evaluate the artist's view and form their own. The researchers chose cartoons for water awareness because "water issue is controversial" and cartoons are "the best tool to present this controversial issue that allow students to argue and try to come up with a rational view." requirements: Students need preliminary instruction in reading and drawing cartoons before using them in subject lessons
constraints: Evidence comes from one school, one grade, and one three-week water unit in Oman
target_learning_goals: Awareness of controversial environmental issues
Critical evaluation of viewpoints
examples: The experimental group read, discussed and drew cartoons about water shortage, desalination and water behavior during the water unit.

article_title: The Effects of a Cross-Age Peer Mentoring Program on School Connectedness with Rural Populations
citation: Kraus, S. E. C., & Cleveland, R. E. (2016). The Effects of a Cross-age Peer Mentoring Program on School Connectedness with Rural Populations. Georgia School Counselor Association Journal.
title: Weekly structured cross-age mentoring session format: icebreaker, connectedness lesson, snack, and group activity over nine weeks
description: The modified CAMP intervention ran once weekly for nine weeks during the middle school exploratory period, facilitated by school counselors. "Weekly classroom activities included an icebreaker, a school connectedness lesson, snack, and a group activity," with mentors and mentees working in pairs and then joining a larger group. Mentors received training and followed a structured list of mentoring activities at each meeting, with activities addressing connectedness to school, teachers, peers, culturally different peers, reading, self in the future, attendance, behavior, and grades.
requirements: Trained high-school peer mentors following a structured activity list
A scheduled recurring period (here the exploratory period) and counselor facilitation
constraints: Nine-week duration is shorter than the 18-week to full-academic-year interventions the authors report in the literature; logistical disruptions (math remediation, athletics) reduced participation
target_learning_goals: school connectedness
student-school belonging

article_title: CAI in Learning Voice in English Grammar among Eighth Standard Students--An Experimental Study
citation: R. Ramesh & B. Sumathi. (2010). CAI in Learning Voice in English Grammar among Eighth Standard Students – An Experimental Study. li-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology.
title: Macromedia Flash 8 tutorial-mode CAI package and 50-item achievement test on Active and Passive Voice
description: The investigators developed and standardized a Computer Assisted Instruction package on Tutorial mode using Macromedia Flash 8 software for learning English Grammar – Voice for eighth-standard students, alongside an Achievement Test on Active Voice and Passive Voice. After item validation through a pilot study, 50 items were retained: 25 items converting Active Voice to Passive Voice and 25 converting Passive Voice to Active Voice. The package served as the experimental treatment and the test as the outcome measure.
requirements: Runs as an individualized self-instructional tutorial allowing students to learn at their own pace depending upon their ability
constraints: Developed and evaluated only for the Active and Passive Voice content unit with eighth-standard Matriculation school students
target_learning_goals: Learning Active and Passive Voice in English grammar

article_title: Efficacy of Using Career and Self-Construction to Help Learners Manage Career-Related Transitions
citation: A Cook and JG Maree. (2016). Efficacy of using career and self-construction to help learners manage career-related transitions. South African Journal of Education, 36(1), Art. #1225. https://doi.org/10.15700/saje.v36n1a1225
title: Career and self-construction theory as a framework for school-based career transition support
description: The article draws on Guichard's self-construction theory, which "sees individuals actively constructing themselves through narration or storytelling in social interaction", and Savickas's career construction theory, which focuses on identity derived from one's career and its career adaptability model covering concern, control, curiosity and confidence. Career and life design counselling translates these theories into practice as clients narrate life stories in dialogue with counsellors and supportive audiences. The study operationalises this framework in an eight-lesson group intervention within the Life Orientation syllabus.
requirements: Group-based dialogue with supportive audiences so individuals can narrate life stories and become authors of their life trajectories
Non-judgmental facilitation in which participants are acknowledged as experts of their own lives
constraints: The article notes Western career facilitation practices characterised by individualism, rationality and empiricism will be irrelevant to many cultures, calling for globalisation rather than westernisation of practices
target_learners: Grade 11 adolescents in contrasting South African school settings (independent and disadvantaged state schools)
target_learning_goals: Career adaptability (concern, control, curiosity, confidence)
Self-knowledge and life-theme identification
Managing career-related transitions
examples: The intervention used the Career Interest Profile, collages, lifelines and reflective journals across eight lessons, with participants sharing narratives in group discussions

article_title: Distortions in Distributions of Impact Estimates in Multi-Site Trials: The Central Limit Theorem Is Not Your Friend
citation: Henry May. (2014). Distortions in Distributions of Impact Estimates in Multi-Site Trials: The Central Limit Theorem is Not Your Friend. SREE Fall 2014 Conference. https://www.sree.org/
title: Interpret visualizations of site-specific impact estimates in multi-site experiments with caution, because low reliability forces them toward normality
description: The paper's stated purpose is "to provide cautionary guidance regarding the interpretation of distributions of site-specific impact estimates in multi-site experiments". Because within-site sample sizes in typical multi-site RCTs are small and reliabilities low, visualized distributions of fixed or random effect estimates reflect normal sampling error rather than the true distribution of impacts. Researchers should therefore not read shape features (skewness, outliers, modality) of such plots as features of true site-level impact variation.
requirements: Users should recognize that unless within-site sample sizes are enormous (e.g., >1,000), the shape of the distribution of estimates is dominated by the normal distribution
constraints: The article states most multi-site RCTs yield within-site sample sizes below 30 and reliabilities below .50 when roughly 30 or more sites are visualized
target_learners: first-graders reading substantially below grade level in the Reading Recovery i3 study
target_learning_goals: early reading achievement (ITBS reading words and reading comprehension)
examples: The paper visualized Empirical Bayes site-specific Glass's D effect size estimates from the 2011-12 and 2012-13 Reading Recovery multi-site randomized trials (Figures 1-2) and showed via simulation how uniform, lognormal, and negative lognormal true distributions were concealed.
key_sources: Henry May. (2014). Distortions in Distributions of Impact Estimates in Multi-Site Trials: The Central Limit Theorem is Not Your Friend. SREE Fall 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562702

article_title: Feedback on Developmental Writing Students' First Drafts
citation: Gulley, B. (2012). Feedback on developmental writing students' first drafts. Journal of Developmental Education, 36(1). https://www.jstor.org
title: Categorized feedback response sheet guiding teacher comments
description: A printed form with sections for thesis statement, content, organization, sensory details, grammar, and style, each with blank space for comments. The instructor used it to deliver written feedback, e-mailed completed copies to the written-feedback group, gave carbon copies to the combined group, and used it "as a guide while providing the students with oral feedback" so all groups received information on the same topics. The author reports it reminds teachers to comment on all assignment goals, leading to more frequent praise.
requirements: Sections covering all assignment goals so teachers comment on areas students succeeded in as well as errors
constraints: Evaluated in this study only for a narrative paragraph assignment
target_learners: developmental writing students at a community college
target_learning_goals: receiving balanced feedback across all assignment goals
examples: The Appendix prints the response sheet used for the narrative paragraph rough draft, with categories from topic sentence through style

article_title: Educational Context: Preparing Accounting Students to Identify Ethical Dilemmas
citation: Mary Jo Billiot, David Daniel, Sid Glandon, TerryAnn Glandon. (2012). Educational Context: Preparing Accounting Students To Identify Ethical Dilemmas. American Journal Of Business Education – May/June 2012 Volume 5, Number 3. https://clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE
title: Weekly case-based ethics education combining active learning, a structured decision-making model, and corrective feedback, delivered in either an ethical or an accounting context
description: A semester-long instructional pattern in which each week the instructor introduces a case, students spend approximately 15 minutes discussing it, complete a seven-step decision-making model adapted from Langenderfer and Rockness (1989), and conclude with classroom discussion of recommendations. The article states the process "incorporates active learning, a structured decision-making model, and corrective feedback." The same case fact patterns were used in both contexts; the ethical context added the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct and labeled cases "Ethics Case," emphasizing Steps 2, 3, 5, and 7, while the accounting context emphasized Steps 1, 4, 6, and 7.
requirements: A new case introduced and discussed each week for 12 weeks, with student discussion time and completion of the seven-step decision-making model
Corrective feedback through concluding classroom discussion in which students present their recommendations
constraints: The article notes a pretest was foregone to avoid sensitizing participants, and students were not randomly assigned to conditions across semesters
target_learners: undergraduate accounting majors in the first Intermediate Accounting course
target_learning_goals: ethical sensitivity to subtle ethical issues in accounting practice
moral reasoning in professional accounting judgment
examples: In one semester all students experienced the accounting context (62 students); in a subsequent semester all experienced the ethical context (76 students), with a comparison group of 55 completing only the survey
key_sources: Mary Jo Billiot, David Daniel, Sid Glandon, TerryAnn Glandon. (2012). Educational Context: Preparing Accounting Students To Identify Ethical Dilemmas. American Journal Of Business Education – May/June 2012 Volume 5, Number 3. https://clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE

article_title: Traditional Instruction versus Virtual Reality Simulation: A Comparative Study of Phlebotomy Training among Nursing Students in Kuwait
citation: Abeer William, Victoria L. Vidal, Pamela John. (2016). Traditional Instruction Versus Virtual Reality Simulation: A Comparative Study of Phlebotomy Training among Nursing Students in Kuwait. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.9. https://www.iiste.org
title: CathSim virtual reality simulator with phlebotomy module
description: The CathSim system is the computer-based virtual reality simulator used to train the experimental group, described as "a computer based simulation of an imagined or real environment, which offers a highly interactive experience to students." Its phlebotomy module has six patients; the learner uses a mouse to select an insertion site, palpate, apply a tourniquet, and insert a virtual needle via the AccuTouch device, with a virtual collection tube filling with blood on screen. The system also supplies the study's six performance metrics.
requirements: A computer with the AccuTouch needle unit device and the CathSim phlebotomy module
constraints: In the VRS, a student clicks on an icon instead of actually tying a tourniquet, so some steps are critically different from real phlebotomy
Students reported it was harder to manipulate both a needle assembly and a mouse simultaneously
target_learners: level-two Associate Degree in Nursing students
target_learning_goals: phlebotomy skill performance on actual patients
examples: The experimental group practiced for a five hour session on at least three case patients under researcher supervision before clinic exposure

article_title: The Effect of Using Storytelling Strategy on Students' Performance in Fractions
citation: Charalambos Lemonidis & Ioanna Kaiafa. (2019). The Effect of Using Storytelling Strategy on Students’ Performance in Fractions. Journal of Education and Learning, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v8n2p165
title: Carefully select stories and include them in teaching in a targeted way to support students' understanding of mathematical concepts
description: The article's instructional implication is that "careful selection of a story and its targeted inclusion in teaching can support students’ understanding of mathematical concepts". Stories should be aligned with the teaching objectives (target-focused) so that the narrative context carries the mathematical ideas, giving students a meaningful context in which to communicate and discuss them. The study's stories were written to match the objectives of a curriculum for rational number teaching.
requirements: stories must be selected carefully and aligned with the mathematical objectives of the lesson
constraints: evidence comes from third-grade fraction teaching over a 4-week intervention in two Greek primary schools
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of fractions
problem solving
examples: The researchers wrote target-focused stories matching the objectives of the new rational numbers curriculum and used them at each new-concept introduction

article_title: Catch Up® Numeracy: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: National Foundation for Educational Research (NFER), evaluation team led by Simon Rutt. (2014). Catch Up® Numeracy: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/evaluation
title: Catch Up Numeracy one-to-one intervention with ten-component diagnostic targeting
description: Catch Up Numeracy is a one-to-one intervention for primary pupils struggling with numeracy, delivered by trained teaching assistants in two 15-minute sessions per week. It "breaks numeracy down into ten components, assesses children's ability on each, and targets subsequent instruction so that the tutor always addresses the exact area of weakness." Components include counting verbally, counting objects, word problems and estimation. Delivery follows four stages: assessments for learning, identifying an appropriate focus, individual sessions (review and introduction, numeracy activity, link recording) and ongoing monitoring. TAs receive detailed session plans and three half-day training sessions.
requirements: TAs are supplied with detailed session plans and receive three half-day training sessions
A Catch Up Numeracy coordinator in each school oversees the intervention and supports the TAs
constraints: The trial required 60 sessions over 30 weeks, which schools struggled to deliver in full; TAs and coordinators suggested the duration, group size and paperwork could be adapted
target_learners: primary school children who are struggling with numeracy
target_learning_goals: component numeracy skills including counting, word problems and estimation
examples: The report describes a sample activity, Cool fans, in which learners use a number fan to make 1-3 digit numbers and order sets of three numbers by size, smallest first and largest first.
key_sources: National Foundation for Educational Research (NFER), evaluation team led by Simon Rutt. (2014). Catch Up® Numeracy: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/evaluation

Time allocation beyond regular course hours for humorous activities

article_title: Effects of 7E Learning Cycle Model and Case-Based Learning Strategy on Secondary School Students' Learning Outcomes in Chemistry
citation: Adesoji, F. A., & Idika, M. I. (2015). Effects of 7E learning cycle model and case-based learning strategy on secondary school students' learning outcomes in chemistry. Journal of International Society for Teacher Education, 19(1). https://jiste.org/
title: Case-based learning strategy for chemistry
description: Case-based learning (CBL) is a pedagogical method that uses case studies as active learning tools, defined in the article as "analysis of a particular case or situation used as a basis for drawing conclusions in similar situations." Cases have two main parts: a case situation (an engaging or controversial story or dilemma requiring basic understanding of scientific principles) and study questions that direct students and facilitate class discussion. Learners solve the presented problem using background knowledge. In the study it was delivered via a Teachers' Instructional Guide for Case-Based Learning Strategy.
requirements: Cases composed of a case situation plus related study questions
Study questions that direct understanding rather than ask only for names, dates, or labels
constraints: The article notes cases have historically been used mostly in medicine, law, psychology, social sciences, and humanities; use in chemistry teaching is a newer development
target_learning_goals: chemistry achievement
critical thinking
interest and enjoyment toward learning chemistry
examples: The researcher observed that students showed signs of emotional attachment to the characters used in the stories during CBL lessons

article_title: Use of Dramatization to Teach Cardiac Cycle Physiology to Medical Students
citation: Dowlati, E., Musick, D. W., Zhang, L., Thornton, K., & Carvalho, H. (2016). Use of Dramatization to Teach Cardiac Cycle Physiology to Medical Students. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i9.1603
title: Cardiac cycle dramatization: students role-play cells and components of a functioning heart
description: An active-learning pattern in which each student physically embodies one component of the cardiac cycle — myocytes, sinoatrial node, atrioventricular node, valve leaflets, red blood cells, or neurotransmitters — with roles and receptors marked by signs, arranged in a figure '8' representing atrium and ventricle. Students act out depolarization, contraction, blood flow, valve closure as a clap simulating heart sounds, and staged scenarios of sympathetic or parasympathetic activity demonstrating inotropy and chronotropy. The article used it to teach cardiac cycle dynamics to first-year medical students, with emphasis on exercise responses.
requirements: An instructor and an assistant facilitate the role-playing
Students are assigned specific roles and receptors noted by signs on their chest or back
The active learning process must be carefully planned and rehearsed in advance
constraints: The nature of a more engaging learning activity such as dramatization may not allow enough time to completely cover the same amount of content as a lecture
target_learning_goals: understanding of cardiac cycle dynamics including electrical activity, mechanical activity, neurotransmitters, receptor sites, heart sounds, and changes with exercise
examples: Students positioned in a figure '8' shape acted out depolarization by lifting their hands, moved inward as chambers contracted, and clapped hands to simulate heart sounds when valves closed
key_sources: Dowlati, E., Musick, D. W., Zhang, L., Thornton, K., & Carvalho, H. (2016). Use of Dramatization to Teach Cardiac Cycle Physiology to Medical Students. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i9.1603

description: The article's Table 1 lesson template for the linear function unit guides students to first familiarise themselves with the Microsoft Math Tool interface, then "use the graphical calculator to draw a graph of the linear function", then "draw the same graph using graph sheet, pencil and eraser", and finally identify and describe the y-intercept point and the gradient. This pairs visual tool-based exploration with manual construction of the same graph.
requirements: Access to the Microsoft Math Tool graphical calculator interface and graph sheets for the parallel manual drawing activity
constraints: The template was described for a linear function unit with objectives of drawing graphs and identifying gradient and y-intercept

identifying and describing gradient and y-intercept

article_title: Concept Attainment Teaching Methodology (CATM)--An Effective Approach for Training Workers on Chemicals Health Hazards
citation: Abdulqadir Mohamad Suleiman. (2016). Concept Attainment Teaching Methodology (CATM) – An Effective Approach for Training Workers on Chemicals Health Hazards. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(11): 2677-2685. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.041122
title: Short, focused workplace training session combining reception and selection concept-attainment activities
description: The training sessions lasted between two and two-and-a-half hours, held during working hours, and combined both CATM paradigms: trainees worked individually with picture-based PowerPoint presentations for the reception strategy and in groups of 3-5 with printed pictures and information cards for the selection strategy. Materials were prepared in English and Norwegian and used interchangeably according to participants' needs. baseline pre-test to establish trainees' prior knowledge

workers of minority background with language challenges

applying hazard concepts to actual work tasks

article_title: The Impact of Online Reading Tasks and Reading Strategies on EFL Learners' Reading Test Scores
citation: Altay, İ. F., & Altay, A. (2017). The impact of online reading tasks and reading strategies on EFL learners' reading test scores. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 13(2), 136-152. http://www.jlls.org
title: Caution stakeholders against high expectations that online reading tasks will raise reading test scores
description: The article recommends that educators temper expectations about technology's effect on reading scores, because its quasi-experiment found no significant gains from six weeks of online reading tasks. It states these "non -significant results caution educators and researchers about the use of technology in the language classroom and expectances regarding online reading tasks potential to bring about changes in reading scores", contributing to a more realistic understanding of instructional technology.
requirements: Decisions about integrating online reading tasks should be informed by evidence of their effect on reading outcomes rather than assumed benefits.
constraints: The caution derives from one small, short-duration quasi-experiment with low-proficiency learners; the authors call for more research before final conclusions.
target_learners: tertiary-level EFL learners at B1+ proficiency
target_learning_goals: L2 reading comprehension
examples: The study assigned 25 B1+ learners emailed online reading tasks for six weeks while 26 controls read on paper, then compared paper-based pre- and post-test scores.
key_sources: Altay, İ. F., & Altay, A. (2017). The impact of online reading tasks and reading strategies on EFL learners' reading test scores. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 13(2), 136-152. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1159168

article_title: The Effect of Call-Based Tasks on EFL Learners' Grammar Learning
citation: Alian, J., Khodabandeh, F., & Soleimani, H. (2016). The effect of CALL-based tasks on EFL learners’ grammar learning. Teaching English with Technology, 18(3), 54-68. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: CALL-based task treatment: computer-produced grammar assignments in sub-groups
description: An instructional element in which learners in sub-groups complete grammar assignments using computers at home — for example making PowerPoint slides illustrating the Simple Past Tense, creating multimedia activities about the lesson's grammatical rules, or using programs such as Swish Max and e-Studio 7 — and submit them by e-mail or CD. The teacher supervises and guides as needed, then presents the tasks in class and asks learners to explain how they did them. It was compared against photocopied written-question tasks over 15 sessions.

constraints: The article does not clearly specify advantages and disadvantages of particular technology-based instruments, per its own limitations statement
