target_learning_goals: English grammar rules (Simple Past Tense, Conjunctions, Present Continuous Tense, Irregular Verbs, Conditional Sentences, Possessive Adjectives)
examples: One sub-group made PowerPoint slides explaining the Simple Past Tense; another made a multimedia activity about the lesson's grammatical rules

article_title: Effectiveness of Flipped Learning: Improving Pre-Service Teachers' Prowess in Producing Videos
citation: Faisal M. Almutairi, Abdullah A. Almodaires & Alaa J. Zeyab. (2020). Effectiveness of Flipped Learning: Improving Pre-Service Teachers' Prowess in Producing Videos. International Education Studies, 13(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v13n7p163
title: Exercise care when structuring pre-service teacher education courses that apply flipped learning
description: The study recommends that "care should be taken when structuring courses in pre-service teachers' education when applying flipped learning", because outcomes comparing flipped and traditional formats were mixed and many students remained averse to the approach. The article also suggests educators should not expect that a move to a flipped learning method would spontaneously inspire students. Structuring should therefore attend to pre-class material availability, relevant videos, adequate viewing time, and in-class clarification of difficult concepts, which the questionnaire items show students valued.
requirements: Videos and lessons must be available on the e-learning portal before the flipped activity, and students need adequate time to view them
constraints: Not all students prefer flipped classes; some feel they lack access to an expert while viewing videos outside class
target_learning_goals: skill and knowledge attainment in applied production tasks
examples: In the study's flipped condition, class time was dedicated to hands-on activities with instructor and peer support, while demonstration videos and readings were studied at home before class

title: CARE for Teachers professional development program
description: CARE for Teachers (Cultivating Awareness and Resilience in Education) is a mindfulness-based professional development program for teachers combining "emotion skills instruction, mindful awareness and stress reduction practices and caring and listening practices". target_learning_goals: stress reduction
emotion regulation
mindfulness
improved classroom interactions
examples: Over 90% of participants attended at least 4 of the 5 training days, and coaching calls averaged 26 minutes

citation: Jennings, P. A., Brown, J. L., Frank, J. L., Doyle, S., Oh, Y., Davis, R., Rasheed, D., DeWeese, A., DeMauro, A. A., Cham, H., & Greenberg, M. T. (2017). title: CARE for Teachers logic model: synergistic program elements producing teacher and classroom outcomes
description: The CARE for Teachers logic model (Figure 1) maps program elements to hypothesized outcomes for K-5 teachers. The article states the "program elements of emotion skills instruction, mindful awareness and stress reduction practices and caring and listening practices are hypothesized to promote increases in adaptive emotion regulation, teaching efficacy and mindfulness and reductions in psychological and physical distress". The elements are hypothesized to act synergistically, such that "no one single program element is hypothesized to have a unique and direct impact on any one outcome".
requirements: All program elements operate together; the model presumes no single element alone drives outcomes
target_learning_goals: adaptive emotion regulation
teaching efficacy
mindfulness
reduced distress
classroom emotional support and organization
examples: A similar logic model was developed and tested in previous CARE studies (Jennings et al., 2011, 2013) and refined slightly for the current trial

description: The study evaluated CARE for Teachers using "a two-level (teachers/classrooms, schools) multisite cluster randomized trial design with intervention at level two (teachers) and schools serving as naturally occurring blocks". Teachers were block-randomized within schools by grade after baseline collection, yielding 118 intervention and 106 control teachers. The authors note this design "has been recommended as a strategy to control between-school variability" and requires fewer schools for adequate power.

constraints: Within-school randomization posed a potential threat to internal validity due to possible contamination or spillover from intervention to control teachers within a school

title: Drill-and-practice and tutorial CAI software for Class XI English
description: The investigators developed CAI software for Class XI English using the drill-and-practice and tutorial program types, chosen as "the most widely used types of computer programs". Diagrams and sketches were incorporated through scanning, concepts and units were given different codes, and the software was validated before use in the experimental treatment. It was designed to let students work at their own pace, measure performance quickly, and provide immediate feedback and reinforcement.

citation: Amosa Isiaka Gambarı, Mudasiru Olalere Yusuf. (2015). Effectiveness of Computer-Assisted Stad Cooperative Learning Strategy on Physics Problem Solving, Achievement and Retention. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, 3(3). https://www.mojet.net

description: CALP is a researcher-developed drill-and-practice CAI package written in html using Macromedia Dreamweaver 8, with Fireworks for graphics and Flash for simulation, covering "two topics subdivided into sixteen lessons". It presented physics content with animation and multiple-choice questions, requiring "at least 100% mastery of one topic before moving on to the next", with logout after three failed attempts. It was used in both the cooperative STAD setting and the individualized setting.

article_title: The Effect of Computer-Assisted Educational Games on Teaching Grammar
citation: Adil Kayan & İbrahim Seçkin Aydın. (2020). The Effect of Computer-Assisted Educational Games on Teaching Grammar. World Journal of Education, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v10n1p117
title: Game-based grammar lesson structure combining implicit rule discovery, group play, and individual tablet practice
description: Each lesson in the experimental condition followed a recurring structure: lessons "started with presenting videos, animations or various visuals" to attract attention, then questions prompted students to discover grammar rules through implicit learning from texts and digital examples. Students then practiced via smart-board applications and games, played in groups of 5 or 6 with rotating membership, discussed and decided jointly, wrote decisions on cardboard, and explained them to the class, followed by individual tablet games and feedback so all students could feel like winners.

cooperation and peer teaching skills
examples: Groups were changed according to the order of the list per week so students of different levels worked together; feedback was given to each student after group games

article_title: Teaching Primary Grade Students Perfectionism through Cartoons Compared to Bibliotherapy
citation: Zousel, M. L., Rule, A. C., & Logan, S. R. (2013). Teaching Primary Grade Students Perfectionism through Cartoons Compared to Bibliotherapy. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 5(2), 199-218. www.iejee.com
title: Cartoon analysis-and-creation lesson sequence for teaching affective concepts
description: A reusable lesson pattern in which each session opens with discussion of printed cartoons using prompts such as 'What is happening?' and 'How does the character feel?', then progresses across lessons to completing partly-finished cartoons, small-group skits applying a cartoon's concept to a new situation, and collaborative completion of a multi-panel strip. The pattern applies academic or affective concepts to new cartoon situations, using humor, wordplay, and creative drawing to motivate students.
requirements: A set of numbered cartoons focused on the target concepts so the teacher can refer to them during discussion
constraints: The article reports the approach tested in one suburban school with primary-grade students; generalizability to other populations is untested
target_learning_goals: acquiring concepts of an affective or academic topic
applying concepts to new situations
examples: Four 30-minute lessons were delivered to each classroom: cartoon discussion in lesson one, completing partly-drawn cartoons in lesson two, group skits in lesson three, and a collaborative three-panel strip in lesson four

article_title: Is Case-Based Instruction Effective in Enhancing High School Students' Motivation toward Chemistry?
citation: Yalçınkaya, E., Boz, Y., & Erdur-Baker, Ö. (2012). Is case-based instruction effective in enhancing high school students' motivation toward chemistry? Science Education International, 23(2), 102-116. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ970613
title: Case-based instruction with small-group discussion of daily-life cases
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern in which students read real-life cases and answer study questions in small groups of four to five, followed by whole-class discussion. In this study "A total of fifteen cases about real-life events, experiments, and specific situations were utilized in the context of gas topic". The teacher guides rather than answers directly, asking open-ended and challenging questions, and groups are mixed by prior achievement and attitude.
requirements: Cases composed of a case situation plus related study questions that direct students to facilitate understanding rather than recall names, dates, or labels
A teacher trained in the method who guides discussion and avoids direct answers
Mixed groups of four to five students formed considering previous chemistry achievement and attitude
constraints: Implemented here only in the gas topic of 10th-grade chemistry over 12 weeks in one Anatolian high school
target_learning_goals: Increased perceived motivation toward chemistry
Connecting abstract chemistry concepts to daily-life situations
examples: Fifteen cases on the gas topic, e.g., an airbag accident case asking about the working principle of airbags and the properties of the gas in an airbag, discussed in groups then as a whole class

description: An instructional component in which preschool science content is taught through computer presentations rather than only traditional methods. Content with educational purpose rather than social media or game use

description: The article presents the case-study method as a learning–teaching method of the constructivist education system, used "to gain knowledge, skills and attitudes about specific issues" by analyzing real-life problems through cause-and-effect relationships. problem-solving skills
environmental knowledge and values

citation: Hamza AKENGİN, Gökhan AYDEMİR. (2012). Effects of Using Case-Study Method in Social Studies on Students' Attitudes Towards Environment. International Electronic Journal of Environmental Education, Vol.2, Issue 2. http://www.iejeegreen.com
title: Use the case-study method in social studies to develop positive environmental attitudes and raise knowledge, values and skills
description: Based on its findings and similar experimental studies, the article recommends that the case-study method be used effectively in learning–teaching processes to improve students' environmental awareness. environmental awareness
knowledge, values and skills in social studies

article_title: The Effectiveness of Dialogic Reading in Increasing English Language Learning Preschool Children's Expressive Language
citation: Diana Brannon, Linda Dauksas. (2014). The Effectiveness of Dialogic Reading in Increasing English Language Learning Preschool Children's Expressive Language. International Research in Early Childhood Education, 5(1). https://www.education.monash.edu.au/irecejournal/
title: Ten-week parent dialogic reading training program combining the CAR strategy with 1, 2, 3 Tell Me What You See
description: The intervention trained ELL parents during the preschool's mandatory 15-minute Family Time, three days a week every other week for ten weeks. It taught the CAR strategy — "Comment and wait (provide a language model), Ask questions and wait (encourage interaction and reflection) and Respond and add more (build expressive language)" — followed by the authors' 1, 2, 3 Tell Me What You See technique, which asks children to comment on what they see, has parents teach new words, and connects the story to the child's life. Parents watched modeling, received sample questions and books, and kept books in English and Spanish.
requirements: Training was delivered in 15-minute sessions with live modeling in front of the child's class, sample questions, and take-home practice books; materials were provided in English and Spanish
constraints: Both groups received a set of 5 random picture books in English and Spanish to ensure equal home access to literature
target_learners: English language learning parents of at-risk preschool children aged three to five
target_learning_goals: Parents' dialogic reading and literacy interaction skills
Children's expressive vocabulary development
examples: Parents from Teacher A's class trained weeks 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9; Teacher B's class weeks 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10; six undergraduate students administered the trainings after a full-day training

article_title: Flipped Learning in an EFL Environment: Does the Teacher's Experience Affect Learning Outcomes?

Closed captions and visual supports should be included to aid comprehension

article_title: Effect of Explicit Language Learning Strategy Instruction on Language-Test and Self-Assessment Scores
citation: Jurkovič, V. (2010). Effect of Explicit Language Learning Strategy Instruction on Language-test and Self-assessment Scores. English Language Teaching, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v3n1p16
title: CALLA (Cognitive Academic Language Learning Approach) as the strategy instruction model for higher-education language courses
description: The article uses the CALLA model (Chamot & O'Malley, 1994) to structure explicit strategy instruction. It was chosen because it "includes three components": study-discipline content, academic language skills, and "explicit scaffolded instruction in language learning strategies". The model rests on the cognitive theory of learning, distinguishing long-term, short-term and working memory, with foreign language learning arising from "strategic behaviour in working memory" (Macaro, 2006). In the study it was implemented through cognitive, metacognitive and memory strategy clusters integrated into regular class work.
requirements: Strategy instruction should be explicit and integrated into regular class work activities, per the models the article cites (Chamot, 2004)
constraints: The article reports that when course time is limited and groups are highly heterogeneous, deducting strategy training time from language teaching may hinder effectiveness
target_learners: first-year higher-education students of English for specific purposes in mixed-ability groups
target_learning_goals: general and discipline-specific English language competence
strategic self-regulated language learning
examples: The treatment group received five to ten-minute strategy discussions two to three times per session, roughly fifteen to twenty minutes per session (about five hours, six percent of total course time), following the CALLA model.

citation: Dilek İlhan-Beyaztaş, Burhanettin Özdemir. (2018). The Effect of Case-Based Curriculum on Cognitive and Affective Characteristics of Students. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 6, No. 3. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i3.3035
title: Case-based curriculum implemented in two sequences: presentation-then-cases (CBL1) and cases-then-presentation (CBL2)

Both variants rest on Wassermann's five fundamental CBL elements: cases, study questions, small group work, class discussions, and activities to ensure permanence.
requirements: Cases, study questions, small group works, class discussions, and activities to ensure permanence as fundamental elements of the CBL process
constraints: Studied only in an Introduction to Educational Science course with freshmen at two Turkish universities; the article states it is necessary to investigate the reflection of this study on different socio-cultural and larger working groups

article_title: The Effect of Explicit Instruction of Meta Cognitive Learning Strategies on Promoting Jordanian Language Learners' Reading Competence
citation: ABEER AL-GHAZO. (2016). The Effect of Explicit Instruction of Meta Cognitive Learning Strategies on Promoting Jordanian Language Learners' reading competence. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.10. https://www.iiste.org
title: CALLA model of metacognitive strategy instruction (Chamot and Rubin, 1994): five instructional phases
description: The Cognitive Academic Language Learning Approach (CALLA) model proposed by Chamot and Rubin (1994) is a strategy-instruction model the article calls "the most effective strategy instruction model". It structures instruction in five phases: Preparation, in which students identify prior knowledge and the teacher explains metacognitive strategies; Presentation, in which the teacher demonstrates the strategies and explains how and when to use them; Practice, in which students use the strategies in regular class activities with teacher guidance; Evaluation, in which students self-evaluate strategy use with rating scales and checklists; and Expansion, in which students apply the strategies to new situations and tasks. The study implemented this model with the experimental group over two and a half months.
requirements: Teacher explanation and demonstration of the strategies across phases, handouts, guided practice, self-evaluation activities, and application to new tasks and contexts
constraints: The article reports the model as implemented in EFL reading instruction with low-proficiency university students over two and a half months
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Metacognitive strategy use in foreign language reading
examples: The experimental group received explicit instruction following the five phases: teacher distributed handouts containing various metacognitive strategies, demonstrated strategies, guided practice with questions and cooperation, rating scales and checklists of strategies used, and application in different tasks and contexts

description: The review recommends that educators and researchers temper enthusiasm for gamification given the state of the evidence base. citation: Cha J, Zhao Y, Zong H. (2026). Large Language Model Performance on Multistep Clinical Cases: Comparative Study Across Question and Case Levels. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/95342
title: Case-level evaluation framework: case pass rate and consistency gap as stricter benchmarks than question-level accuracy
description: The article proposes a multidimensional metric framework that goes beyond simple per-question accuracy. The case pass rate (CPR) defines success only when the model answers all subquestions associated with a case correctly, treating partial correctness as failure. The consistency gap, the arithmetic difference between QPR and CPR, quantifies performance degradation from question-level to case-level aggregation. The authors argue this shift "provides a more stringent and clinically meaningful benchmark, thereby revealing limitations of current LLMs that are masked by high accuracy scores in traditional assessments."
requirements: Cases must comprise multiple logically interdependent questions covering stages of clinical management within a shared patient vignette
constraints: The CPR does not directly assess whether answers are logically compatible with one another
Because each question was submitted independently without conversation history, results reflect independently answered questions aggregated at the case level rather than true sequential performance
target_learning_goals: assessing LLM readiness for multistep clinical tasks
examples: Applied to 189 CNMLE cases, the framework revealed consistency gaps of 10% to 17.9% across four state-of-the-art models

description: The article describes a manufacturing pipeline for case-specific 3D-printed temporal bone models: cadaveric temporal bones were scanned on a cone-beam CT scanner, DICOM data were imported into "VESTool (in-house software for 3D segmentation)", which resampled the virtual models to 0.2 mm voxel size and segmented the bony volume using "interactive and localized thresholding features with minimal manual effort required"; models were exported as STL files and 3D-printed with identical specifications, then individually drilled to validate accuracy against CT imaging data.

constraints: The authors state manufacturing case-specific models requires considerably more resources and effort than standard models, with 1–4 h spent per model, making routine use unlikely to be cost-effective for initial training until automation reduces manual steps

examples: Models for the CM group were produced from CBCT scans of the cadaveric temporal bones and printed with identical specifications for both groups

description: The CSC is a structured, multi-session simulation curriculum for OHNS residency comprising five sessions—pediatric airway foreign body, neck dissection, functional endoscopic sinus surgery, nasal fracture/sphenopalatine artery ligation, and rhinoplasty—delivered annually during protected academic time using cadaveric and mannequin-based models with juniors paired with senior residents. article_title: Cartooning in Biological Learning.
citation: Bahsoun Soukaina, Morris Mhairi, Akam Elizabeth. (2026). Cartooning in Biological Learning. Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/bmb.70040
title: Cartooning seminar pattern: lecture, recall quiz, team cartoon creation, presentation and peer-ranked competition
description: A reusable seminar-level design for making abstract multi-step topics approachable. After a lecture introducing topics and subtopics, students take a brief multiple-choice recall quiz via an online polling platform, form teams of two to six, randomly choose one of the offered subtopics, and create a cartoon of it. Presentations are followed by peer assessment in which each group ranks the other groups' cartoons; rankings are converted to aggregated points and the highest cumulative score wins, run as a friendly competition with small prizes. The authors report the activity was easy to set up, low cost, and required no specific technical skills.
requirements: Topics should be complicated, multistep processes that can be divided into subtopics
Only a subset of subtopics is offered for cartooning to allow comparative evaluation
Peer-assessment ranking rules and point aggregation must be set up in advance
constraints: The authors note that in the absence of additional seminar time, a guided hybrid homework approach may be needed
target_learning_goals: understanding of complex multi-step biological processes
active learning and engagement
teamwork
examples: Part A students cartooned DNA repair mechanisms, Part B signaling life and death, and Part C molecular hallmarks of cancer; the activity was also run with colleagues from various backgrounds at the Horizons in STEM Higher Education Conference, University of Bristol, June 2024

citation: Roszipal Benjamin, Szelesi Gabriella, Ernst Martin, Hoffelner Alexander, Wagner Michael. (2025). Competency development in early nursing training: a cross-sectional OSCE study of self-assessment versus examiner ratings. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08279-0
title: Calibration-as-monitoring account within self-regulated learning: transparent criteria support accurate self-assessment, tacit interpersonal standards foster overestimation
description: The article grounds calibration accuracy — "the alignment between self-assessed competence and externally assessed performance" — in Zimmerman's SRL framework, where calibration operates as a core monitoring mechanism linking performance appraisal to strategy adjustment. It interprets the domain-specific findings as showing that "transparent, criterion-based tasks foster more accurate monitoring", while miscalibration localizes to domains where standards are tacit and relational. Weaker or delayed feedback cues in interpersonal domains constrain the monitoring phase and foster overconfidence.
requirements: Learners must receive external performance ratings to compare against self-ratings for calibration to be measured or trained
constraints: Stated for early-stage, first-year nursing cohorts under OSCE conditions with explicit checklists; cross-sectional design precludes inferences about developmental change
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of clinical competencies
metacognitive monitoring and calibration
examples: The OSCE study operationalized calibration as self minus examiner discrepancy scores across three domains in a summative second-semester examination

title: Formalin-embalmed cadaver simulation stations with embedded synthetic cysts for ultrasound-guided procedure training
description: A low-cost simulation setup in which 7-inch latex balloons filled with 15 to 20 CCs of tap water are embedded about 1 inch below the skin of formalin-embalmed cadavers to create target cysts. Each station was equipped, per the article, with "a supine formalin-embalmed cadaver, an ultrasound machine, and linear transducer covered with a nonsterile plastic cover," with black plastic sheeting obscuring the cadaver except at procedure sites. Three stations supported a 20-minute supervised training period and a separate cyst used for skills testing.
requirements: Cadavers with more adipose tissue make subcutaneous cyst placement easier
Careful blunt dissection to minimize air infiltration and preserve sonographic image quality
One cyst per contralateral side reserved for the skills test separate from training cysts
constraints: The training protocol did not address sterile technique needed in clinical settings
The model cannot perfectly mimic performing the procedure on a live patient

target_learning_goals: ultrasound-guided needle placement and percutaneous cyst access and drainage
tactile procedural skills for ultrasound-guided procedures
examples: Three Mindray MX7 ultrasound systems with L12-3RC linear transducers guided 18 g 2-inch needles on 30cc syringes during cyst aspiration

title: Calgary-Cambridge model of medical consultations as the framework anchoring communication skills measurement
description: The Calgary-Cambridge model is a framework for medical consultations "focused on marrying content and process within medical consultations, not excluding either the content of the consultation or the processes of communication at the expense of the other." Its task framework includes "initiating the session, gathering information, physical examination, explanation and planning, and closing the session," with running pillars of providing structure and flow while building relationships, rapport, and involving the patient. In this study it served as the anchor for an in-house 11-item pre-post survey of self-reported communication skill attainment, developed iteratively by 6 experienced medical educators and mapped to the model in a supplementary table.
requirements: Survey items mapped to the model's tasks and objectives to support conceptualization and help learners organize communication process skills
constraints: The article notes no succinct externally validated tool for measuring communication skills attainment was identified, motivating the in-house instrument
target_learning_goals: Structured medical consultation communication skills
Building rapport and involving the patient
examples: The study's 11-item survey used 10-point linear scales with anchored end points, piloted for usability with 5 students, and housed on Microsoft Forms

diagnostic accuracy
examples: In EYE-ECG2, participants were presented with either case 1, 2, 3, or 4 as their first case, followed by the remainder of the cases in original order

title: Stoll's capacity building framework as a lens for the institutional role of teaching-focused faculty
description: The article frames PoT roles within Stoll's capacity building framework, couched in ecological systems theory, which "describes universities as dynamic and adaptive systems that are influenced by both internal and external forces at a variety of levels". Internal capacity for educational change is influenced by individual faculty, the institution's social and structural learning context, and the external context. The authors argue PoTs are uniquely situated to influence internal capacity more than research-focused colleagues or adjunct lecturers, and map their findings onto factors such as motivation to learn and sense of interdependence.
requirements: Understanding the role and perspectives of the teaching-focused faculty themselves, which the article says is essential to maximize their impact
constraints: The framework's application is speculative in places; the article explicitly uses it to speculate about PoTs' impact
target_learners: undergraduate students in STEM at research-intensive universities
target_learning_goals: institutional capacity for educational change and improved STEM education
examples: The article maps respondents' education-focused scholarly activities to the framework's motivation-to-learn factor and self-reported influence to the sense-of-interdependence factor.

description: The article offers an explanatory account for why the two daVinci Xi components showed different learning patterns. citation: Manav Esra Yildirim, Akbiyik Sema Yazici, Ceylan Aydan Büşra, Çakiroğlu Ayfer Ezgi Yilmaz, Tuncer Duygu. (2025). title: Caviprep layered tooth model with enamel, dentin, and pulp layers
description: Caviprep (Edudent, Turkey) is a physical layered simulation model for preclinical restorative dentistry training. The article states it "replicates enamel, dentin, and pulp with materials of varying hardness" and that "The red layer simulates the pulp and provides distinct tactile feedback, enhancing anatomical awareness." As students reach the red pulp layer they receive strong tactile feedback, supporting anatomical awareness and depth control without a VR system.
requirements: Varying-hardness material layers so learners receive distinct tactile feedback at each anatomical depth
constraints: The article notes limited studies have directly evaluated Caviprep specifically; compared to 3D-printed teeth it offers internal layering but is positioned as a lower-cost alternative rather than an advanced individualized tool

examples: Group 2 students completed three cavity preparations using only the layered model before final assessment on extracted teeth

citation: Qiu Kangli, Zeng Tianshu, Xia Wenfang, Peng Miaomiao, Kong Wen. (2025). Interdisciplinary medical education practices: building a case-driven interdisciplinary simulation system based on public datasets. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07631-8
title: Case-based interdisciplinary simulation practice system built on public datasets
description: A data-driven virtual simulation practice system composed of data, processing, and presentation models. The data model draws on TCGA, GEO, and UK Biobank; the processing model integrates differential, enrichment, survival, and machine-learning analyses; the rendering model is 'bifurcated into teacher and student components, primarily responsible for dataset management and result display.' It runs on nine virtualized cloud servers and uses R for TCGA/GEO analysis and Python for UK Biobank modeling.
requirements: Cloud computing hardware with dynamically adjustable resources and R/Python software environments
constraints: UK Biobank data requires a paid download to obtain; the dataset is restricted and should be expanded to more common diseases
target_learners: fourth-year clinical medicine students on internal medicine rotations
target_learning_goals: end-to-end biomedical data analysis
integrating bioinformatics with clinical reasoning
examples: The gout case links GSE160170 for differential gene screening, UK Biobank for biochemical modeling, and TCGA-CHOL for survival validation

title: CAE Vimedix ultrasound simulator
description: The CAE Vimedix (CAE Healthcare, Montreal, QC, Canada) is an ultrasound simulator used as a supplement in the surveyed echocardiography, practical-year, and DEGUM-certified abdominal courses. It is "designed to support the development of psychomotor and cognitive skills, particularly regarding the handling of ultrasound probes, image interpretation, diagnosis, and decision-making", consisting of an ultrasound probe connected to a computer and screen plus a plastic phantom providing anatomical-topographical correlation by probe position. It offers animations, supports in-person and remote exercises, and depicts pathologies in selected cases (Fig. 1).

constraints: Realism and direct transferability of its display to real conditions received lower user ratings (4.02–4.69 on a 7-point scale) than its physical characteristics and image presentation

image interpretation
sono-anatomical knowledge
diagnosis and decision-making in ultrasound

British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 496–512. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12735
title: CASEL framework of five student social–emotional competencies
description: The Collaborative for Academic, Social and Emotional Learning (CASEL) framework defines five student social–emotional competencies that inform most formal school SEL curricula internationally. The five competencies are Self-Awareness ("Ability to understand one's own emotions, thoughts and values and how they influence behaviour across contexts"), Self-Management, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills and Responsible Decision-Making. This study operationalised all five via the 20-item self-report MCS-SEL and tested each against later academic achievement.

constraints: The brief 20-item MCS-SEL provides only limited coverage of the skills in each of the five competencies, per the article's limitations
target_learners: Students in middle childhood (~age 11, final year of primary school)
target_learning_goals: Social–emotional development supporting academic engagement and achievement
examples: The study measured the five competencies with 20 MCS-SEL items (Self-Awareness 4 items, Self-Management 3, Social Awareness 5, Relationship Skills 5, Responsible Decision-Making 3).

title: CanMEDS 2015 framework as an organizing lens for patient-generated feedback content
description: The CanMEDS 2015 framework defines physician competencies across seven roles. The article describes it as "comprised of seven roles: Scholar, Professional, Health Advocate, Communicator, Collaborator, Leader, and Medical Expert" and uses it deductively to categorize patient comments from low-rating reviews. It functions here as a coding taxonomy showing that lay patient complaints map onto formally defined physician competency domains, enabling frequency summaries such as Professional (59.7%) and Leader (45.3%).
requirements: A competency framework whose role terminology can be applied deductively to patient narrative comments
constraints: Applied here to comments associated with low ratings (≤2/5) for one specialty, otolaryngology, in Canada
target_learning_goals: identifying areas for practice improvement from patient feedback
examples: 878 written reviews deductively coded to the seven CanMEDS roles with frequencies reported in Table 1

The article states that "The capillarization of training allowed the adaptation of interventions to regional needs, promoting collaborative practices among different health professionals." article_title: Advancing skills and confidence in ultrasound-guided injection techniques: the impact of a cadaveric workshop.
citation: Zure Mert, Topaloğlu Mahir, İş Enes Efe, Sezikli Selim, Sarıkaya Deniz, Dıraçoğlu Demirhan. (2025). Advancing skills and confidence in ultrasound-guided injection techniques: the impact of a cadaveric workshop. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07270-z
title: One-day cadaveric musculoskeletal ultrasound-guided injection workshop with theoretical sessions and four hands-on stations
description: A one-day workshop combining theoretical instructional sessions on USG basics, regional anatomy, probe and needle placement, and joint-specific injection techniques with hands-on practice on cadaveric specimens. Practice ran in "four stations, three of them representing the anterior and lateral aspects of the major joints— hip, knee, and ankle— and one station for the posterior aspect of all joints", each with a high-resolution ultrasound device, a cadaver, one instructor, and a maximum of ten participants. Protocols followed the EURO-MUSCULUS/USPRM and European Society of Musculoskeletal Radiology scanning and injection protocols.
requirements: Each station requires a high-resolution ultrasound device, a cadaver, one instructor, and a maximum of ten participants
Formalin-preserved cadavers screened for infectious diseases and compliant with national ethical donation guidelines
constraints: Needle positions were not documented via imaging or dissection due to ethical and logistical constraints
The study focused on self-reported confidence rather than objective procedural accuracy
target_learning_goals: Sonoanatomical knowledge of hip, knee, and ankle joints
Ultrasound-guided injection technique and procedural confidence
examples: Three one-day workshops with 109 attendees; participants practiced scanning and injections under instructor supervision after demonstrations

citation: Navlekar Anisha S., Theobald Elli J., Griffith Ken, Limeri Lisa B. (2025). Strategically creating maximally heterogeneous lab groups did not improve group performance in an introductory biology lab class. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0323799
title: CATME team-maker tool for instructor-managed student team formation
description: CATME is "a system of online tools designed to help instructors manage student teams effectively"; its team-maker sorts students into teams from survey responses and instructor-selected criteria. In this study, students completed a survey on identities, GPA, schedules, and goals, and CATME settings were assigned to create groups dissimilar in race, gender, generation in college, and GPA while keeping schedules similar. It served as the intervention mechanism for strategic group assignment in the lab sections.
requirements: Students must complete the CATME survey providing identity, prior preparation (GPA), schedule, and goal information for the team-maker to sort them
constraints: Only the sections assigned maximally heterogeneous groups completed the CATME survey, which the authors note could have been a confounding effect if completing the survey affected teamwork
target_learners: undergraduate students in large-enrollment introductory biology lab sections
target_learning_goals: collaboration and teamwork skills in laboratory coursework
examples: Instructors at a Hispanic-serving institution used CATME to form maximally heterogeneous groups in half of lab sections across two semesters, with random assignment in the other half

article_title: Comparison of case-based learning and traditional lecture in teaching residents on research misconduct: a controlled before-and-after study.
citation: Chen Lulin, Li Yizhao, Guo Xiaoyan, Liu Wei. (2025). Comparison of case-based learning and traditional lecture in teaching residents on research misconduct: a controlled before-and-after study. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0322336
title: Use case-based analysis and discussion rather than lecture alone when the goal is to change attitudes toward severe research misconduct
description: The article's discussion recommends against relying on lecture alone for moral education and behavioral-norm promotion, arguing that "traditional lecture has not shown statistically significant improvements in participants' attitudes towards these three behaviors" most dangerous to research integrity. It recommends deep analysis and discussion of real-life cases so residents "more intuitively understand the harms of research misconduct", forming aversion and vigilance. The principle applies when instructional goals include attitude and ethical-concept change rather than only knowledge transmission.
requirements: Real-life cases requiring in-depth analysis and group discussion; instructor facilitation and summarization
constraints: Study conducted only with residents at two Chinese tertiary hospitals, so generalizability to other populations is uncertain per the authors
target_learning_goals: Rejecting research misconduct behaviors
Understanding harms of misconduct to research integrity
examples: The CBL course had residents analyze two misconduct cases in small groups, whereas the lecture group saw the same PowerPoint without case discussion; only the CBL group changed on all attitude items.

article_title: European expert consensus on a structured approach to circular stapling anastomosis in minimally invasive left-sided colorectal resection.
citation: Tou S, Gallagher AG, Bislenghi G, Farinha R, Wolthuis A. (2025). European expert consensus on a structured approach to circular stapling anastomosis in minimally invasive left‐sided colorectal resection. Colorectal Disease. https://doi.org/10.1111/codi.70037
title: CAPITAL A performance metrics set for circular stapling anastomosis
description: A set of performance metrics characterizing a reference approach to circular stapling anastomosis during minimally invasive left‐sided colorectal resection, comprising three procedural phases (transection of the rectum; preparation of proximal colon for anastomosis; anastomosis), 36 steps, 42 errors and 39 critical errors after Delphi refinement. The article defines performance metrics as "units of observable behaviour which together constitute a stepwise description of a reference approach to a procedure", with errors as deviations from optimal performance and critical errors as major deviations likely to cause harm. Accompanying didactic material covers the mechanics and science of anastomosis.
requirements: A reference procedure restricted to straightforward, uncomplicated cases per the stated patient selection and procedure‐specific criteria
constraints: The metrics describe a standardized reference approach and the authors acknowledge the variety of individual surgical practices, for example using a purse‐string applicator instead of a manual purse‐string
target_learners: trainees in minimally invasive colorectal surgery
junior surgical team members who introduce the circular stapling device
target_learning_goals: stepwise mastery of circular stapling anastomosis
avoidance of errors and critical errors during anastomosis
examples: The three phases each have a defined beginning and end, e.g. Phase III begins when the proximal bowel is moved to the pelvis and ends with checking the anastomosis for leakage.

citation: Roche Adam F., Kavanagh Dara O., Crimmins Darach, Healy Vincent, Zilani Gulam, Konge Lars, Nayahangan Leizl Joy, Khan Danyal Z., Murray Daniel, Cuello Javier Francisco, Cahir Caitriona, Murphy Niamh, Condron Claire M. (2025). A Delphi-based needs assessment to identify and prioritise procedural skills through consensus for simulation-based learning in neurosurgery. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06922-4
title: CAMES Needs Assessment Formula applied through a modified Delphi process for prioritising procedures for simulation-based training
description: The Copenhagen Academy for Medical Education and Simulation (CAMES) Needs Assessment Formula (NAF) is a consensus methodology the article describes as a "modified Delphi method" consisting of three iterative survey rounds. It quantifies procedure importance across four equally weighted domains (Doctors, Frequency, Risk, Feasibility), each given 25%, producing an overall score that generates a prioritised procedure list. Domain scores are obtained on 5-point scales, with a steering committee quantifying feasibility factors of cost, availability and suitability. The article states this approach "is well established" and aligns with comparable studies in the literature.
requirements: A five-person steering group to oversee the process and ensure a robust methodological approach at all stages
Three iterative survey rounds with participant ranking on 5-point scales and a 75% majority to determine the final prioritised ranking list
constraints: The article applies and evaluates it specifically for neurosurgical technical skills in the UK and Ireland, using multi-jurisdiction KOLs whose training bodies collectively utilise the JCST curriculum
target_learners: Neurosurgical trainees (senior trainees and consultants served as expert respondents)
target_learning_goals: Identifying and prioritising technical procedural skills for simulation-based learning curricula
examples: The study extracted 71 procedures from the JCST/ISCP curriculum plus KOL brainstorming, excluded procedures with mean scores of 2.95 or lower after round one, and produced a final prioritised list of 47 procedures

Well-prepared, good-quality exercises with instructor encouragement

description: The article recommends cautious application of generative AI in medical education and practice, especially in non-English contexts, because measured performance falls short of reliability thresholds. It states the findings "emphasize the need for cautious application and further refinement, especially in non-English medical contexts." The principle directs educators to treat AI answers as unverified until checked, given the predominance of informational errors among incorrect answers.
requirements: Human verification of AI-generated answers before educational use, given the observed error profile
constraints: GPT-4 did not meet the recommended >95% performance level for educational tools in this examination context
Performance is lower for Korean-language questions than English translations
target_learning_goals: medical knowledge assessment
problem solving in anesthesiology and pain medicine
examples: The study tested GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and CLOVA X on 398 Korean in-training examination questions and found GPT-4 scored 67.8% overall, below the cited educational-tool threshold

title: Fixed-length computer adaptive progress test (CA-PT) with Rasch-calibrated item bank
description: A 135-MCQ digital progress test built from a bank of 3400 Rasch-calibrated questions drawn from 30 previous linear tests, delivering "120 calibrated questions, and 15 non-adaptive pretest questions" per student according to the PT blueprint. Six non-adaptive starter questions give a first ability estimate, after which the algorithm adapts item difficulty; navigation is unidirectional and the score is the estimated ability level (theta). It was administered in TestVision in an authentic exam setting.

A pre-determined item-selection algorithm and digital delivery platform
constraints: Navigation is only unidirectional, unlike the conventional PT where students could review and change answers
The question-mark option of the conventional PT is absent
target_learners: medical students across all years of a six-year curriculum
target_learning_goals: reliable assessment of end-of-curriculum medical functional knowledge at each student's ability level
examples: Administered voluntarily alongside the mandatory May 2022 conventional PT in three Dutch medical schools under full study conditions, with the highest outcome counting for study progress

title: Casper: an online open-ended response format Situational Judgement Test assessing ten personal characteristics

Responses are rated by trained raters on a 9-point global rating scale relative to other participants

BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05801-8
title: CARE scale as an external patient-rated empathy assessment instrument
description: The Consultation and Relational Empathy (CARE) scale, designed by Mercer et al., is used in this study as the external behavioural measure of empathy, rated by the group-associated patient immediately after the encounter. The article describes it as "an external assessment tool for empathy rated by an involved person" containing 10 items on a 5-point Likert scale, where a low score indicates high experienced empathy. It complemented the self-report JSPE and IRI instruments, which detected no group differences.
requirements: The rating patient must be trained on how to use the CARE scale; in this study all patients were recruited from a trained SP-pool
constraints: The question design yields a low score when experienced empathy is subjectively high, which must be interpreted inversely
target_learning_goals: assessment of empathetic behaviour in medical consultations
examples: All patients (SPs, IPs, RPs) were recruited from the trained SP-pool and trained on the CARE scale before rating students

article_title: [Repetitio est mater studiorum-implementation of ENT cases in case-based e-learning].
citation: Engert J, Backhaus J, Henig L, Spahn B, Voelker J, Ickrath P, Scherzad A, Rak K, Hagen R, König S, Hackenberg S, Kaulitz S. (2024). Repetitio est mater studiorum—implementation of ENT cases in case-based e-learning. HNO. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00106-023-01409-4
title: CaseTrain web-based case player for case-based e-learning in WueCampus
description: CaseTrain is a web-based case player developed at the University of Würzburg to enable case-based learning within blended-learning concepts; the article describes it as "einen webbasierten Fallplayer, der in die Lehrangebote der Plattform WueCampus" integrated. Each case opens with a clinical case introduction, followed by 6–12 self-test questions including image and video material, with feedback explaining correct and incorrect options after each answer. Cases could be restarted at will and counted as successfully completed from 60% correct answers. Fifteen ENT patient cases aligned with exam-relevant lecture topics were implemented.
requirements: Integration into the WueCampus learning platform and playback via the Adobe Flash Player plugin, as the article describes the technical setup
constraints: Cases were designed to cover only exam-relevant (klausurrelevant) lecture topics, per the article's stated design rule
target_learning_goals: Clinical case-based knowledge and self-assessment in ENT lecture content
examples: 15 HNO patient cases based on winter 2022/2023 lecture topics were implemented and offered voluntarily to 157 students
key_sources: Engert J, Backhaus J, Henig L, Spahn B, Voelker J, Ickrath P, Scherzad A, Rak K, Hagen R, König S, Hackenberg S, Kaulitz S. (2024). Repetitio est mater studiorum—implementation of ENT cases in case-based e-learning. HNO. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00106-023-01409-4

citation: Engert J, Backhaus J, Henig L, Spahn B, Voelker J, Ickrath P, Scherzad A, Rak K, Hagen R, König S, Hackenberg S, Kaulitz S. (2024). Repetitio est mater studiorum—implementation of ENT cases in case-based e-learning. HNO. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00106-023-01409-4
title: Case-based e-learning case structure: introduction, self-test questions with media, explanatory feedback, and a 60% completion threshold
description: The article's cases follow a uniform design scheme: an introduction leads into the clinical case, then "zur Selbsttestung Fragen (6–12) mit Einbezug von Bild- und Videomaterial" follow, and after each answer learners receive feedback with explanations of correct and incorrect options. Single-, multiple-choice and text question formats are used, cases can be repeated and restarted any number of times, and a case counts as successfully completed from 60% correct answers. This structure lets students check their progress at any time and access structured feedback, which the authors say reduces the complexity of learning.
requirements: Questions and explanations perceived as structured and comprehensible, which the evaluation rated highly (M 4.49 and 4.50 on a 5-point scale)
constraints: Completion threshold set at 60% correct answers, as defined in the article
target_learning_goals: self-testing, exam preparation, and recapitulation of lecture content
examples: The 15 CaseTrains each contained 6–12 questions with image and video material and per-answer feedback

article_title: The application of human reliability analysis to carpal tunnel decompression.
citation: Lucey Á, Kennedy S, Hussey A, McInerney N, Kelly JL, Joyce KM. (2024). The application of human reliability analysis to carpal tunnel decompression. Ann R Coll Surg Engl. https://doi.org/10.1308/rcsann.2023.0038
title: HTA and SHERPA analysis artifact for open carpal tunnel decompression with remedial strategies
description: The article produced a hierarchical task analysis of carpal tunnel decompression comprising 13 principal tasks (from WHO sign-in through WHO sign-out) and 46 subtasks, published as tables with a complete version in supplemental material. For every subtask the SHERPA analysis records the credible error, its probability and criticality ratings, the computed risk score, and a remediation, such as 'Have checklist readily available in theatre' for uncompleted WHO checklists. The artifact is offered as a tool for surgical trainers and trainees.
requirements: Remedial strategies are devised for each potential error, spanning individual, equipment, environmental and organisational levels
constraints: The article notes there will inevitably be some variation in clinical practice across surgical specialities and across different surgical units, and recommends each unit refine the HTA while reaching internal agreement
target_learning_goals: learning the standardised sequence of carpal tunnel decompression steps and the error-prone, high-criticality steps within it
examples: Table 2 presents the simplified HTA, including subtasks such as identifying Kaplans cardinal line, aspirating the syringe before infiltrating tissue, and cutting through TCL centrally to identify the underlying median nerve.
key_sources: Lucey Á, Kennedy S, Hussey A, McInerney N, Kelly JL, Joyce KM. (2024). The application of human reliability analysis to carpal tunnel decompression. Ann R Coll Surg Engl. https://doi.org/10.1308/rcsann.2023.0038

article_title: From summative MAAS Global to formative MAAS 2.0 - a workshop report.
citation: Stamer Tjorven, Essers Geurt, Steinhäuser Jost, Flägel Kristina. (2023). From summative MAAS Global to formative MAAS 2.0 – a workshop report. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2023-40/zma001591.shtml
title: Calgary-Cambridge model as the underlying framework for structuring communication assessment
description: The Calgary-Cambridge approach is an internationally established method for teaching and training clinical communication skills, created by Kurtz and Silverman in 1996. The article describes it as "a five-step guide which, if followed, should facilitate successful doctor-patient communication", focusing on constructive structuring of consultations and building relationships. MAAS 2.0 explicitly emphasizes this scheme as its underlying model, e.g. by moving the empathy item between emotions and imparting information.
requirements: Assessment items must be ordered and worded so as to reflect the model's consultation phases and relationship-building focus
target_learning_goals: structured doctor-patient consultations
relationship building during consultations
examples: In MAAS 2.0 the item "empathy" is now placed between "emotions" and "imparting information", making the instrument "more adapted to the Calgary-Cambridge-Modell".

article_title: Measuring attitudes towards biology major and non-major: Effect of students' gender, group composition, and learning environment.
citation: Almasri Firas, Hewapathirana Gertrude I., Ghaddar Fatme, Lee Nick, Ibrahim Bashar. (2021). Measuring attitudes towards biology major and non-major: Effect of students’ gender, group composition, and learning environment. PLoS ONE 16(5): e0251453. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0251453
title: Instructors should carefully select gender grouping and develop gender-specific, context-specific pedagogies in undergraduate science
description: Because the effect of collaborative versus traditional learning on biology attitudes reversed direction by gender and group composition, the article recommends that instructors deliberately choose gender grouping when teaching undergraduate science. The article concludes "there is a need for developing gender-specific and context-specific learning pedagogies, and instructors carefully select gender grouping in teaching undergraduate science subjects". This follows from the three-way interaction among gender, teaching method, and gender composition reported in the study.
requirements: Knowledge of students’ gender and the gender composition of classes and groups
Willingness to adapt pedagogy (CL vs TL) to the composition context
constraints: Evidence base is one randomized study in a Kuwaiti university where single-gender classes are the norm; the interaction was reported for nonmajor students
target_learners: Undergraduate science students, particularly biology majors and nonmajors
target_learning_goals: Cultivating positive attitudes toward learning biology and science careers
examples: The study randomly assigned men and women into single-gender classes, mixed-gender classes, single-gender groups (4M or 4W), and mixed-gender groups (2M+2W) under CL or TL

article_title: Learning to diagnose accurately through virtual patients: do reflection phases have an added benefit?
citation: Fink Maximilian C., Heitzmann Nicole, Siebeck Matthias, Fischer Frank, Fischer Martin R. (2021). Learning to diagnose accurately through virtual patients: do reflection phases have an added benefit? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02937-9
title: CASUS-based virtual patients on dyspnea causes for learning history-taking and diagnosis
description: Nine validated virtual patients "suffering from different causes of dyspnea" were embedded in the digital learning environment CASUS. Each encounter starts with an introductory video presenting prior diagnostic information and the chief complaint; participants take the history "by selecting from a menu of 69 questions", with answers streamed as short videos. Diagnostic accuracy is scored on a long menu of 180 possible dyspnea-related diagnoses (1 point correct, 0.50 partially correct), compared to an expert sample solution.
requirements: Requires validated cases, (semi)-professional actors trained for their roles, and the CASUS environment
constraints: Cases limited to dyspnea-related diagnoses; a limited number of cases may allow case specificity
target_learners: third to fifth year medical students
target_learning_goals: history-taking
accurate diagnosis of dyspnea causes
examples: Participants diagnosed three virtual patients each at pretest, learning phase, and posttest, with a 10-minute time limit per simulation

article_title: Learning to diagnose collaboratively: validating a simulation for medical students.
citation: Radkowitsch A, Fischer MR, Schmidmaier R, Fischer F. (2020). Learning to diagnose collaboratively: validating a simulation for medical students. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001344.shtml
title: CASUS-based simulation of internist-radiologist collaboration for assessing information sharing
description: A computer-based simulation on the case-based learning platform CASUS in which learners, in the role of an internist, scan a patient file, request a radiologic test by filling in a request form choosing among 42 different combinations of methods and body parts, and share patient information or differential diagnoses. Only learners who appropriately justify their request receive the radiologic findings. It separately assesses information sharing (collaborative) and final diagnosis (individual).
requirements: A fiction contract and technical familiarization were added to increase perceived control after pilot testing showed low dependability ratings
constraints: Developed for the specific context of radiologic test requests identified as problematic in interviews with seven practitioners
target_learning_goals: information sharing skills
diagnostic accuracy
diagnostic efficiency
examples: Paper prototypes were evaluated by an expert committee; case material for ten patient cases was revised in a one-day expert workshop

article_title: Simulation training for emergency skills: effects on ICU fellows' performance and supervision levels.
citation: Zante Bjoern, Schefold Joerg C. (2020). Simulation training for emergency skills: effects on ICU fellows’ performance and supervision levels. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02419-4
title: Two-phase, five-step emergency skill training combining flipped pre-training preparation, cadaver-lab practice with formative assessment, and summative supervision-level assessment
description: The program follows a two-phase, five-step structure for procedural skill training: a cognitive phase of reading/visualization and viewing demonstrations, then a psychomotor phase of formative simulator assessment, summative assessment, and performance on patients. Fellows received "literature and video documents along with the departmental standard operating procedures (SOP)" individually before training, then practiced on human cadavers in groups of "a maximum of six fellows with two experienced attending consultants", with formative assessment during training and a summative post-training supervision-level assessment.
requirements: Pre-training individual preparation with literature, videos, and departmental SOPs
Small learner-to-teacher ratio (maximum six fellows with two attending consultants)
Cadaver laboratory setting for safe repetition of emergency skills
constraints: The article notes "try and error" for emergency skills should be avoided in direct patient care and performed in simulated training instead
Retention of emergency skills is time-dependent, with repetition (e.g. every 6 months) likely required to sustain performance
target_learners: ICU fellows in a tertiary care academic hospital
target_learning_goals: Emergency procedural skills: chest tube insertion, pericardiocentesis, cricothyroidotomy
examples: Full-day skill training performed twice per year since 2017 at the Inselspital, University of Bern, with 31 ICU fellows participating over the period
key_sources: Zante Bjoern, Schefold Joerg C. (2020). Simulation training for emergency skills: effects on ICU fellows’ performance and supervision levels. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02419-4

citation: AlKhaibary AA, Ramadan FZ, Aboshaiqah AE, Baker OG, AlZaatari SZ, AlZaatari SZ. (2021). Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.633
title: Clinical Assessment Tool for Nursing Education (CAT-NE) with 13 rubric items
description: The CAT-NE, proposed by Skúladottir and Svavarsdottir (2016), is the study instrument: an assessment tool "comprises of rubrics that list the criteria for the expected performance of students". It contains 13 items categorized as personal factors (6 items: enthusiasm, initiative, realistic confidence, competence with staff, competence with clients, caring) and professional factors (7 items including documentation, clinical competence, critical thinking, self-control). It was used to compare the two learning-approach groups.
requirements: Rubric criteria are clarified with students to make evaluation objective-oriented
constraints: Its validation cannot predict the limited number of students who failed clinical study, per the article's stated limitation
target_learners: Nursing students and intern nurses in clinical courses
target_learning_goals: Clinical performance evaluation across personal and professional development factors
examples: Scores on the tool's 13 items were compared between the interactive and traditional learning groups using independent sample t tests.

article_title: Satisfaction, Enjoyment and Boredom with Physical Education as Mediator between Autonomy Support and Academic Performance in Physical Education.
citation: Baños Raúl, Fuentesal Julio, Conte Luis, Ortiz-Camacho María del Mar, Zamarripa Jorge. (2020). International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17238898
title: CAA-EF and SSI-EF questionnaires measuring autonomy support and satisfaction/enjoyment–boredom in PE
description: Two validated Spanish-language instruments for Mexican PE contexts were used. The CAA-EF, adapted from the Learning Climate Questionnaire, "contains 15 items to measure the professor’s support for autonomy through one dimension: autonomy support" on a seven-point scale. The SSI-EF is composed of eight items, five measuring satisfaction/enjoyment and three measuring boredom, on a five-point Likert scale. Confirmatory factor analysis supported acceptable fit for both instruments in this sample (e.g., CAA-EF CFI = 0.98, RMSEA = 0.056).
requirements: Administered to students in classroom sessions of 15–20 minutes in the presence of the lead researcher
constraints: The boredom subscale has only three items, and its α was 0.68 in this sample, which the authors deem acceptable only because of the limited number of items per factor
target_learners: Third-grade secondary school students in Mexico
target_learning_goals: Measuring perceived teacher autonomy support and intrinsic satisfaction (enjoyment and boredom) in physical education
examples: PE grades were taken from teachers' latest test score records on a 1–10 scale rather than from students themselves

article_title: Assessing the instructional quality of private tutoring and its effects on student outcomes: Analyses from the German National Educational Panel Study.
citation: Guill Karin, Lüdtke Oliver, Köller Olaf. (2019). Assessing the instructional quality of private tutoring and its effects on student outcomes: Analyses from the German National Educational Panel Study. The British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12281
title: Do not recommend private tutoring as a generally effective strategy for improving academic achievement; monitor whether grades actually improve
description: Based on their null global effects and null quality effects on grades, the authors conclude that "neither the current state of research (Park et al., 2016) nor our own analyses provide convincing support for recommending private tutoring as a generally effective strategy to improve academic achievement". They advise that parents and students who opt for tutoring should regularly evaluate whether grades really improve, and that public subsidies should be monitored closely. Tutoring may still relieve stress from insufficient achievement and stabilize well-being.
requirements: Longitudinal data controlling for prior achievement and motivation when evaluating tutoring effectiveness
constraints: Findings may not transfer to countries with very different tutoring attendance patterns, such as South-East Asian countries where high-performing students also attend tutoring
target_learners: secondary school students and their families considering private tutoring
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in school subjects
student well-being
examples: The NEPS regression and structural equation models found no positive grade effects, supporting the caution against recommending tutoring for achievement gains

article_title: Improving Cardiovascular Workforce Competencies in Cardio-Obstetrics: Current Challenges and Future Directions.
citation: Sharma G, Zakaria S, Michos ED, Bhatt AB, Lundberg GP, Florio KL, Vaught AJ, Ouyang P, Mehta L. (2020). Improving Cardiovascular Workforce Competencies in Cardio‐Obstetrics: Current Challenges and Future Directions. J Am Heart Assoc. https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.119.015569
title: Cardio-obstetrics curriculum design pattern: five content areas for fellowship-level training
description: The article enumerates five content areas that cardio-obstetrics curricula should cover: "cardiovascular pharmacotherapies in pregnancy", physiologic and pathological cardiovascular changes of pregnancy, basic obstetrical modes of delivery, echocardiographic changes and pregnancy-specific normal values, and case-based reviews of pregnant and postpartum patients with simple or complex CVD. It functions as a lesson/unit-level curriculum blueprint for cardiology fellowship education, to be incentivized through ACGME standards, ABIM blueprints, and Core Cardiology Training Statement requirements.
requirements: Joint multisocietal guidelines and incorporation into ACGME standards, ABIM blueprints, and COCATS requirements to incentivize training programs
constraints: Limited time in training to gain competencies; no formalized training requirements currently exist in COCATS, ACGME, ACC, or AHA educational statements
target_learning_goals: Preconception risk stratification and counseling
Cardiovascular pharmacotherapy in pregnancy
Management of pregnancy complications with CVD
examples: The article's Table 1 proposes developing cardio-obstetrics multidisciplinary grand rounds and didactics in general cardiology fellowship training and intensive sessions at national meetings

article_title: Teaching Endotracheal Intubation Using a Cadaver Versus a Manikin-based Model: a Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Pedigo Ryan MD, Tolles Juliana MD, MHS, Watcha Daena MD, MS, Kaji Amy H. MD, PhD, MPH, Lewis Roger J. MD, PhD, Stark Elena MD, PhD, Jordan Jaime MD. (2020). Teaching Endotracheal Intubation Using a Cadaver Versus a Manikin-based Model: a Randomized Controlled Trial. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2019.10.44522
title: Cadaver-based ETI testing and training protocol with blinded video review
description: This element is the study's training-and-assessment protocol: fourth-year medical students were stratified by prior ETI experience (<10, 10–24, 25+ attempts), randomized 1:1 to a 30-minute instructor-led session on an unembalmed cadaver or a Laerdal airway management trainer, then tested on a separate unembalmed cadaver using direct laryngoscopy. Two intervention-blinded reviewers assessed video recordings of time to successful ETI and POGO, with reviewer correlation coefficients of 0.99 and 0.98 and no systematic bias on a Bland-Altman plot.
requirements: An unembalmed cadaver used as the testing medium for all learners to eliminate between-group differences in airway difficulty
Blinded video review with student identifying information blurred
constraints: POGO could not be judged in cases where the camera became obscured; one session's data was lost to camera malfunction
target_learners: fourth-year medical students on EM sub-internship or procedures electives
target_learning_goals: endotracheal intubation procedural competency
examples: Students did not have access to the video monitor during the ETI attempt; the screen was turned away but recorded for data collection

citation: Dubosh NM, Hall MM, Novack V, Shafat T, Shapiro NI, Ullman EA. (2020). A Multimodal Curriculum With Patient Feedback to Improve Medical Student Communication: Pilot Study. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2018.11.44318
title: Communication Assessment Tool (CAT) used as a patient-rated measure of medical student communication
description: The CAT is "a 15-item questionnaire that assesses communication skills from the patient perspective and has validity evidence to support its use," using a 1–5 rating scale across communication and interpersonal domains. The study omitted the final team-level item and scored students out of 70 points, dichotomizing into maximal (70) vs sub-maximal scores because of a ceiling effect. Its utility in medical students had not previously been studied.
requirements: Patients must be able to identify the student by photo, not require interpreter services, and be alert and oriented; administration takes about five minutes
constraints: The article notes an inherent ceiling effect, with mean scores skewed toward the upper end of the 5-point scale, which may minimize group differences
target_learners: fourth-year medical students assessed by their ED patients
target_learning_goals: communication and interpersonal skills from the patient perspective
examples: Trained research assistants administered 321 CAT questionnaires; the median number per student was five

article_title: Codebook for rating clinical communication skills based on the Calgary-Cambridge Guide.
citation: Iversen Else Dalsgaard, Wolderslund Maiken Overbeck, Kofoed Poul-Erik, Gulbrandsen Pål, Poulsen Helle, Cold Søren, Ammentorp Jette. (2020). Codebook for rating clinical communication skills based on the Calgary-Cambridge Guide. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02050-3
title: The Calgary-Cambridge Guide as a six-domain framework structuring the clinical communication consultation
description: The Calgary-Cambridge Guide (C-CG), introduced by Kurtz and Silverman in 1996 and updated to a third edition in 2013, is a well-known framework for teaching and training clinical communication skills. The article organizes communication assessment around its structure, with the OS-12's "12 items covering the following six domains: initiating the session, gathering information, building the relationship, explanation and planning, providing structure, and closing the session." Although not intended as an assessment tool, it is used to guide structured feedback and rating, and it contains 73 micro-skills from which the OS-12 selected a priority subset.
requirements: Effective use for assessment assumes raters understand the micro-skills as described in the C-CG.
constraints: The C-CG was not originally intended to be an assessment tool; C-CG-based tools differ in number of items, response scales, settings and aims.
target_learners: Health care providers and medical students in communication skills training
target_learning_goals: Clinical communication competence across the consultation
examples: The 'Clear Cut Communication with Patient' training programme at a large regional hospital in Denmark was based on the C-CG, and OS-12 items were content-validated against that programme.

Codebook for rating clinical communication skills based on the Calgary-Cambridge Guide. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02050-3

article_title: Peer assessment to improve medical student's contributions to team-based projects: randomised controlled trial and qualitative follow-up.
citation: Biesma Regien, Kennedy Mary-Claire, Pawlikowska Teresa, Brugha Ruairi, Conroy Ronan, Doyle Frank. (2019). title: CATME Likert Short Version tool for team-member effectiveness
description: The validated Comprehensive Assessment Team Member Effectiveness (CATME) Likert Short Version tool served as the trial's outcome measure. It is a "behaviorally anchored rating scale" describing behaviors typical of performance levels in five categories: contributing to the team's work, interacting with teammates, keeping the team on track, expecting quality, and having relevant knowledge, skills, and abilities. Students rated each teammate on Likert scales at baseline (week 2) and follow-up (week 10).
requirements: Completion by all participating students at baseline and end of project
constraints: Rated on Likert scales from strongly disagree to strongly agree; used here as self- and peer-rated perception rather than observed behaviour
target_learning_goals: teamwork effectiveness
team contribution
examples: Both arms scored teamwork quality highest and having relevant KSAs lowest at baseline and follow-up
