article_title: Promoting medical competencies through a didactic tutor qualification programme - a qualitative study based on the CanMEDS Physician Competency Framework.
citation: Homberg Angelika, Hundertmark Jan, Krause Jürgen, Brunnée Merle, Neumann Boris, Loukanova Svetla. (2019). Promoting medical competencies through a didactic tutor qualification programme – a qualitative study based on the CanMEDS Physician Competency Framework. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1636-5
title: CanMEDS Physician Competency Framework as an analytical tool for curricular mapping
description: The CanMEDS framework, developed by the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada, "describes key competencies, grouped thematically under seven professional roles" of the physician, each role represented by two to five key competencies. The study uses it as an analytical tool: module components are mapped to key competencies and results reported at the role level to increase reliability. The authors conclude it "is proved to be an appropriate analytical tool for presenting the acquisition of competencies" in the qualification programme, while noting its suitability for structuring teaching units is critically discussed.
requirements: Raters study the detailed CanMEDS role competency framework before allocating module components to key competencies
Consensus must be reached within but not between rater groups
constraints: Its suitability for structuring teaching units is critically discussed in the literature, as the article notes
target_learners: Medical students and medical educators using competency-based curricula
target_learning_goals: Mapping and making visible physician role competency acquisition across curriculum components
examples: Two tutors and three training coordinators independently assigned the four modules' components to CanMEDS key competencies in a table with one column per component and one row per key competency
key_sources: Homberg Angelika, Hundertmark Jan, Krause Jürgen, Brunnée Merle, Neumann Boris, Loukanova Svetla. (2019). Promoting medical competencies through a didactic tutor qualification programme – a qualitative study based on the CanMEDS Physician Competency Framework. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1636-5

article_title: Critical Appraisal Worksheets for Integration Into an Existing Small-Group Problem-Based Learning Curriculum.
citation: O'Neil Jessica, Croniger Colleen. (2018). Critical Appraisal Worksheets for Integration Into an Existing Small-Group Problem-Based Learning Curriculum. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10682
title: Eight critical appraisal worksheets tailored to specific study types, with faculty answer keys
description: The article describes "These eight worksheets" adapted from Center for Evidence-Based Medicine templates, tailored to specific preselected studies and to study types CEBM does not cover, such as case reports. Each worksheet contains six to eight questions assessing purpose, validity, importance, and applicability, with guidance passages under each question. Faculty facilitators receive answer keys (Appendices I-P) so they can support group discussion, and students gain access to the keys after the session.
requirements: Worksheets are paired with a preselected health science research article relating to the weekly PBL learning objectives, and faculty facilitators are assigned to read the study and the answer key.
constraints: An effort was made to select studies with manuscripts under five pages in length because of constraints on the students' existing workload.
target_learning_goals: critical appraisal of health science literature
evidence-based medicine skills
examples: Week 1 used a systematic review on insulin and glucagon physiology; week 7 used a randomized controlled trial on oncogenes (Table 1).
key_sources: O'Neil Jessica, Croniger Colleen. (2018). Critical Appraisal Worksheets for Integration Into an Existing Small-Group Problem-Based Learning Curriculum. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10682

article_title: Fighting adult illiteracy with the help of the environmental print material.
citation: Iqbal Tassawar, Iqbal Saqib, Hussain Syed Sajid, Khan Iftikhar Ahmed, Khan Hikmat Ullah, Rehman Attiqa. (2018). Fighting adult illiteracy with the help of the environmental print material. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0201902
title: Computer Assisted Learning application presenting EPM-based alphabet content
description: Two CAL applications were developed for the experiment: one supporting alphabet-letter learning using EPM-based content (logos, brand names, and everyday objects such as Pepsi, Geo, Bread, Refrigerator), and one using traditional content borrowed from mainstream education. The applications were "designed to minimize the role of instructors and to reduce the cognitive load in addition to giving immediate feedback". A separate computer-assisted assessment application presented a picture and required learners to select the correct alphabet letter by clicking.
requirements: A 30-minute demo on the application interface was given before learning sessions
constraints: The EPM content was presented in context; the article notes non-literates are not good at reading EPM out of context
target_learners: adult non-literate participants in Pakistan aged over 15
target_learning_goals: recognition, pronunciation, and recall of Urdu alphabet letters
examples: Learning sessions ran one hour a day on weekdays for four weeks, with all alphabet letters covered on a given day
key_sources: Iqbal Tassawar, Iqbal Saqib, Hussain Syed Sajid, Khan Iftikhar Ahmed, Khan Hikmat Ullah, Rehman Attiqa. (2018). Fighting adult illiteracy with the help of the environmental print material. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0201902

article_title: Does the Podcast Video Playback Speed Affect Comprehension for Novel Curriculum Delivery? A Randomized Trial.
citation: Song K, Chakraborty A, Dawson M, Dugan A, Adkins B, Doty C. (2018). Does the Podcast Video Playback Speed Affect Comprehension for Novel Curriculum Delivery? A Randomized Trial. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2017.10.36027
title: Do not assume faster podcast playback speeds save learners time when novel material must be retained
description: The article challenges the assumption that sped-up video lectures are a free time saving: time is only saved "if the retention of the material is comparable." Since objective quiz performance was worse or no better at 1.5× speed for novel material, designers of self-paced video curricula should not default to faster playback without checking retention. The trial was a small pilot, so the recommendation is provisional.
requirements: Retention of material must be assessed objectively when recommending faster playback speeds, since survey-reported subjective benefits may not reflect actual retention.
constraints: Evidence comes from a single-center pilot randomized trial with 54 students testing only immediate recall of two novel ultrasound lectures at one accelerated speed (1.5×).
target_learning_goals: immediate retention of factual lecture content
examples: In the trial, students watching the artifacts video at 1.5× speed averaged 61.4% correct versus 72.7% at 1.0× speed, a significant decrement.
key_sources: Song K, Chakraborty A, Dawson M, Dugan A, Adkins B, Doty C. (2018). Does the Podcast Video Playback Speed Affect Comprehension for Novel Curriculum Delivery? A Randomized Trial. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2017.10.36027

article_title: Viewpoint matters: objective performance metrics for surgeon endoscope control during robot-assisted surgery.
citation: Jarc Anthony M., Curet Myriam J. (2017). Viewpoint matters: objective performance metrics for surgeon endoscope control during robot-assisted surgery. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-016-5090-8
title: Three camera metrics for endoscope control during RAMIS simulation (CFrq, CDur, CInt)
description: The article defines three novel performance metrics, called camera metrics, computed from endoscope movement data recorded on the da Vinci Skills Simulator. Camera movement frequency (CFrq) is "the average number of endoscope movements made by a surgeon per second over the entire exercise"; camera movement duration (CDur) is the average time in seconds of all endoscope movements; and camera movement interval (CInt) is the average time in seconds between endoscope movements over an entire exercise. They are computed alongside conventional metrics (overall score, completion time, economy of motion, master workspace range) for all 25 exercises.
requirements: Requires kinematic and event data recording of endoscope movements from the surgical system and virtual environment for the full duration of each exercise
constraints: The viewpoint measures used were simply the gross positions of the endoscope, not field of view, point of view, or focal point
target_learners: RAMIS surgeon trainees (new, intermediate, and experienced surgeons)
target_learning_goals: Proficient endoscope control and effective visualization of the operative field during robot-assisted surgery
examples: Computed for 39 surgeons across 25 dVSS exercises including Camera Targeting, Match Board, Ring Walk, Suture Sponge, and Tubes
key_sources: Jarc Anthony M., Curet Myriam J. (2017). Viewpoint matters: objective performance metrics for surgeon endoscope control during robot-assisted surgery. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-016-5090-8

article_title: Using social media to support small group learning.
citation: Duncan C, Rengasamy ER, Batchelor S, Pope C, Riley S, Cunningham AM. (2017). Using social media to support small group learning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1060-7
title: Campus Pack wiki within the VLE for group collaboration on case-based learning records
description: The Campus Pack wiki is a VLE add-on described as "Good for group collaboration tasks on same document" with auditable edits showing who contributed, easy addition of pages, and document upload. A wiki was set up for each CBL group within Blackboard, accessible only by group members and the facilitator, and used by some groups to record agreed learning outcomes, share flipchart photos, and build comprehensive revision notes.
requirements: Students need to be familiar with the document structure to navigate effectively
constraints: Accessing can be difficult with multiple steps; sharing of documents does not occur outside of the wiki group; no alert system for updates
target_learners: year 1 undergraduate medical students in case-based learning groups
target_learning_goals: creating a record of group learning
collaborative note-taking and revision resource building
examples: Some groups used the wiki to record agreed learning outcomes and share photos of flipcharts from face-to-face sessions, and individuals used it for revision in a directory-like format
key_sources: Duncan C, Rengasamy ER, Batchelor S, Pope C, Riley S, Cunningham AM. (2017). Using social media to support small group learning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1060-7
